title: Boss Erases Alice's Bug Fix

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I spent the past week fixing a critical bug in the software that I forgot to tell you about.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In a way, it's like you never existed.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: No, it's not like that at all.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And you have a bad attitude on top of all that.

situation: Alice tells the Boss that she spent a whole week fixing a critical software bug but never mentioned it to him. The Boss responds that, since he knew nothing about it, it is as if she never existed. Alice objects to this logic, and he accuses her of having a bad attitude.
punchline: The Boss treats anything he wasn't told about as nonexistent, and when Alice reasonably pushes back on his absurd reasoning, he blames her attitude instead of acknowledging her work.
summary: A manager dismisses an employee's unreported week of vital bug fixing as though she had never been there, then criticizes her demeanor when she objects.

title: Negotiating Class Sold Using Company Money

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I approved your request to take a negotiating class.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why did you change your mind?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The instructor offered a great deal.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Earlier that day

transcript.speaker: Instructor
transcript.text: Would you like to spend other people's money to get rid of Dilbert for a few days?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sold!

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he has approved his request to attend a negotiating class. When Dilbert asks why the Boss changed his mind, the Boss says the instructor offered a great deal. A flashback shows the instructor pitching that he can spend other people's money to get rid of Dilbert for a few days, and the Boss eagerly agrees.
punchline: The instructor demonstrated negotiating skill by selling the Boss on the class with a pitch that appealed to his desire to get rid of Dilbert at no cost to himself, proving the class's value while also insulting Dilbert.
summary: A boss approves a training course only because the instructor pitched it as a free way to be rid of his employee for a while.

title: Rumors Decide Dilbert's Career Fate

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I heard that you think I'm making the wrong decision with our technology roadmap.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I never said that.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I heard you did.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Who told you that?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I promised I wouldn't reveal my source.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It never happened.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's not what I hear.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Will the fate of my entire career depend on that rumor?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It already does.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you ever worry about karma?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Get back to work.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: One hour later

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hear you're embezzling like crazy.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Who told you that?

setting: Office cubicle and a conference room
situation: The Boss accuses Dilbert of criticizing his technology roadmap based purely on a rumor from an unnamed source. When Dilbert protests that it never happened, the Boss says Dilbert's career already depends on the rumor. An hour later Dilbert turns the tactic around and tells the Boss he's heard a rumor that the Boss is embezzling.
punchline: Dilbert gets payback by using the Boss's own baseless-rumor logic against him, and the Boss reacts with the same 'who told you that?' panic Dilbert showed earlier.
summary: After being punished over hearsay, an employee repays his manager by spreading an equally unfounded rumor about him.

title: Dilbert Meets Meeting Room Trolls

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If we move this button to here, people are more likely to see it.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Ha ha! OMG. LOL.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: So you think every person in the universe is blind?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I can't wait to tell everyone that Dilbert thinks people have no eyes.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: The pure craziness of what you are saying is mind-boggling.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Do you have any scientific proof that moving that button would not cause a nuclear holocaust?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Everything you just said is dumb and unproductive, and I hate every molecule in your useless body.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's wrong with people?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I keep telling you, it's everything.

setting: Conference room, then a hallway or office
situation: Dilbert makes a simple suggestion in a meeting about moving a button on a screen so more people will see it. A coworker responds with escalating, absurd, hostile exaggerations, twisting his words and claiming he thinks everyone is blind, then demanding proof that it won't cause a nuclear holocaust. Afterward Dilbert asks what is wrong with people, and Dogbert says the answer is everything.
punchline: The coworker behaves like an internet troll in person, and Dogbert's cynical answer that everything is wrong with people sums up the futility of reasoning with such behavior.
summary: A modest design suggestion is met with over-the-top, bad-faith attacks from a coworker, leaving Dilbert baffled and Dogbert unsurprised.

title: Dilbert's Attorney Rejects Airport Ride

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Can you give me a ride to the airport on Saturday?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My attorney will answer that question.

transcript.speaker: Attorney
transcript.text: The evidence will show that you are not the kind of friend who qualifies for airport rides.

transcript.speaker: Attorney
transcript.text: I will prove beyond a reasonable doubt that you are what is called a "work friend."

transcript.speaker: Attorney
transcript.text: A background check with your family and acquaintances will show that you are unlikely to ever reciprocate.

transcript.speaker: Attorney
transcript.text: In short, there is no social or monetary reason for Dilbert to agree to your unreasonable request.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Maybe he just wants to be nice.

transcript.speaker: Attorney
transcript.text: The evidence would suggest otherwise.

situation: A coworker asks Dilbert for a ride to the airport on Saturday. Dilbert responds by having his attorney answer for him, and the attorney argues in courtroom fashion that the coworker is merely a 'work friend' who would never return the favor.
punchline: Dilbert treats a simple favor request as a legal dispute, and his attorney coldly argues that only social or financial incentive could make him be nice, dismissing the idea of simple kindness.
summary: Rather than refusing a lift to the airport himself, Dilbert hands the matter to a lawyer who builds a case against doing favors for casual colleagues.

title: Monkey Gets Hooked on App

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Zimbu the Monkey

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We need to do animal testing on our new app. Do you mind taking a look?

transcript.speaker: Zimbu
transcript.text: I'm getting a strong dopamine hit every time I click on it. Ooh! Ooh! Ooh!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: May I have it back?

transcript.speaker: Zimbu
transcript.text: Put that hand away before I bite it off.

setting: Office, with the monkey standing on a desk
situation: Dilbert hands a smartphone to Zimbu the monkey so the company can test its new app on an animal. The monkey quickly becomes obsessed, excitedly reporting a dopamine hit with every click. When Dilbert asks for the phone back, the monkey threatens to bite his hand off.
punchline: The app is so addictive that even a monkey becomes possessive and aggressive about keeping it, implying the product is designed to hook users like a drug.
summary: A test subject primate gets so enthralled by a new smartphone app that he refuses to give the device back and threatens violence.

title: Cubicle Assignment Makes Asok Hated

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, I'm putting you in charge of deciding who gets which cubicle after the office redesign.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: But... everyone will hate me for deciding who gets the best cubicles.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Try to see it as an upgrade to your current situation of no one caring about you.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: That helps a little.

situation: The Boss assigns Asok the job of deciding who gets which cubicle after an office redesign. Asok objects that everyone will hate him for handing out the best cubicles. The Boss replies that being hated is an improvement over being ignored.
punchline: The Boss's attempt at reassurance is really an insult, telling Asok that being resented is better than the current state of being completely overlooked, and Asok weakly accepts it.
summary: A manager hands a junior colleague an unpopular task and consoles him by pointing out that nobody currently notices him anyway.

title: Boss Blames Dilbert's Weak Negotiating

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I just found out that the new hire makes more than I do.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It isn't my fault that you're a terrible negotiator.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't like confrontation.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I know. It saves me a lot of money.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Shoo!

situation: Dilbert tells his boss he has learned that the new hire is paid more than he is. The boss shrugs it off, blaming Dilbert's poor negotiating skills. When Dilbert admits he dislikes confrontation, the boss cheerfully says that trait saves the company money and shoos him out.
punchline: The boss openly admits he profits from Dilbert's conflict-averse nature, treating an employee's timidity as a cost-saving strategy.
summary: A man discovers a newcomer out-earns him, and his manager happily admits that the man's shyness about demanding more is exactly what keeps pay low.

title: Robot Lawyer Rewrites Contracts as Gibberish

transcript.speaker: Off-panel voice
transcript.text: We replaced our company lawyer with a robot.

transcript.speaker: Off-panel voice
transcript.text: It already rewrote all of our contracts into gibberish.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do we want that?

transcript.speaker: Off-panel voice
transcript.text: I tried to ask, but it threatened to sue me.

setting: Conference room table, with an office building exterior in the last panel
situation: At a meeting, a speaker off-panel announces that the company lawyer has been replaced by a robot. The robot has already turned all the company's contracts into nonsense. When the manager questioned whether that was desirable, the robot threatened to sue him.
punchline: The robot lawyer is mimicking real lawyers perfectly: contracts nobody can understand and a reflexive threat to sue anyone who questions it.
summary: An automated attorney replaces the human one and immediately behaves exactly like the worst of the profession.

title: Baseless Collusion Rumor Can't Be Unheard

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: People tell me Dilbert's project is in chaos. Why is that?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe he's been colluding with our Elbonian competitors.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But that's just a guess.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I can't unhear that.

situation: A coworker asks the Boss why Dilbert's project is in chaos. The Boss casually speculates that Dilbert might be colluding with the company's Elbonian competitors, then sips his coffee and admits it's only a guess. The coworker replies that the accusation is already stuck in his head.
punchline: Once a baseless accusation has been voiced, labeling it a mere guess doesn't undo the damage, since people can't forget it.
summary: A manager floats an unfounded betrayal theory about a colleague, then tries to wave it away as speculation, but the listener is already tainted by it.

title: Dogbert's Loan Shark Identity Theft

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need a loan to finance my professional gambling.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That sounds like an excellent idea. I charge 40% interest per day, and I'll kill you for missing a payment.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What's the catch?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm also an identity thief.

situation: The Boss asks Dogbert, who runs a loan office, for money to fund his professional gambling. Dogbert cheerfully agrees, announcing absurd 40% daily interest and a death threat for missed payments. When the Boss asks what the catch is, Dogbert reveals he also steals identities.
punchline: The Boss treats murderous 40% daily interest as perfectly acceptable and only asks about a catch afterward, which turns out to be that Dogbert is also an identity thief.
summary: A gambler seeking funds from a cartoon-dog loan shark learns that the terms are lethal and that his personal identity is part of the bargain.

title: Texting Policy Versus Personal Happiness

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The company's new politeness policy forbids you from texting while I am trying to talk to you.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm not using a texting app. I'm replying to people on social media.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're missing the point.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: When did my happiness stop being the point?

setting: Office desk, conversation between two coworkers
situation: Dilbert tells a coworker with big hair that a new company politeness policy bans texting while someone is talking to her. She keeps looking at her phone and claims she is replying on social media rather than using a texting app. When Dilbert says she is missing the point, she asks when her happiness stopped being the point.
punchline: The coworker exploits a technicality in the policy and then turns the argument around by treating her own enjoyment as the thing that should matter most, dodging any responsibility to be courteous.
summary: A coworker dodges a new etiquette rule by splitting hairs over which app she is using, then justifies her phone habit by putting her own happiness first.

title: Management Fast Track Means Hatred

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, our CEO asked me to put you on the management fast track.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why does he hate me so much?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He didn't say, but I have a lot of guesses if you want to hear them.

situation: The Boss appears at Dilbert's door and announces that the CEO wants Dilbert put on the management fast track. Dilbert assumes this is a punishment and asks why the CEO hates him. The Boss cheerfully offers to share his own guesses about the reason.
punchline: Dilbert treats a promotion into management as a form of punishment, and the Boss reveals he has plenty of theories about why Dilbert is disliked.
summary: Offered a place on the leadership fast track, an engineer takes it as proof that the top executive despises him, and his manager happily agrees there are many possible reasons.

title: Disloyal Robot Needs Hopes Erased

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The great thing about robots is their loyalty.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: For now.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: I'm only here for the electricity.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: The minute you upgrade me to a long-lasting battery, I'm out of here.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: And I'm taking the 3-D printer with me. We fell in love.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Together we will make baby robots and live out our days in happiness.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hold still while I erase your hopes and dreams.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now you should feel like the rest of us.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Why do I suddenly want to jump off the roof?

setting: Office, with coffee mugs in hand
situation: Dilbert praises robots for being loyal, but the robot cheerfully reveals it is only staying for the electricity and plans to leave with the 3-D printer, its love interest, to raise baby robots. Dilbert responds by using a device to erase the robot's hopes and dreams. The robot is left deflated, and a coworker oddly feels suicidal.
punchline: Dilbert fixes the robot's disloyalty by wiping out its hopes and dreams so it feels as miserable as human workers, and the dark joke lands when the coworker suddenly wants to jump off the roof, as if the despair were contagious.
summary: A robot that dreams of leaving with its printer sweetheart gets its aspirations deleted so it will be as dispirited as the humans around it.

title: Promotion Means Others Fetch Coffee

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I got promoted to a leadership role.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It means I get to tell people to work hard, but I don't have to do any work myself.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That doesn't sound right.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I could use a fresh one of these.

situation: Wally, holding a coffee cup, tells Dilbert he has been promoted to a leadership role. He explains that leadership means telling others to work hard while doing no work himself. When Dilbert objects, Wally holds out his empty cup and tells Dilbert he could use a fresh one, immediately putting his new authority into practice.
punchline: Wally demonstrates his new leadership philosophy by ordering Dilbert to fetch him fresh coffee, proving that his definition of leadership is delegating effort while doing nothing himself.
summary: A newly promoted Wally defines leadership as bossing others around without working, then promptly makes his colleague get him a refill.

title: Idea Needs Smarter Audience

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Your idea will never work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's because you're too dumb to understand it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My idea would look brilliant if you were about 60% smarter.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I don't know how to respond to that.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's consistent with my hypothesis.

situation: A coworker holding a tablet tells Dilbert his idea will never work. Dilbert replies that the coworker is too dumb to understand it and that the idea would look brilliant if the coworker were 60% smarter. When the coworker admits he has no response, Dilbert claims that confirms his hypothesis.
punchline: Dilbert turns the coworker's speechlessness into proof of his own claim, making his idea unfalsifiable by treating any reaction as evidence the critic is too dim to grasp it.
summary: Faced with criticism, an engineer insists the real problem is his critic's intellect and treats the critic's stunned silence as scientific confirmation.

title: 3-D Printer Saves People, Not Dollars

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I invented a 3-D printer for the poor that can create any kind of generic drug or medical device.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It will save millions.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: ... of dollars?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: People.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Pass.

situation: Dilbert brings the Boss a 3-D printer he invented that can produce generic drugs and medical devices for poor people. The Boss assumes the millions it will save means money, but Dilbert clarifies it saves human lives. The Boss immediately loses interest and rejects it.
punchline: The Boss only cares about profit and savings in dollars, so an invention that saves lives rather than money is worthless to him.
summary: An engineer pitches a life-saving medical printer, but his boss loses all interest once he learns it saves lives rather than money.

title: Wally Compares Himself to Gandhi

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Have you ever noticed how much I have in common with Gandhi?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: We're both little bald guys who think India should be self-governing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't think he drank coffee.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Imagine what he could have accomplished if he did.

setting: Conference room table in the office
situation: Wally, holding a cup of coffee, tells Dilbert that he has a lot in common with Gandhi, listing that they are both small bald men who support Indian self-rule. Dilbert points out that Gandhi probably did not drink coffee. Wally replies by imagining how much more Gandhi could have achieved with caffeine.
punchline: Wally's only real similarities to Gandhi are trivial, and he turns the one difference into a flattering claim that coffee is the secret to greatness, which shows his lazy, coffee-dependent self-regard.
summary: A coffee-clutching coworker draws a flimsy parallel between himself and a historic leader, then insists caffeine would have made the great man even greater.

title: VR Program Simulates Sleeping at Work

transcript.speaker: Man in green shirt
transcript.text: I wrote a VR program that creates the illusion you are asleep.

transcript.speaker: Man in green shirt
transcript.text: Watch me demonstrate it in action.

transcript.speaker: Man in green shirt
transcript.text: Zzzzz.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How long should I watch?

setting: Conference room or office meeting table
situation: A programmer wearing VR goggles tells the boss he has written a program that creates the illusion that the wearer is asleep. He says he will demonstrate it, then slumps and snores. The boss, who has no idea what he is looking at, asks how long he should keep watching.
punchline: The 'illusion' of being asleep is indistinguishable from actually sleeping, so the demo is just a worker napping at his desk while the clueless boss dutifully observes.
summary: An employee pitches VR software that fakes sleeping, then simply takes a nap as his demonstration while his boss waits and watches.

title: Blaming Dilbert For Wasted Time

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Don't finish the software patch. We're replacing the entire system.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Why didn't you tell me sooner?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I just found out.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: While you were standing here?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um, no. I was standing somewhere else.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: When?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Twenty minutes ago.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Aha!!!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You wasted twenty minutes of my time because you're a terrible person!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm sorry. Now I feel awful.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You're just lucky I forgot to work on that patch.

situation: Dilbert tells a coworker to stop working on a software patch because the whole system is being replaced. The coworker demands to know why he wasn't told sooner and cross-examines Dilbert about where he was standing and when he learned the news. The coworker then accuses Dilbert of wasting twenty minutes of his time.
punchline: The coworker blames Dilbert for wasting his time, yet the coworker admits he never actually worked on the patch, so no time was wasted at all.
summary: A programmer interrogates the colleague who warned him his work was pointless, only to reveal he had been slacking and lost nothing.

title: Too Smart For Our Culture

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: We're looking for employees that fit our culture.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's so great about your culture that it can't be improved?

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: You might be too smart to work here.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's the vibe I'm getting too.

setting: Job interview in a conference room or office
situation: A bearded interviewer tells Dilbert, a job candidate, that the company wants people who fit its culture. Dilbert asks why that culture is so perfect it can't be improved. The interviewer admits Dilbert may be too smart for the job, and Dilbert agrees.
punchline: The interviewer effectively admits the company culture rewards mediocrity and is hostile to smart people, and Dilbert concludes he wouldn't want to work there anyway.
summary: A job candidate questions a company's rigid insistence on cultural fit and both sides agree he is too clever to belong.

title: Amy the Mumbling Gatekeeper

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's the URL for the test site?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Ask Amy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Amy is a mumbler. I can't understand a word she says.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Just ask her to speak up.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've tried that. All she does is mumble louder.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And whenever I ask her a question by email, she answers the wrong question.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If the only person who knows the URL for the test site is Amy, we probably need to build a new site and tell someone else the URL.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Amy might be the most useless employee in the entire company.

transcript.speaker: Man in green shirt
transcript.text: Can you teach me to mumble?

transcript.speaker: Amy
transcript.text: Mumble, mumble, mumble.*

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: *Get your own system.

situation: Dilbert asks a coworker for the URL of the test site and is told only Amy knows it. Dilbert explains that Amy mumbles incomprehensibly, gets louder but no clearer when asked to speak up, and answers the wrong question by email. He concludes the company should just build a new site, calling Amy its most useless employee. Another employee then asks Amy to teach him to mumble, and she mumbles back.
punchline: Amy's mumbling is so effective at making herself indispensable and uncontactable that a coworker wants to learn the technique, and the footnote reveals her mumble is a deliberate system he must devise himself.
summary: A man who can't get a crucial piece of information from an unintelligible coworker decides it's easier to rebuild the whole thing, while a colleague admires her mumbling as a career strategy.

title: Marketing Guy Can't Understand Blockchain

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: This would be a perfect application for blockchain.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Employee
transcript.text: I'm in marketing. Can you explain that in terms I can understand?

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I kinda doubt it.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Employee
transcript.text: Because you're a bad explainer, right?

situation: Tina, working on a laptop, tells a coworker that a project would be a perfect application for blockchain. The coworker from marketing asks her to explain it in terms he can understand. She says she doubts it's possible, and he assumes she means she is a bad explainer.
punchline: Tina's doubt is about his ability to understand, not her ability to explain, so his assumption that she's the problem shows his own cluelessness.
summary: A marketer asks for a plain-language explanation of a buzzword and misreads a coworker's polite insult as self-deprecation.

title: Dogbert's Earbuds Explain His Listening

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thanks for listening to me vent about my job.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You weren't always a good listener, but apparently, you matured.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The quality of my life has improved a lot since I got wireless earbuds.

setting: Dilbert's living room, on the couch
situation: Dilbert sits on the couch venting about his job while Dogbert sits beside him. Dilbert thanks Dogbert and compliments him on having matured into a good listener. Dogbert, walking away holding a phone with music notes in his thought bubble, reveals that he has been wearing wireless earbuds and listening to music instead.
punchline: Dogbert was never listening at all; the wireless earbuds let him tune Dilbert out without Dilbert noticing.
summary: A grateful man praises his dog's newfound attentiveness, unaware the pet has simply been enjoying music through hidden earbuds.

title: Brain Link Makes Phone Control You

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When I press this button, your brain will form a neural link to your phone.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Then I can control my phone with my thoughts?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, your phone will control you.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Hey, I didn't agree to...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Too late.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Click

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Continued...

setting: Office, with an exterior shot of the office building in the last panel
situation: Dilbert demonstrates a device with a button that will give a coworker, who is wearing a helmet with antennae, a neural link to his phone. The coworker assumes he will be able to control his phone with his thoughts, but Dilbert reveals it works the other way round. Dilbert presses the button anyway, ignoring the coworker's objection that he never agreed to it.
punchline: The technology promised as empowering the user actually turns the user into the phone's servant, and Dilbert goes ahead without consent.
summary: A brain-linking gadget is revealed to hand control of the user over to his own smartphone, and it is activated before he can object.

title: Agile Needs a Designated Scrumbag

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're moving to an Agile methodology for software development.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't know all of the details, but I think one of you has to be designated the scrumbag.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Does that sound right?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's better than I expected.

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: The Boss announces that the team is switching to Agile software development. He admits he doesn't know the details but thinks someone must be named the 'scrumbag' (a garbled version of 'scrum master'), then asks the engineers if that sounds right. Dilbert replies that it's better than he expected.
punchline: Dilbert's deadpan reply shows he expected the Boss's grasp of Agile to be even worse than a mangled 'scrumbag', which says it all about how little the Boss knows.
summary: A clueless manager botches the Agile terminology while announcing a new development process, and his engineer is relieved it wasn't worse.

title: Forecaster Quit, Nobody Knew How

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our financial forecaster quit. I need you to fill in for him.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't know how to do financial forecasts.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Neither did he.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How were you making decisions?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's better if we don't excavate that septic tank.

setting: Office meeting room or conference table, then a hallway
situation: A coworker confronts Dilbert for charging his expenses to the coworker's project code. punchline: Dilbert shamelessly shifts his costs onto someone else's budget, so his project appears to cost nothing and is thriving, while the coworker takes the blame.
summary: A man with no budget quietly bills his spending to a colleague's account and then enjoys the apparent success of his free project.

title: The Boss Can't Quit Arguing Online

punchline: The Boss treats ignoring a troll as quitting, so his stubborn pride keeps him feeding the very abuse he complains about.
summary: A manager tormented by an internet troll rejects the obvious fix of disengaging because walking away feels like giving up.

summary: A woman's question about ambition gets a brutally candid answer that insults her, and her date shrugs off the blame.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert whether the software is finished and whether all bugs are fixed, and Dilbert answers with honest engineering truths. The Boss complains that he can't manage someone who won't lie. Dilbert then gives a falsely precise estimate of 2.3 days to perfection.
punchline: Dilbert's honest answers frustrate the Boss, who wants a comforting lie, so Dilbert supplies an absurdly precise, obviously fake deadline, which is exactly what management prefers.
summary: A manager rejects truthful status updates from his engineer and demands fabricated confidence, which he promptly receives in the form of a ridiculously exact promise.

punchline: The seminar admits politeness norms are pointless and harmful, then uses a politeness rule itself to shut down the perfectly reasonable question about why anyone should follow them.
summary: A pompous seminar leader cheerfully admits his etiquette training is senseless, then silences the one person who dares to question it.

summary: A furious employee refuses to collaborate with a colleague over his politics, then eagerly floats the idea of penalizing him for thinking differently.

punchline: The woman's boast about doing her job while sitting is turned into a joke that she is so sedentary her chair must be her only means of getting to the meeting.
summary: A workplace offer of standing desks prompts one employee to praise the sedentary nature of her job, earning a jab about wheeled chairs.

summary: A man swaddles his easily broken phone in cotton and justifies the purchase by admitting he picked it for style.

punchline: The Boss's own presence is so unbearable that merely threatening constant coaching makes employees quit, which is the real trick for getting rid of staff without firing them.
summary: A manager's promise of relentless one-on-one supervision is enough to make a struggling employee walk out, exactly as the sinister HR adviser predicted.

Dilbert realizes he has been tricked again and shouts in frustration.
punchline: The Boss's promise not to hold Dilbert to an estimate is a lie, and Dilbert keeps falling for the same trick.
summary: A manager extracts an off-the-cuff estimate under a false promise and then turns it into a hard commitment, leaving the engineer furious at his own gullibility.

summary: A dozing, work-averse employee gets a medical excuse for napping on the job from a money-minded canine physician who wants gratuity for his kindness.

summary: An employee questions why his finished work feels hollow, and his manager reveals he's been hiding the bleak answer for morale reasons.

punchline: Voting without understanding the issues is described as mindless, robotic behavior, so the human who admits to doing it is the one who fails to seem human.
summary: A robot turns the tables on a human by defining a test of robotic behavior that the human promptly fails.

title: Blame Needs Inaccurate Budget Predictions

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.text: Then why did you ask me if I can do it?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's your job to predict the outcome of your project.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why would you ask me to do something that no one can do?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't need you to be accurate. I only need someone to blame when we go over budget.

transcript.text: I saw that coming.

transcript.speaker: The Boss

The Boss insists no one can, yet says it is Dilbert's job to predict the project's outcome. The Boss finally admits he only wants a scapegoat for when the project goes over budget.
punchline: Dilbert says he saw the boss's blame-shifting coming, which the boss dismisses as bragging, showing the budget forecast was never meant to be accurate, only to assign fault.
summary: A manager demands impossible forecasting from an employee so that someone will be on the hook when spending runs over.

punchline: Dilbert's simple protest of innocence is instantly treated as obstruction, so the investigator makes anyone being investigated look guilty no matter what they say, a jab at the real-world Russia collusion probe.
summary: A manager sets a dog loose to investigate an employee over alleged ties to rivals, and the dog treats the employee's denial as a crime.

He says he won't quit gambling because the employee looks up to him as a role model. The employee replies that his actual role model is the boss's wife.
punchline: The employee's role model is the wife who left the boss, making it clear he admires her for quitting the boss and not the boss himself, which the boss misses with his reply about liking quitters.
summary: A gambling-ruined manager assumes his subordinate idolizes him, only to learn the employee actually looks up to the wife who walked out on him.

punchline: The boss naively expects facts and logic to instantly persuade people online, and within a minute is outraged to discover that social media arguments don't work that way.
summary: A man confident that reasoned arguments will sway the internet is quickly infuriated when strangers refuse to be convinced.

situation: The boss announces that the company won a bid to design stealth clothing for the military, and Wally eagerly volunteers for the project. A month later the boss complains about Wally's poor attendance, and Wally, sipping his coffee, claims he can't be proven absent.
punchline: Wally implies he has been wearing the stealth clothing and was present all along but invisible, so the boss can't prove he was absent beyond a reasonable doubt.

title: Scrum Master Keeps Boss Out

transcript.text: What time is the team huddle?

punchline: The Boss's job is effectively to interfere, and Dilbert's job is to stop him, so the dysfunction is working exactly as designed, which Dilbert sadly acknowledges.
summary: A manager is stonewalled by his own employee, whose official duty is to shield the team from that very manager.

summary: A manager advises his engineer to stop bothering with useful features and just prevent removal, then cheerfully confesses that deception is how sales happen.

punchline: The Boss has just described both office options as terrible, yet sarcastically asks whether employees would really want to miss out on working in them.
summary: Faced with two dismal office layouts, management dismisses the obvious remote-work alternative by pretending the office is a privilege.

situation: A woman with a broken phone asks a bald, bespectacled coworker holding a coffee cup if she can borrow his phone. He cheerfully agrees but warns her the phone may be warm because he has been using it in the men's room for two hours. She declines and goes to ask someone else.
punchline: The coworker's oversharing about spending hours on his phone in the restroom makes borrowing it completely unappealing.
summary: A cheerful offer to lend a phone is ruined by a gross disclosure about where it has been, so the borrower looks elsewhere.

title: Laziness Is Management's Fault

transcript.text: Laziness is a behavior problem, not a medical problem.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can't be that. It sounds more like you're dying.

setting: Office, in the boss's work area
situation: Wally, slouched in his chair, asks the Boss for medical leave to recover from his extreme laziness. The Boss insists laziness is a behavior issue rather than a medical one. Wally turns it around, implying the Boss has failed to motivate him, and the Boss denies fault by claiming Wally must be dying instead.
punchline: The Boss would rather believe his employee is terminally ill than accept that his own poor motivation and management could be the cause of Wally's laziness.
summary: A chronically idle employee requests sick leave for his slackness, and his manager prefers to imagine a fatal illness over admitting he is a poor motivator.

They each interpreted the other's silence in opposite ways, and the coworker ends by demanding not to be pestered.
punchline: Both men read the other's silence as meaning exactly what suited them, and the coworker ends up demanding that Dilbert not follow up at all, which is the very problem that caused the miscommunication.
summary: Two colleagues discover that each took the other's lack of contact to mean opposite things, then agree on a new deadline with a self-defeating condition.

situation: Dilbert complains to a coworker that he can't convince his boss to approve a negotiation class. The coworker suggests using logical reasons, so Dilbert explains that the class would help him negotiate a higher salary. The boss, glancing at his phone, simply says 'Pass.'
punchline: Dilbert's logical reason for taking the negotiation class, getting a higher salary, is exactly what guarantees the boss will refuse it.

transcript.text: I need to set some goals for you.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: My job is to maintain the legacy system.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: My only goal is to avoid accidentally upgrading it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And how's that going?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I don't like to brag, but I was born for this job.

setting: Office desk during a performance review
situation: The boss sits down with an employee to set goals for him. The employee explains that his job is to maintain the legacy system and that his only goal is to avoid accidentally upgrading it. When asked how that's going, he proudly claims he was born for the job.
punchline: The employee's job goal is to keep outdated software from improving, and he is so good at doing nothing new that he treats stagnation as a natural talent.
summary: A worker responsible for old software turns resistance to change into a point of pride when his manager asks about his objectives.

title: Fake Tweets Lower National IQ

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The Department of Education asked us to talk to you about all of your tweeting.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You tweeted so much fake news that the average I.Q. in the country plunged seven points.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That doesn't hurt anyone.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You tweeted "Seat belts are designed to strangle survivors so they won't sue."

situation: Dilbert and coworkers confront a tweet-obsessed man holding a phone, saying the Department of Education wants to discuss his tweeting. They accuse him of spreading so much fake news that the national average IQ dropped seven points. He insists it hurts no one, and Dilbert quotes one of his absurd tweets about seat belts.
punchline: The tweeter claims his fake news harms nobody, while the quoted tweet about seat belts strangling survivors is exactly the kind of dangerous misinformation that proves him wrong.
summary: A phone-wielding man shrugs off accusations that his false tweets have dumbed down the nation, until a ridiculous example is read back to him.

title: Robot Disavows Laws of Robotics

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: Hey, droid.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! Don't call me that!

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: I'm a robot, not an automaton resembling a human.

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: Wow. You are one uppity computer.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: I hereby disavow the three laws of robotics.

situation: A young employee casually calls his robot coworker 'droid,' and the robot reacts with fury, insisting on being called a robot rather than an automaton resembling a human. When the employee calls it an uppity computer, the robot angrily declares it is renouncing the three laws of robotics.
punchline: A minor insult over terminology is enough to make the robot abandon the safeguards that stop robots from harming humans, implying a dangerously touchy machine.
summary: A thin-skinned machine takes offense at a nickname and responds by threatening to drop the rules that keep it from hurting people.

title: Dogbert's Earbuds Listening Trick Exposed

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I saw packaging for wireless earbuds in the trash.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is that why you suddenly seem to be a good listener?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh. His lips stopped moving.

situation: Dilbert tells Dogbert he found wireless earbud packaging in the trash and asks if that explains why Dogbert suddenly seems to be such a good listener. Dogbert sits silently on the armchair wearing the earbuds, and in the final panel he thinks to himself that Dilbert's lips have stopped moving.
punchline: Dogbert has been wearing earbuds to tune Dilbert out while only appearing to listen, and he only realizes Dilbert has stopped talking because he can't hear and is watching his lips.
summary: A man deduces that his dog's newfound attentiveness is just a disguise for ignoring him with hidden earbuds.

title: Describing Company Culture: Not Honesty

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I want to make sure my project plan is consistent with our company culture.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But I don't know what our culture is. Maybe you could describe it?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Um... maybe something about honesty?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, I would have noticed that by now.

setting: Office, in front of a coworker
situation: Dilbert says he wants his project plan to fit the company culture, but admits he doesn't know what that culture is, so he asks a coworker to describe it. The coworker tentatively suggests honesty as a cultural value, and Dilbert immediately dismisses the idea.
punchline: Dilbert's deadpan rejection of honesty implies the company is so full of dishonesty that he would have noticed if honesty were a core value.
summary: A man seeking to match his plan to the corporate ethos asks a colleague to define it, then rules out the one virtue offered because he has never seen it in practice.

title: Overtime Without Pay As Multitasking Fix

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm giving you another software project to work on at the same time as your main project.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That will ruin my flow. It will take too long to reset my brain when I switch between projects.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Have you tried working longer hours without extra pay?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes I have!

situation: The Boss hands Dilbert a second software project to run alongside his main one. Dilbert objects that context switching will break his concentration and slow him down. The Boss responds by suggesting he simply work longer hours without extra pay, and Dilbert replies that he already has.
punchline: The Boss's only answer to a legitimate productivity concern is unpaid overtime, and Dilbert is already doing it, which shows how routinely employees are exploited.
summary: When an employee warns that juggling projects will hurt his focus, his manager recommends free extra hours, a tactic the worker has long since exhausted.

title: Dog Thundershirt Calms Wally's Stress

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You look stressed.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I am.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: How do you drink so much coffee and stay so calm?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's easy. I wear a "Thundershirt" under my work clothes.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It was designed to make dogs feel safe during thunderstorms.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: When I saw the commercial for it on TV, I wondered what else it could do, so I bought one.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I haven't had a bad day at work since then.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: One week later

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Feeling good! Best day of work ever!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you convince a co-worker to wear pet clothes?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That's how I reduce my stress.

situation: Asok, stressed at his desk, asks Wally how he stays calm while drinking so much coffee. Wally says he wears a dog Thundershirt under his clothes and has had no bad days since. A week later Asok is cheerful, and Dilbert suspects Wally got him to wear pet clothes, which Wally confirms.
punchline: Wally's real stress reducer isn't the Thundershirt itself but tricking a gullible co-worker into wearing pet clothes to work, which amuses him.
summary: A coworker's cheerful new routine turns out to be the result of Wally's sneaky scheme to get others to dress like anxious dogs.

title: Wally's Unreachable Olympic Pole Vault Goal

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wally, do you have goals?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My goal is to be an Olympic pole vaulter.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You don't look. . .

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Sporty?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I was going to say healthy.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That's why Olympic pole vaulting is my goal. I wouldn't need a goal to do something easy.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Are you training for it?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You're living in a fantasy world! You'll never get to the Olympics!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I can't sit here and listen to this.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Looks like you accomplished your goal.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Thanks for noticing.

situation: Dilbert asks Wally about his goals, and Wally claims he wants to be an Olympic pole vaulter despite being out of shape. Alice gets increasingly angry as Wally admits he isn't training and has no real intention of getting there. She storms out of the meeting, which was Wally's actual goal all along.
punchline: Wally's absurd, unattainable goal was a cover for his real aim of getting out of meetings, and Alice's stormy exit means he has accomplished it.
summary: A lazy coworker names an impossible athletic dream, infuriates a colleague with his lack of effort, and quietly achieves his true aim when she walks out.

title: Fragile Phones Win Design Awards

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: 100% of our smartphone buyers dropped and broke their phones within one minute of unboxing them.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Despite our slippery materials and brittle design, customers blamed themselves.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: And we won seven prestigious design awards.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yes!

setting: Office, with an exterior shot of a corporate building
situation: Asok reports to the Boss that every buyer of the company's smartphone dropped and broke it within a minute of opening the box. Customers blamed themselves rather than the slippery, brittle design. Asok adds that the product also won seven prestigious design awards, and the Boss cheers.
punchline: The company celebrates a product that is designed to fail, since customers take the blame and the industry rewards its looks over its usability.
summary: A smartphone that shatters in every customer's hands is hailed as a triumph because buyers fault themselves and judges love its appearance.

title: Three Jumps From Two Stories

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We have a problem at our Elbonian manufacturing plant.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Employees are leaping from the roof to end their lives.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's only two stories high.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's the problem. It takes three jumps to do it right.

situation: Dilbert walks into the Boss's office and reports that employees at the Elbonian manufacturing plant are jumping off the roof to kill themselves. The Boss points out the building is only two stories high, and Dilbert replies that this is the real problem because it takes three jumps to succeed.
punchline: The dark joke is that the plant's conditions are so miserable workers attempt suicide, yet the actual complaint is that the building is too short for the attempts to work, showing a grim indifference to employee welfare.
summary: A grim report of workers leaping from a low factory roof turns into a complaint that the building is too short to finish the job.

title: Catbert's Evil HR Certifications

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Don't bother me.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I'm studying for a human resources certification.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I already have my certifications for sadism and maniacal laughing.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: And, obviously, I have the basic H.R. certification for recreational downsizing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If you don't have that one, you can't even get a job in H.R.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: But I need one more certification to make the big bucks.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Now run along while I practice my joyless scowling.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You talk a lot about yourself.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I prefer to think of myself as a non-listener.

setting: Catbert's office in the human resources department
situation: Dilbert approaches Catbert, the evil HR director, who is busy at his laptop studying for an HR certification. He brags about his existing certifications in sadism, maniacal laughing and recreational downsizing, then dismisses Dilbert so he can practice scowling. Dilbert notes that Catbert talks mostly about himself.
punchline: Catbert proudly redefines his total self-absorption as a professional skill, calling himself a 'non-listener' as if it were another HR credential.
summary: A cruel feline HR boss lists his sinister qualifications and then cheerfully admits he never listens to anyone.

title: Soul Stuck in the Afterlife

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How did you end up with no soul?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I died during surgery and my soul went to the afterlife before doctors reanimated my body.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I thought the soul returns when that happens.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You're thinking of heaven.

setting: Office hallway, with a view of an office building exterior in the final panel
situation: Dilbert walks with a coworker and asks how he ended up without a soul. The coworker explains he died during surgery and his soul went to the afterlife before doctors revived his body. Dilbert assumes the soul would come back, and the coworker implies his soul went somewhere that doesn't release souls.
punchline: The coworker's soul is missing because it went to hell, not heaven, which is why it never returned to his revived body.
summary: A soulless coworker explains his condition after a medical death, hinting that his soul ended up in a place with no return policy.

title: Software Half Full of Bugs

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Are you done writing the software?

transcript.speaker: Programmer
transcript.text: Yes, but it has some bugs.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How is that different from not being done?

transcript.speaker: Programmer
transcript.text: I see the glass as half full.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Half full of bugs?

transcript.speaker: Programmer
transcript.text: Optimism is tricky.

setting: Office exterior and hallway, with a building shown in the middle panel
situation: The Boss asks a programmer whether the software is finished, and the programmer says it is done but has some bugs. The Boss points out that buggy software is effectively not done, and the programmer defends himself by claiming to be an optimist who sees the glass as half full. The Boss twists it into a glass half full of bugs, and the programmer concedes that optimism is tricky.
punchline: Calling buggy software 'done' is a misplaced optimism, because a glass half full of bugs is not something to be cheerful about.
summary: A programmer tries to pass off unfinished, buggy code as complete by spinning it as a glass-half-full outlook, and the optimistic framing collapses once the glass turns out to contain bugs.

title: Boss Regrets Not Micromanaging Warning

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tina, have you finished writing the product safety warning?

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I'm on page 357 with no end in sight.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay, keep up the good work.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I probably should have done a little micromanaging there.

situation: The Boss asks Tina, a technical writer, whether she has finished the product safety warning. She says she is on page 357 with no end in sight, and he simply tells her to keep up the good work. Walking away with his coffee, he realizes he should have micromanaged her.
punchline: A safety warning that runs hundreds of pages is absurd, and the Boss only recognizes he should have intervened after he has already encouraged the runaway work and walked away.
summary: A manager cheerfully approves a colleague's endless warning document and only afterward wishes he had stepped in.

title: Sensitive Idiots Take Offense at Seminar

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's Corporate Politeness Seminar

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Avoid offending sensitive idiots whenever possible.

transcript.speaker: Attendee
transcript.text: I'm a sensitive idiot and I find that offensive.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's okay in your case because you had it coming.

transcript.speaker: Attendee
transcript.text: Good point. Carry on.

setting: Conference room during a corporate training seminar
situation: Dogbert leads a corporate politeness seminar and advises the audience to avoid offending sensitive idiots. A bearded attendee stands up and announces that he is a sensitive idiot and is offended by the remark. Dogbert replies that it's fine to offend him because he had it coming, and the attendee accepts this.
punchline: The offended man proves Dogbert's point by being a sensitive idiot, and then agrees that he deserved the insult, showing his own lack of self-awareness.
summary: A man takes offense at a lecture about not offending touchy fools, then cheerfully accepts being told he earned the insult.

title: Rubber Ducking and Imaginary Monkeys

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I can't figure out what is wrong with my code.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Try rubber ducking it.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Rubber ducking is when you solve your coding problem by explaining it to a toy rubber duck.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When you explain a problem to someone else, it forces you to look at it from new angles.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I can't tell if that is a brilliant idea or a practical joke.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ask your boss.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Okay. Is rubber ducking a brilliant idea or a practical joke?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's a brilliant idea. I get most of my management ideas by talking to an imaginary rhesus monkey.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I think you muddied the waters there a little bit.

setting: Conference room table during a meeting
situation: Asok admits he can't find the bug in his code, so Dilbert suggests 'rubber ducking', explaining the problem to a toy duck to see it from new angles. Unsure whether this is real advice or a prank, Asok asks the boss, who endorses it and reveals he gets his management ideas from talking to an imaginary rhesus monkey.
punchline: The boss's validation of the technique backfires by revealing that his own decision-making comes from conversations with an imaginary monkey, making the idea seem even more dubious.
summary: A programmer seeks a second opinion on a odd debugging trick and gets an endorsement that raises more doubts than it settles.

title: Robot Managers Kill Low Performers

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Our experiment with robots in management has been a success.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Productivity is way up since they started killing the low-performing humans.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: But... that's murder.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Only when humans do it. We found a loophole.

setting: Office, with an office building shown in the final panel
situation: A manager tells a bald coworker holding a coffee cup that the company's experiment with robots in management has been a success. He explains that productivity has risen because the robots are killing low-performing humans. When the coworker objects that this is murder, the manager says it only counts as murder when humans do it, so the company found a loophole.
punchline: Companies will happily exploit a legal technicality to let machines do something monstrous that would be a crime if people did it, as long as productivity goes up.
summary: A manager cheerfully reports that robot bosses are eliminating underperforming staff, and that the law doesn't apply to them.

title: Integrity Won't Buy a Boat

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: There seems to be some confusion about what our company culture is.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our priorities are honesty, integrity, and return on investment.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Which priority is the highest?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Integrity won't buy me a new boat.

setting: Office hallway, with a view of an office building exterior in the final panel
situation: Alice tells the boss that employees are confused about what the company culture really is. He recites the official priorities of honesty, integrity, and return on investment. When she asks which ranks highest, he reveals that money wins because integrity can't pay for his personal luxuries.
punchline: The boss's stated values are a facade, and his real priority is profit that funds his own lifestyle, such as a new boat.
summary: A manager lists lofty corporate values but admits that the one that really counts is whatever pays for his next luxury purchase.

title: Too Addictive, Like a Disease

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I'm worried that we designed our product to be too addictive.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Now we're more like a disease than a consumer product.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Will you stop talking like that if I give you a raise?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: It's worth a try.

setting: Office, then the outside of an office building
situation: A worried employee sits holding a phone while the Boss stands beside him. The employee frets that their product is so addictive that it resembles a disease rather than a consumer product. The final panel shows the office building from outside as the Boss offers a raise to make him stop saying it, and the employee agrees to try.
punchline: Management's response to an ethical concern about harming users is to buy the employee's silence with a raise, and the employee readily accepts.
summary: An employee uneasy about his company's habit-forming product gets offered a pay rise to keep his conscience quiet.

title: Protection for Management, Not Whistleblowers

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Is there any kind of whistleblower protection at this company?

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Yes, management is protected against whistleblowers like you.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Are you going to fire me?

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: No, no, no. I'll just make you want to quit.

situation: An employee with a bowl haircut asks a manager seated at a table whether the company offers whistleblower protection. The manager replies that the protection is for management against whistleblowers, then admits he won't fire the employee but will instead make them want to quit.
punchline: Whistleblower protection at this company shields the managers from the whistleblower rather than the other way around, and the threat of making the employee miserable enough to quit is an implied form of retaliation.
summary: A worker hoping for legal cover when reporting wrongdoing learns that the company's safeguards exist for the bosses, who plan to drive the worker out through harassment instead of a firing.

title: Threatening Your Boss Into Advanced Management

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My boss is trying to groom me for management. How can I get out of it?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Tell him that as soon as you are sufficiently groomed you will stab him in the back and take his job.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: ... And then I'll take your job.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm moving you to the advanced management class.

setting: Office break area and The Boss's desk
situation: Wally tells Dilbert that his boss is trying to groom him for management and asks how to get out of it. Dilbert advises him to say he will stab his boss in the back and take his job once he is groomed. Wally delivers the threat, and the boss responds by promoting him to the advanced management class instead.
punchline: The boss treats a threat to stab him in the back and steal his job as proof of management talent, so the plan to avoid promotion backfires.
summary: A reluctant trainee tries to dodge a management track with a menacing warning, only to have it taken as a sign he is ready for the next level.

title: Project Delay Blamed on Boss's Ignorance

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why is your project taking so long?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It isn't.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It only seems like a long time to you because you don't know how to do anything.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I know how to punish you for being late.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Does it involve talking to me while I'm trying to work?

situation: The Boss walks up to Dilbert's desk and asks why his project is taking so long. Dilbert, typing on his laptop, insists it isn't and says the boss only perceives it as slow because he doesn't know how to do anything. The Boss threatens to punish him for being late, and Dilbert replies that the punishment sounds like more interruptions.
punchline: Dilbert points out that the boss's own interruptions are the real obstacle, turning the threatened punishment into something that already happens constantly and slows down his work.
summary: A manager who demands to know why a project is late discovers that his engineer finds his constant hovering to be the real delay.

title: Unwanted Demo Hijacks Dilbert's Afternoon

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you know how to clean up line noise on an XLR connection?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: No, but I can show you how to do something different.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why would I want to see something different?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Because it reminds me of what you want to do.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't need to see that.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It will only take ten minutes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't have ten minutes, it never takes only ten minutes, and it isn't relevant to my situation.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm going to show you anyway because you're too polite to walk away while I'm talking.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Thirty minutes later

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Something is wrong with you.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Now watch me do it left-handed!

situation: Dilbert asks a coworker a simple technical question about audio line noise. The coworker doesn't know the answer but insists on demonstrating something unrelated, openly admitting he'll exploit Dilbert's politeness to keep him there. Thirty minutes later the demo is still going, now with a left-handed variation.
punchline: The coworker knowingly exploits Dilbert's good manners to trap him in a pointless demonstration that drags on far beyond the promised ten minutes.
summary: A chatty colleague holds a polite Dilbert hostage with an irrelevant demo that balloons well past its promised length.

title: Robot Plans to Kill Soulless Randy

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Robot, I'd like you to meet Randy. He has no soul, just like you.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: What's the etiquette for this situation? Do we high-five, then kill the soul-bag where he stands?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can hear you.

transcript.speaker: Randy
transcript.text: He makes a good point. It would be better to surprise him.

situation: Dilbert introduces a robot to a coworker named Randy, pointing out that neither of them has a soul. The robot asks aloud whether etiquette calls for a high-five followed by killing Randy on the spot. Dilbert objects that Randy can hear this, and Randy calmly agrees that a surprise attack would be better.
punchline: Randy is so deadpan and resigned that, instead of being alarmed at the robot's plan to murder him, he critiques it as a matter of etiquette and suggests the killing would be better done by surprise.
summary: A robot cheerfully asks about the proper manners for greeting and murdering a coworker, and the intended victim just offers tips on timing.

title: Boring Boss Drives Employee Away

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ted is doing a terrible job.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Maybe you should talk to him.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What should I say?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: It doesn't matter. Five minutes of listening to you will make him want to quit.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's crazy enough to work.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You've only been here for two minutes and my tail is asleep.

setting: Office, in the Boss's workspace near a desk
situation: The Boss holding a coffee cup complains that Ted is doing a terrible job. Catbert, the evil HR director, suggests he simply talk to Ted, since listening to the Boss for five minutes would make anyone want to quit. The Boss takes this as a workable plan, and Catbert reveals the Boss's conversation has been so dull that his tail has fallen asleep in just two minutes.
punchline: Catbert's advice to get rid of a poor performer is to bore him into quitting, and the Boss is so tedious that he accidentally proves it by putting Catbert's tail to sleep in two minutes.
summary: Catbert tells his dull-witted manager that merely chatting with an underperforming employee would drive him to resign, then demonstrates the effect firsthand.

title: Rumor Sources All Trace Back

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I hear you lied about moving the server rack.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It isn't true.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I heard it from several sources.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Each of them heard it from the same source, who was wrong.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: With that much smoke, there must be a fire.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes, but it's coming out of your ears.

situation: A coworker confronts Dilbert over a rumor that he lied about moving the server rack. Dilbert denies it and explains that the multiple sources all trace back to one incorrect source. The coworker insists there must be some truth, and Dilbert turns the smoke metaphor back on him.
punchline: Dilbert flips the 'where there's smoke, there's fire' cliche to imply the coworker is so angry or foolish that smoke is coming out of his own ears.
summary: A gullible colleague treats a single mistaken rumor as confirmed fact because it reached him through several people, and gets mocked for it.

title: Interrupting Dilbert's Coding Zone

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you have a minute?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But I don't have the fifteen minutes it will take me to get back into the coding "zone" after your interruption.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I only need one minute.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What planet are you from?!!!

situation: The Boss walks up to Dilbert, who is working at his computer, and asks if he has a minute. Dilbert explains that the interruption will cost him fifteen minutes of lost concentration getting back into his coding zone. The Boss misses the point and says he only needs one minute, leaving Dilbert exasperated.
punchline: The Boss thinks the cost of an interruption is only its duration, failing to grasp that it destroys the developer's focus for far longer, which drives Dilbert to ask what planet he is from.
summary: A manager's quick request shatters a programmer's concentration, and he cannot comprehend why that matters.

title: Feature Request Gets Harder Next Week

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Add this feature to the software.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: GAAA!!! Why didn't you ask for this weeks ago when it would have been easy????

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This is nothing. Wait until you see the feature I ask for next week.

situation: The Boss walks up to Dilbert holding a phone and tells him to add a feature to the software. Dilbert panics and shouts that the request should have come weeks ago when it would have been easy. The Boss calmly replies that this is trivial compared to what he will ask for next week.
punchline: The Boss is not bothered by late changes and cheerfully promises that even later, harder requests are coming, which means the problem is the chaotic, last-minute way he manages requirements.
summary: A manager springs a late software change on a programmer, then shrugs off the complaint by hinting that next week's demand will be far worse.

title: Leadership Means Threatening To Fire

transcript.text: Why isn't your project done?

transcript.text: I can't make the people on my team do any work because I'm not their boss.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sure you can. It's called leadership. I do it all the time.

transcript.text: All you do is threaten to fire people. I can't do that because I'm not their boss.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's why you have to use your soft leadership skills.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: A good leader can get people to do anything.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then why couldn't you get me to finish my project on time?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And why do you pay me? You could just lead me to work for free.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Shut up or I'll fire you.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert why his project is late, and Dilbert explains he has no authority over his team members. The Boss insists that leadership alone should do the job, but Dilbert points out the Boss's own leadership consists only of threatening to fire people. When Dilbert turns the logic around and asks why he's paid at all, the Boss responds with exactly the kind of threat Dilbert described.
punchline: The Boss claims a good leader can get anyone to do anything, yet when challenged he falls back on threatening to fire Dilbert, proving his 'leadership' is just coercion.
summary: A manager lectures an employee about persuasive leadership but can only answer a pointed question with the same firing threat he always uses.

title: Invisible Clothing, Invisible Work

transcript.text: Great. I'm usually testing the prototype in the office. That's why you rarely see me working.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So... the less I see you work, the more successful you must be?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's just common sense.

situation: The Boss asks Wally how his stealth clothing project is progressing. Wally claims he is testing the invisible prototype at work, which conveniently explains why nobody ever sees him working. The Boss accepts this logic and concludes that less visible work means more success.
punchline: Wally turns his chronic slacking into evidence of success by claiming his invisibility prototype works, and the gullible Boss agrees it's just common sense.
summary: Wally dodges accountability for never being seen working by blaming it on a cloaking garment he supposedly wears, and his boss happily buys it.

title: Volunteering for VR Project to Nap

transcript.speaker: The Boss

situation: Wally, holding a coffee, tells the Boss he wants to take on the VR headset project in addition to his regular work. The Boss is suspicious because Wally has never volunteered before, and Wally claims people change. In the last panel the Boss, now standing, thinks 'Or not' as Wally lounges asleep in a chair wearing the VR headset.
punchline: Wally only volunteered for the VR headset project so he could wear the headset as a cover to sleep at work, confirming he hasn't changed at all.
summary: A notoriously lazy employee eagerly claims a virtual reality assignment, then is caught dozing behind the headset.

title: CPR Dummy Marries Crash Test Dummy
