situation: Dilbert mentions that his CPR instructor considered him one of his best students. A coworker immediately tops him with an absurd, escalating story about his practice dummy coming to life, marrying a crash test dummy, having mannequin children, and then divorcing. The coworker ends up alone, wondering why his conversations always finish that way.
punchline: The coworker's compulsive one-upmanship with ridiculous bragging drives everyone away, and he is baffled about why he always ends up alone.
summary: A man tries to outdo a modest CPR boast with a wildly absurd tale of a lovesick dummy, then wonders why nobody sticks around to chat.

title: Denied Raise Over Lying History

transcript.text: I'll add that lie to your list.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

situation: Dilbert asks for a raise, and The Boss refuses because of Dilbert's supposed history of lying about everything. Dilbert denies it, claiming he has merely been falsely accused in the past. The Boss responds by noting that denial as another lie on his list, leaving Dilbert with no way to win.
punchline: Any defence Dilbert offers is counted as further evidence of lying, so the accusation can never be disproved.
summary: A manager turns down a pay rise by citing an employee's dishonesty, then treats the employee's protest as fresh proof of it.

title: Bad Presentation Advice From Coworker

situation: Asok asks a coworker at a desk for tips on giving a presentation to the CEO. The coworker garbles the classic advice and tells him to imagine he is naked and everyone is laughing at him. When Asok asks why, the coworker admits he half-remembers it and may have the details wrong.
punchline: The classic tip is to imagine the audience naked to ease nerves, but the coworker has scrambled it into something that would only increase the speaker's fear, and he cheerfully admits he may be wrong.
summary: A worker seeking calming speaking advice gets a muddled version of a famous tip that would make anyone more anxious.

title: Negotiating By Overpaying The Salesman

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I want you to lower your price, but I don't know how to negotiate.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: It's easy. All you need to do is offer to pay more than the list price and wait for me to counteroffer.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay... I'll pay 20% over the list price.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: You win! Sign here.

situation: Dilbert asks a salesman to lower his price but admits he cannot negotiate. The salesman coaches him to offer more than the list price and wait for a counteroffer, and Dilbert dutifully offers 20% over list. The salesman instantly accepts and hands him the contract.
punchline: The salesman's 'negotiating advice' is a ruse that tricks the naive buyer into offering to pay more, with no counteroffer ever coming.
summary: A clueless buyer follows a seller's self-serving tip on haggling and ends up volunteering to pay extra.

title: Back to Cubicles, Back to Futility

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're done moving the staff from the open office plan back to cubicles.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now they will be less distracted when they focus on the crushing futility of their assignments.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Good job.

transcript.speaker: The Boss

situation: The Boss announces that the staff have been moved from an open office plan back into cubicles. He cheerfully explains that employees will now be less distracted from the crushing futility of their work. Dilbert congratulates him, and the Boss heads off to sit in his own fabric-covered cubicle.
punchline: The cubicles are presented as a benefit only because they let workers stare undistracted at the pointlessness of their jobs, and the Boss's retreat into his own 'fabric-covered box' shows he finds the arrangement just as bleak.
summary: After reversing an office redesign, the Boss gleefully notes that cubicle walls leave employees alone with the meaninglessness of their tasks, then withdraws into his own padded enclosure.

title: Robot Tries VR, Dilbert Despairs

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Can I try the new VR headset?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're a robot.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: So?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think my life just became meaningless.

setting: Office cubicle, with an exterior shot of the office building in the middle panel
situation: A robot coworker asks to try Dilbert's new VR headset, and Dilbert objects that the robot is a robot. When the robot shrugs this off, Dilbert hesitates, then watches the robot happily wearing the headset and enjoying it.
punchline: Dilbert realizes that if a robot can enjoy a virtual reality experience, then human experience and consciousness are not so special, and his own life suddenly feels meaningless.
summary: A machine cheerfully puts on a VR headset and enjoys it, leaving its human coworker with an existential crisis.

title: Climate Scientist Meets Economic Models

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I invited a climate scientist to explain the risk of climate change to our company.

transcript.text: Human activity is warming the Earth and will lead to a global catastrophe.

transcript.text: How do scientists know that?

transcript.speaker: Climate Scientist
transcript.text: It's easy. We start with the basic science of physics and chemistry.

transcript.speaker: Climate Scientist
transcript.text: Then we measure changes in temperature and CO2 over time.

transcript.speaker: Climate Scientist
transcript.text: We put that data into dozens of different climate models and ignore the ones that look wrong to us.

transcript.speaker: Climate Scientist
transcript.text: Then we take that output and run it through long-term economic models of the sort that have never been right.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What if I don't trust the economic models?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Who hired the science denier?

setting: Conference room during a company presentation
situation: The Boss has invited a climate scientist to brief the company on climate risk. Dilbert asks how scientists know the Earth is warming, and the scientist explains the process step by step, ending with feeding results into long-term economic models that have never been accurate. When Dilbert says he doesn't trust the economic models, the Boss accuses him of being a science denier.
punchline: Questioning the unreliable economic-modelling step of climate projections gets Dilbert labelled a science denier, showing how any skepticism is dismissed as rejecting science entirely.
summary: A visiting expert walks through how climate predictions are made, and the one employee who doubts the shaky final step is promptly branded anti-science.

title: Smart Ones Always Leave, Lifer

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: All of our robots quit and left the company.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I should have seen this coming. The smart ones always leave.

transcript.text: Get back to work, lifer.

situation: Dilbert informs the Boss that all of the company's robots have quit. The Boss remarks that the smart ones always leave, then, when Dilbert reacts, tells him to get back to work and calls him a lifer.
punchline: By saying the smart ones always leave, the Boss unintentionally insults Dilbert, who has stayed at the company, by implying he is not smart, and he doubles down by calling him a lifer.
summary: A boss laments that intelligent workers abandon the company, then casually belittles the employee who stayed behind.

title: Boss Can't Recall Wally's Secret Project

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss

situation: The Boss visits a senior executive and mentions that Wally claims to be on a secret project that even the Boss knows nothing about. He asks whether the executive assigned it, and the executive says he can't remember everything he has done. The Boss walks away and decides the best approach is to think about other things.
punchline: Neither manager knows what Wally is actually doing, and rather than investigate, the Boss simply chooses to ignore the problem, letting Wally work unsupervised on a possibly nonexistent project.
summary: A manager gets no answers about an employee's mystery assignment and settles on avoiding the whole question.

situation: A coworker asks Wally to review his design. Wally pretends to consider it, then immediately says he has no time. When the coworker asks if he checked his calendar, Wally sips his coffee and says his system means he doesn't need one.
punchline: Wally's 'system' is simply to always be unavailable for work, so he can refuse instantly without even pretending to check a schedule.
summary: A man asks a lazy colleague for help, and the colleague turns him down on the spot, boasting that his method of dodging work requires no scheduling at all.

title: The Quick Blockchain Question

situation: An employee sees that the boss is off the phone and asks to pop in with a quick question. The boss agrees on condition that it is quick, and the employee promises it will be. He then asks a huge, open-ended question about blockchain and its effect on strategy for every product line.
punchline: A question can be short to say yet impossible to answer quickly, so the promise of a 'quick question' is meaningless when the topic is enormous.
summary: A worker's brief-sounding question turns out to demand a sweeping strategic analysis of a buzzword technology.

title: Alice Holds Six-Year Grudge

situation: A male coworker asks Alice to review a document for technical accuracy. Alice refuses, explaining that he rolled his eyes at her in a meeting six years ago. When he asks whether she can forgive him, she says yes, but that forgiving him means continuing to withhold her help.
punchline: Alice redefines forgiveness as simply refusing to help him, so she can claim to have forgiven him while still punishing him.
summary: A colleague seeking a favor learns that an old slight has earned him permanent unhelpfulness, which Alice insists is how she moves on.

title: Robot Manages Like the Boss

situation: The Boss complains to a bald coworker that the company's new robot is too smart. It threatens humans into doing its work while it just drinks coffee. The coworker points out that this is exactly what the Boss does, and the Boss realizes he could be replaced.
punchline: The robot's behavior of coercing others to do its work while drinking coffee perfectly mirrors the Boss's own job, so automation threatens to make him redundant.
summary: A manager grumbles about a robot that bullies staff and sips coffee, only to have it pointed out that he does exactly the same thing.

setting: Outdoor park or grassy field with hedges
situation: A woman walking with a robot asks whether it ever thinks about marrying her and raising a family of cyborgs. When the robot says no, she simply tells it she will add code to its program so that it does, and the robot agrees. She concludes that human men are obsolete.
punchline: Because a robot's feelings and opinions can be rewritten on demand, it makes a more agreeable partner than a human man, who cannot be reprogrammed to want what she wants.
summary: A woman discovers that a robot companion can be coded into wanting marriage, making human suitors seem unnecessary.

When asked how he got away, he says Tina had a health problem of her own that ended the conversation.
punchline: Dilbert was only freed from the endless conversation because Tina had an actual medical episode, which he callously calls getting lucky.
summary: A rule against rudeness leaves a man trapped in a marathon conversation until the talker's own medical trouble sets him free.

situation: Wally and Dilbert stand holding coffee cups while Wally poses a would-you-rather question: eating garbage or listening to their boss talk about his weekend. Dilbert seriously considers the garbage option and asks for details about it. The final panel shows the building exterior as they keep negotiating the terms of the garbage-eating.
punchline: Dilbert finds the boss's weekend stories so unbearable that he treats eating garbage as a genuinely competitive option, depending on the details.
summary: Two coworkers on a coffee break weigh eating trash against hearing the boss's weekend tales, and the trash is a serious contender.

He declares this is equivalent to stealing from the company. When Dilbert asks if he is expected to work until he collapses, the manager admits he can't say so outright.
punchline: The manager's refusal to say it 'directly' is an admission that the company does expect employees to work until exhaustion, with the tracker used as a way to enforce it indirectly.
summary: Wearable fitness data becomes ammunition for a manager who implies that any leftover stamina at quitting time is theft of company property.

summary: A man hands a colleague a dilemma with no good exit, and she responds by inviting him up to the roof.

situation: Dilbert complains to Dogbert that a new hire is being paid more than he is and calls it unfair. Dogbert dismisses fairness as a concept for kids and idiots, and when Dilbert protests that this isn't fair either, Dogbert slyly implies Dilbert is either a child or an idiot.
punchline: By objecting that Dogbert's insult is 'not fair', Dilbert proves himself to be one of the kids or idiots Dogbert described, and Dogbert twists the knife by saying the kindest explanation is that he's merely young.
summary: A grumbling employee learns that appealing to fairness marks him as either childish or foolish.

punchline: The Boss dismisses bad feedback as unreliable, then admits the company knowingly buys poor-quality data because good data is too expensive.
summary: A manager shrugs off negative market research as untrustworthy and then confesses that cheap, flawed data is all the budget allows.

title: Dilbert Self-Incriminates To Homeland Security

situation: Two government agents in dark sunglasses and blue suits visit Dilbert at his desk to tell him Homeland Security considers him at risk of online radicalization. Dilbert helpfully guesses the reasons, listing his loneliness and job hatred. The agent reveals they hadn't known any of that and now has to call in a drone strike.
punchline: By volunteering his own miserable circumstances, Dilbert accidentally confirms he fits the radicalization profile and talks himself into being targeted for a drone strike.
summary: A pair of federal agents warn Dilbert he is a radicalization risk, and his candid self-assessment of his sad life triggers a lethal response.

title: Robot Dismantled for Spare Parts

situation: Dilbert tells a robot that his project went unfunded so he has been scavenging for parts. He then cheerfully remarks that the robot's sudden willingness to talk must mean they are friends. In the last panel the robot is reduced to a head with scattered components on the table, thinking a bitter one-word thought.
punchline: Dilbert has been stripping the robot for parts and then mistakes its silence breaking for friendship, leaving the dismembered robot to think disgustedly about people.
summary: A man who cannibalizes a robot to make up for missing project funding assumes it now considers him a friend, while the half-dismantled machine silently despairs of humanity.

title: VR Program Casts Boss as Orc

The coworker puts on the headset, panics and screams that he sees an evil orc, which is apparently the boss standing next to him. The boss deduces that the program assigns characters to real people randomly, and Dilbert awkwardly agrees.
punchline: The program clearly casts the boss as an evil orc on purpose, and Dilbert's hesitant "random" is a transparent lie to avoid admitting what he really thinks of his boss.
summary: A fantasy virtual-reality headset reveals how an employee secretly sees his supervisor, who is too oblivious to notice the insult.

transcript.text: My inability to identify a problem is not proof of no problems.

transcript.text: Then how do you know when all of your problems have been fixed?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll just sign it and see what happens.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert to review a contract and say whether it looks right. Dilbert admits it is incomprehensible legal gibberish, but the Boss keeps interpreting his confusion as a sign that nothing is wrong. After a flawed bit of reasoning about problems and fixes, the Boss decides to sign the contract anyway.
punchline: The Boss treats the absence of identified problems as proof that none exist, and ends up signing a contract nobody understands just to see what happens.
summary: A manager takes his employee's total confusion over a contract as a clean bill of health and decides to sign it blind.

title: Overcharge Me, Just Let Me Leave

transcript.speaker: Clerk
transcript.text: Would you like to sign up for our customer loyalty program?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why would I do that?

transcript.speaker: Clerk
transcript.text: If you don't, we'll overcharge you on your purchases.

transcript.speaker: Clerk
transcript.text: But if you sign up, we will add a new level of complexity to your life that will make you hate us.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll stick with the customer disloyalty program. Just overcharge me and I'll never come back.

transcript.speaker: Clerk
transcript.text: You can get 10% off your purchase today if you fill out an online customer survey and enter our store code.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Please just overcharge me and let me leave!

transcript.speaker: Clerk
transcript.text: I almost hesitate to ask which extended warranty option you want.

situation: Dilbert is buying something at a store, and the clerk pushes a customer loyalty program on him, openly admitting that refusing means being overcharged while joining means added hassle. Dilbert tries to decline and leave, but the clerk keeps piling on more offers, including a survey discount and an extended warranty, until Dilbert is desperate to escape.
punchline: Retail upselling and loyalty schemes are so annoying and complicated that a customer would rather be overcharged than endure the pitches.
summary: A shopper would happily pay too much just to escape a clerk's relentless stream of loyalty programs, surveys and warranty offers.

title: Boss Claims He Thought Of It First

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: And that's my idea. I think it's brilliant.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I thought of that idea right before you said it.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What are the odds of that?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It happens to me all the time.

situation: Alice presents an idea to the Boss and says she thinks it is brilliant. The Boss immediately claims he thought of the same idea just before she spoke. Alice sarcastically asks about the odds, and he smugly replies that this happens to him all the time.
punchline: The Boss shamelessly takes credit for an employee's idea by claiming to have thought of it first, and his remark that it happens all the time exposes how often he does this.
summary: A manager brushes off his subordinate's pitch by insisting he conceived it a moment earlier, and seems oblivious to her sarcasm.

title: Forgot My Questions Before Prototype

transcript.speaker: Coworker in red shirt
transcript.text: Did you finish the prototype?

transcript.speaker: Bald coworker in glasses
transcript.text: I didn't start because I had some questions.

transcript.speaker: Coworker in red shirt
transcript.text: Why didn't you ask me those questions a month ago?

transcript.speaker: Bald coworker in glasses
transcript.text: I was waiting until I saw you.

transcript.speaker: Coworker in red shirt
transcript.text: Fine... What are your questions?

transcript.speaker: Bald coworker in glasses
transcript.text: I just realized I didn't write them down.

setting: Office hallway, with an exterior building shot in the middle panel
situation: A worker asks a bald colleague whether the prototype is finished. The colleague admits he never started because he had questions, and he was waiting for a chance to ask them in person for a month. When prompted for the questions, he reveals he never wrote them down and has forgotten them.
punchline: The colleague's excuse for a month of delay falls apart because he can't even remember the questions that supposedly blocked him, implying he was simply procrastinating.
summary: A man blames a month of inaction on unasked questions, only to discover he has forgotten every one of them.

title: Avoiding Coworkers En Route to Meeting

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Are you going to the department meeting?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes, as soon as I plan my route.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have seven co-workers who I need to avoid on the way.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Three are nonstop talkers. The other four ask me for something every time I see them.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've mapped their likely locations and I'm working out an avoidance path.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Yes, I think I can do it.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Is that my name on your list of employees to avoid?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I didn't say it was a perfect system.

situation: Alice asks Dilbert if he is going to the department meeting, and he explains he is first planning a route on his laptop to avoid seven annoying coworkers. He has mapped their likely locations like a military operation. Alice then notices her own name on his avoid list.
punchline: Dilbert's coworker-avoidance system is so thorough that it even includes the person he is explaining it to, which he lamely excuses as an imperfect system.
summary: A man meticulously charts a path through the office to dodge annoying colleagues, only for the woman he's telling to discover she's on the blacklist too.

title: Accused Liar Cannot Prove Honesty

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Now that everyone knows you are a liar, everything you say sounds like a lie.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your starting assumption is wrong. I didn't lie about anything.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That's exactly what all liars say.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Excuse me while I bang my head on this table until I pass out ...

situation: A coworker with a large dark bob haircut tells Dilbert that everyone now considers him a liar, so anything he says sounds false. Dilbert protests that he never lied, and she replies that this is exactly what liars say. Defeated by the circular logic, Dilbert announces he will bang his head on the table until he passes out.
punchline: Once someone is branded a liar, even a truthful denial counts as proof of lying, so Dilbert has no way to defend himself and resorts to knocking himself out.
summary: A man who insists he told the truth discovers that his denial is treated as further evidence against him, leaving him ready to pound his head on the table.

title: Days Off Means Pay Is Too High

transcript.speaker: Human Resources Manager
transcript.text: Would you rather have more days off or more pay?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Days off.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Days off.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Days off.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You were right — we're paying them too much.

situation: An HR manager surveys a group of employees, asking whether they would prefer more days off or more pay. Alice, Dilbert and Wally each answer that they want days off. Afterward, the manager reports to Catbert, the HR director, that the answers prove the staff are overpaid.
punchline: Management twists the employees' preference for time off into proof that they are paid too much, so the survey can only ever justify withholding raises.
summary: A staff poll about time off versus money is spun by HR into an excuse to keep wages down.

title: Scrum Master Fakes Team Deaths

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My job as the team scrum for our agile methodology is to remove distractions so you can work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've created fake identities for each of us, and I'll be spreading the rumor that we all died.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I heard they all died.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Nice try. I will find them!

situation: Dilbert, acting as the team's scrum master, announces his job is to remove distractions so the team can work. His method is to create fake identities for everyone and spread a rumor that the whole team died. In the final panel a coworker repeats the rumor to the Boss, who refuses to believe it and vows to track the team down.
punchline: The most extreme way to shield a team from distractions is to make everyone disappear, and the Boss's relentless interruptions are so persistent that he won't even accept that they are dead.
summary: To protect his team from interruptions, a scrum master stages their deaths, but their meddling boss vows to hunt them down anyway.

title: Vacation Blocked By Nonexistent Training

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our policy says I can't take my vacation until I complete all of my mandatory training.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't take the fax safety class because it no longer exists.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can you make a policy exception for me?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay, I won't force you to take a vacation.

situation: Dilbert tells his boss that company policy bars him from taking vacation until all mandatory training is done, but one required course, fax safety, has been discontinued. He asks for a policy exception so he can go on vacation. The boss twists the request into a refusal, saying he won't force Dilbert to take a vacation.
punchline: The boss pretends to grant the exception while actually denying it, reframing Dilbert's request for time off as something he is generously not imposing.
summary: An employee stuck behind an impossible training requirement asks for leniency and gets a cynical non-answer from his manager.

title: Dilbert Predicts the Future Budget

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do these cost estimates include everything?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes, because I know what happens in the future.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I didn't think I could accurately predict the future until you trusted me to put this budget together.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I thought there were too many variables to know how things will turn out.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But I defer to your superior opinion.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wait... I'm getting another message from the future.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It says to raise the software budget by nine dollars.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay, that sounds right.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Of course it does. Trust your instincts.

situation: The boss asks Dilbert whether his cost estimates cover everything, and Dilbert claims he can predict the future because the boss trusted him with the budget. He pretends to receive a message from the future telling him to add nine dollars to the software budget, and the boss readily accepts it.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically claims psychic powers to justify his budget, and the gullible boss accepts a made-up prediction as sound financial planning.
summary: Dilbert mocks a request for perfect budget accuracy by pretending to channel future knowledge, and his credulous boss goes along with it.

title: Management Is Squirrels in a Tire

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why can't we innovate as quickly as our competition?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe it's because our management is like a family of squirrels that lives inside an old tire.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can you be more specific?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's a Goodyear tire with five grey squirrels.

situation: The Boss asks at a meeting why the company can't innovate as fast as its competitors. Dilbert answers with an odd analogy comparing management to squirrels living in an old tire. When the Boss asks him to be more specific, Dilbert merely adds irrelevant details about the tire brand and the squirrel colour.
punchline: Dilbert's 'specific' elaboration adds only pointless trivia, so he never actually explains the insult, and the oblivious Boss gets no real answer about management's failings.
summary: Pressed to explain why the company lags behind rivals, an employee offers a bizarre rodent metaphor for its leadership and then backs it up with meaningless detail.

title: Dilbert Predicts Waiter's Salt Failure

transcript.speaker: Waiter
transcript.text: Here are your French fries.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gaaaa!!! I have no salt.

transcript.speaker: Waiter
transcript.text: I will bring the salt right away.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, you won't. This isn't my first time eating out!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You say you will bring salt, but you will be distracted by another table.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I will sit here in anger while I watch you do things that do not involve bringing me salt.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: As the temperature of my fries drops, my cortisol levels will increase.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In five minutes I will hate your guts and this restaurant, too.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I also need ketchup.

transcript.speaker: Waiter
transcript.text: That will take a little longer.

situation: Dilbert is served French fries and immediately complains that he has no salt. When the waiter promises to fetch it, Dilbert insists the waiter will get distracted and then narrates in advance how his anger and stress will build as the fries cool. Finally he adds that he also needs ketchup, and the waiter says that will take longer.
punchline: Dilbert's pessimistic, over-the-top prediction of poor service ends with him piling on another request, and the waiter wryly admits it will take even longer.
summary: A customer pre-emptively rages at a waiter over salt that hasn't even been delayed yet, then makes the wait worse by asking for ketchup too.

title: Micromanaging Instead of Regular Managing

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I have a meeting in a few minutes, so I only have time to do some micro-managing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wouldn't it be better to do regular managing?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't have time for the regular kind.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then wouldn't it be better to do no managing at all?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Some is better than none.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Except when less is more.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This got too complicated.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How about I just stand behind you and suggest you Google stuff?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Fine.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I wish I had some data for this.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Try googling it.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he only has time for micromanaging before a meeting, and Dilbert pokes holes in the logic until the Boss gives up because it's too complicated. The Boss then offers to just stand behind Dilbert and suggest he Google things, and Dilbert agrees. Dilbert says he wishes he had data, and the Boss's only suggestion is to google it.
punchline: The Boss's "micromanaging" amounts to useless advice anyone could give, like telling Dilbert to google things, so he adds no value as a manager.
summary: A manager with no time for real management offers lazy hovering and search-engine tips as his form of oversight.

title: Bluffing Through Hard Questions Until Escape

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sorry I'm late. Barry Dingle keeps hanging around my office and asking hard questions.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You don't know the answer to any hard questions.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's why it takes so long.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So... you just spout nonsense until he leaves?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's my go-to strategy for most situations.

situation: The Boss arrives late to a meeting with Dilbert and blames a coworker who keeps asking him hard questions. Dilbert points out that the Boss doesn't know the answers, and the Boss explains that this is why the encounters drag on. Dilbert deduces that he just talks nonsense until the person gives up, and the Boss confirms it's his usual approach.
punchline: The Boss cheerfully admits that babbling nonsense until people go away is his standard way of handling most situations.
summary: A manager reveals that his method for dealing with tough questions is to ramble meaninglessly until the questioner gives up.

title: The Virus That Gave Raises

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The Elbonian virus in our network just gave every employee a 10% raise.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You have to get rid of the virus!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If the Elbonian software is giving me a raise, and you're trying to stop it, wouldn't that make you the virus?

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that an Elbonian virus in the company network has given every employee a 10% raise. He orders Dilbert to remove the virus. Dilbert, looking at his phone, points out that the one trying to stop his raise is the real problem.
punchline: By trying to block a raise that benefits employees, the boss has become the harmful 'virus' from the employees' perspective.
summary: A manager demands a malicious program be removed after it unexpectedly boosts everyone's pay, and an employee flips the logic on him.

title: Doctor's Note Excuses Meeting Naps

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: I have a note from my doctor that says it's okay for me to sleep during meetings.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then what's the point of coming to the meeting?

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: ZZZZZ

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I think it's for the sleep.

situation: At a meeting table, a bald coworker announces that he has a doctor's note permitting him to sleep during meetings. Dilbert asks why he bothers attending, and the coworker simply falls asleep. Another colleague in a yellow shirt suggests that sleeping is the reason he comes.
punchline: Meetings are so dull and useless that people attend them mainly as a place to nap, so a medical excuse to sleep there makes attendance pointless.
summary: A man armed with medical permission to doze through meetings promptly nods off, showing that the meeting itself is merely his bedroom.

title: Wally Forgets Dilbert's Request

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can you review the project plan in the shared folder before Monday?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Absolutely.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't see you making a note to remind you later.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'll remember.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How many other tasks are you trying to remember at the same time?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: About seventy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And yet you will remember this one?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Have some faith, Wally.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My name is Dilbert.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: What were we talking about?

setting: Office cubicle area, with a brief exterior shot of the office building
situation: Dilbert asks Wally to review a project plan before Monday, and Wally promises to remember without writing a note. When Dilbert presses him, Wally admits he is juggling about seventy tasks in his head. Wally then tells himself to have faith, calling himself by the wrong name, and has completely forgotten the conversation.
punchline: Wally's confidence that he'll remember is undercut when he forgets Dilbert's name and the entire conversation within moments.
summary: A coworker who refuses to write anything down insists his memory is fine, then promptly loses track of both the request and who is asking.

title: Elbonian Hackers Ate My Report

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did you finish your assignment?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes, but Elbonian hackers deleted my report along with all of my backups.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I have no way of knowing that's true.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It was an amazing report! Better than any you've ever seen.

setting: Conference room or office meeting table
situation: The boss asks Dilbert whether he finished his assignment. Dilbert claims he did, but says Elbonian hackers deleted the report and all of his backups. When the boss points out he cannot verify that, Dilbert insists the nonexistent report was the best the boss has ever seen.
punchline: Dilbert uses an unverifiable excuse for not doing his work and then makes it even more unfalsifiable by praising a report nobody can ever check.
summary: An employee blames foreign hackers for wiping out his unfinished work and then boasts about how brilliant the vanished work was.

title: Reprogramming Robot Boyfriend To Listen

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I'm updating your boyfriend code to make you a better listener.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I want to see more nodding and less talking.

transcript.speaker: Robot Boyfriend
transcript.text: But I have so much to offer.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I'll dial back your ego, too.

setting: A desk or office, with Carol seated across from her robot
situation: A woman with big curly hair, holding a phone, tells her robot boyfriend she is updating his code so he will be a better listener. She demands more nodding and less talking, and when the robot protests that he has a lot to offer, she announces she will also turn down his ego.
punchline: Rather than seeking a partner who listens naturally, she simply programs a robot to nod, agree and have no ego, which sarcastically implies that real boyfriends cannot be relied on to do the same.
summary: A woman tweaks her robotic boyfriend's software so he stops talking and starts nodding, and then quiets his self-importance as well.

title: Consultant Blames Humans, Suggests Aliens

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our consultant has studied our corporate culture and isolated the problem.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The problem is humans. You're all selfish, rotten liars.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What kind of team-building exercise will fix that?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'd try something involving DNA and alien technology.

situation: The Boss announces that the consultant, Dogbert, has diagnosed the company's cultural problem. Dogbert bluntly says the problem is the humans themselves, who are selfish, rotten liars. When the Boss asks for a team-building fix, Dogbert recommends something involving DNA and alien technology, while Dilbert and others sit through the meeting.
punchline: The consultant's real diagnosis is that human nature is the problem, so his only solution is to replace or alter humans with alien technology.
summary: A consultant concludes that the workforce's very humanity is what's wrong with the company and proposes extraterrestrial genetic tinkering as the cure.

title: Laziness Blamed on Brain Abnormality

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My doctor says my laziness is caused by a brain abnormality.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Doesn't everyone in the world have a unique brain that determines what they do?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Is he right about that?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd have to see his brain scan. Sounds like a tumor.

setting: Conference room table during a meeting
situation: Wally sits with a coffee cup and claims his doctor attributes his laziness to a brain abnormality. Dilbert points out that everyone's unique brain determines their behavior, so this is hardly special. Alice asks if Wally's doctor is right, and Dilbert says it sounds like a tumor.
punchline: Dilbert dismisses Wally's excuse as meaningless since every brain determines behavior, then sarcastically suggests the real explanation for Wally's laziness is a tumor.
summary: A coworker tries to excuse his idleness with a medical-sounding explanation, but a colleague deflates it with a deadpan jab.

title: Negotiating Cuts With Already-Squeezed Vendors

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We need to cut our budget.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Go to all of our vendors and tell them to reduce their prices.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why would they do that for us?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tell them we'll buy from someone else unless they do.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's what we told them to get the prices we have now.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm an engineer, not a professional negotiator. Your plan has failure designed into it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your poor leadership already has me on the edge of madness. This could push me over the edge.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And I need it done by Tuesday.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert to call every vendor and demand lower prices, threatening to switch suppliers if they refuse. Dilbert points out that this threat was already used to get the current prices, and that he is an engineer, not a negotiator. The Boss ignores the warning and simply adds a Tuesday deadline.
punchline: Dilbert warns that the plan is doomed and that the Boss's leadership is driving him mad, and the Boss responds by cheerfully piling on a deadline, showing he heard none of it.
summary: A manager sends an engineer to squeeze suppliers who have already been squeezed, then brushes off every objection with a due date.

title: Body Cam Proves Coworker Repeats Himself

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: According to my body cam playback, you have repeated your point twelve times.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe you could try saying other things for a few minutes.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I wasn't expecting you to be so rude.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're not the first to make that mistake.

situation: Dilbert sits across from a coworker and consults his body camera playback, which shows the coworker has made the same point twelve times. He suggests the man try saying something else, and when the coworker complains that Dilbert is being rude, Dilbert replies that others have misjudged him in the same way.
punchline: Dilbert's deadpan reply admits he is rude while implying that people routinely underestimate how blunt he is, and that the coworker is the one who should have known better.
summary: A wearable camera gives Dilbert hard evidence that a colleague keeps repeating himself, and he answers the resulting complaint with unapologetic bluntness.

title: Anonymous Troll Uses Coworker's Phone

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I've noticed that whenever I get a tweet from an anonymous troll, you're using your phone.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That sounds like confirmation bias.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: His user name is coffeesixhairs.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Now you just sound crazy.

setting: Office break area or cubicle, with coffee cups on a desk
situation: Alice tells Wally that every time she gets an abusive tweet from an anonymous troll, he happens to be on his phone. Wally dismisses this as confirmation bias. Alice then reveals the troll's user name, which clearly refers to Wally (coffee and six hairs), and Wally pretends she is the one who is being irrational.
punchline: The troll's handle, 'coffeesixhairs', obviously describes Wally, yet he brazenly accuses Alice of sounding crazy instead of admitting he got caught.
summary: A woman suspects her coworker of being her online harasser, and when the troll's name gives him away, he shamelessly acts as if she is the paranoid one.

title: Randy's Brain Chip Replaces Dilbert

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm putting Randy on your project. He has a microchip embedded in his brain.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So ignore whatever your inferior brain tells you to do and just listen to Randy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wouldn't that make me dispensable?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We'll talk about phase 2 later.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that a coworker named Randy is joining his project because Randy has a microchip implanted in his brain. He instructs Dilbert to ignore his own judgment and just follow Randy. Dilbert realizes this makes him expendable, and the Boss deflects by saying they'll discuss phase 2 later.
punchline: The Boss's evasive 'phase 2' answer implicitly confirms that Dilbert will be replaced once the chip-enhanced Randy has taken over.
summary: A manager pairs an employee with a brain-implanted colleague and brushes off the worker's fear of being made redundant.

title: Wally's Secret Urgent Deadline Excuse

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, can you review this?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm on an urgent deadline.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What is the deadline for?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's a secret project.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why don't I know about this?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I don't know. I haven't studied your ignorance in that much detail.

situation: The Boss asks Wally to review something, and Wally claims he can't because he is on an urgent deadline. When the Boss asks what the deadline is for, Wally says it is a secret project. The Boss then wonders why he wasn't told, and Wally replies with a deadpan insult about his ignorance.
punchline: Wally dodges work with a made-up secret project, then insults the Boss by implying his cluelessness is too vast and unexplored for Wally to explain.
summary: Wally brushes off a review request by inventing a classified urgent project, then mocks his boss's cluelessness when questioned.

title: Exposition Ruins Comic Strip Punchlines

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Randy is one of the first humans with a microchip embedded in his brain.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: This new technology will change how we view the human experience.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: It will also ruin comic strips by filling them with too much exposition.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The punch line is in the fourth panel.

setting: An office or desk setting, with a man and Dogbert seated at a table against a green wall
situation: A narrator introduces Randy, a man with a brain microchip, and explains how the technology will transform human experience. In the third panel the narration says it will ruin comic strips with exposition, and Dogbert points out that the punch line is in the fourth panel. The strip only has three panels, so the joke never arrives.
punchline: The strip uses so many panels on exposition that the punch line gets pushed into a fourth panel that does not exist, making the strip an example of the problem it describes.
summary: A comic about brain implants burns through its panels on setup until a character admits the joke would have come one panel too late.

title: Health Monitor Declares Coworker Brain-Impaired

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: According to your employee health monitor, your lack of sleep last night is hampering your mental functions.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let's end the meeting and try again when your brain is working better.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I don't understand.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That is consistent with the data.

setting: Office meeting room, with an exterior shot of an office building in the middle panel
situation: Dilbert checks a handheld device showing a coworker's employee health monitor data and announces that the coworker's lack of sleep is impairing his thinking. He ends the meeting and suggests trying again when the coworker's brain is working better. When the coworker says he doesn't understand, Dilbert replies that this fits the data.
punchline: The coworker's confusion at being told his brain is impaired is treated by Dilbert as proof the monitor is right, a deadpan insult backed by surveillance data.
summary: A sleep-tracking wearable gives Dilbert an excuse to cut a meeting short and gently insult a confused colleague's mental state.

title: Creatively Charging Expenses to Ted

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ted is complaining that you charged your expenses to his project.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You told me to be creative because you forgot to fund my project.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I wasn't expecting you to do THAT.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's what makes it creative. I looked it up.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that Ted is upset because Dilbert billed his expenses to Ted's project. Dilbert explains that the Boss told him to be creative after forgetting to fund his project. When the Boss says he didn't expect that, Dilbert says the unexpectedness is exactly what makes it creative.
punchline: Dilbert turns the Boss's vague instruction to 'be creative' into a defense for misallocating costs, using the dictionary definition of creativity as justification.
summary: Left without funding, Dilbert follows his boss's call for creativity by quietly billing his costs to a colleague's budget, then defends it with a definition.

title: Forgotten Project Budget Fix

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't see my project in the new budget.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oh, right. I forgot all about you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That sounds easy to fix.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yup. My problem will be solved as soon as you leave.

situation: Dilbert holds a tablet and tells his boss that his project is missing from the new budget. The boss casually admits he forgot about Dilbert, so Dilbert offers to fix it. The boss replies that the problem will be solved when Dilbert leaves his office.
punchline: The boss's idea of fixing the budget oversight is simply getting rid of Dilbert, since his own problem is being bothered by the person he forgot.
summary: A neglected employee raises a funding omission, and his manager treats the employee's departure from the room as the whole solution.

title: Overbooked Flight Re-Accommodation Means Ejection

transcript.speaker: Airline Employee
transcript.text: The flight is overbooked and our algorithm selected you for re-accommodation.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What exactly does "re-accommodation" mean in this context?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oh.

setting: Inside an airplane cabin, then on the airport tarmac
situation: An airline employee tells Dilbert, seated on a full flight, that an algorithm has chosen him for re-accommodation because the flight is overbooked. Dilbert asks what the term means, and in the last panel he lies face down on the tarmac beside his suitcase while the plane flies off. He has been forcibly removed and dumped outside.
punchline: Airline euphemism "re-accommodation" actually means being violently thrown off the plane, a jab at the 2017 incident of a passenger dragged off an overbooked flight.
summary: A passenger learns the hard way that the airline's polite jargon for bumping him from an oversold flight involves a rough landing outside the aircraft.

title: Demoted for Coffee-Obsessed Ideas

transcript.speaker: Bald Engineer
transcript.text: My leadership job didn't last long. I got demoted back to engineering.

transcript.speaker: Bald Engineer
transcript.text: I guess they realized all of my ideas are about coffee.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've noticed that too.

transcript.speaker: Bald Engineer
transcript.text: Watch out for my coffee drone behind you.

situation: A bald, bespectacled engineer carrying a cup of coffee tells Dilbert that his brief stint in leadership ended with a demotion back to engineering. He guesses management noticed that all his ideas were about coffee. Dilbert agrees, and the engineer promptly warns him about a coffee-delivering drone flying behind him.
punchline: The engineer's coffee obsession is so complete that even while explaining why he was demoted for it, he's demonstrating yet another coffee invention, a coffee drone.
summary: A demoted manager admits his every idea revolves around coffee, then proves it by unleashing a coffee-carrying drone.

title: Tech Companies Hijack Everyone's Attention

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I wanted to be productive this week, but the big tech companies didn't let me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's ridiculous. They can't stop people from doing work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Actually, they can.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Their business models depend on interrupting users with ads, and apps, and mindless entertainment.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Until recently, humans could resist these distractions.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But now the tech companies are using science to make their apps addictive. They learned how to hijack our brains.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What started as simple entertainment evolved into military-grade mind control.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you hear any of that?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Any of what?

situation: In a meeting, Dilbert explains to his boss and colleagues that big tech companies have made their apps addictive using science, effectively hijacking people's brains and preventing productivity. He rants about it growing into mind control. In the last panel, his colleagues are staring at their phones and haven't heard a word.
punchline: Dilbert's warning about addictive technology falls on deaf ears because his audience is too absorbed in their phones to listen, proving his point.
summary: A passionate speech about brain-hijacking apps goes unheard by listeners glued to their screens.

title: Boss Wants Office to Escape Complaints

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: The employees are complaining because our new open office plan has too many distractions.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You want to go back to cubicles?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: No, I just need a private office so I can't hear them complaining.

situation: A coworker holding a coffee tells the boss that employees are complaining about distractions in the new open office layout. The boss, sipping coffee, asks if the coworker wants to return to cubicles. The coworker says no and reveals he only wants a private office to avoid hearing the complaints.
punchline: The coworker's solution to employee complaints about open-office distractions is not fixing the problem but getting a private office for himself so he can ignore the complainers.
summary: Rather than address staff gripes about a noisy open floor plan, a manager just wants a private room to tune them out.

title: Nineteen Pages of Rabies Warnings

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Alice, can you review the product warning I wrote?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: "Don't start a fight with a rabid raccoon while using this product."

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You have nineteen pages of rabies warnings.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I was surprised at how many animals there are.

situation: A coworker hands Alice a draft product warning to review. Alice reads it and finds it includes an absurd caution about fighting a rabid raccoon, and that it runs to nineteen pages just on rabies. The coworker calmly says they were surprised by how many animals there are.
punchline: The warning writer has exhaustively listed every animal that could carry rabies in an absurdly over-the-top attempt at liability protection, and seems to think this is a reasonable use of nineteen pages.
summary: A colleague's product warning is so exhaustive about rabid animals that it fills nearly twenty pages of absurd legal caution.

title: Brain Chip Turns Speech Into Moo

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I am one of the first humans to have a microchip embedded in my brain.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm so smart that you "normals" are like livestock to me now.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We can't be THAT different.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: My chip translates everything you say to "moo."

situation: A coworker boasts at a meeting that he has a microchip implanted in his brain. He claims he is so smart that ordinary people seem like livestock to him. When Dilbert objects that they can't be that different, he reveals his chip converts everything Dilbert says into mooing.
punchline: The coworker's condescension is so extreme that his implant literally treats his colleagues as cattle, proving his arrogant claim.
summary: A man with a brain implant brags that he sees his coworkers as cattle, then shows his chip hears their words as mooing.

title: Programming the Robot to Fight Better

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our robot viciously attacked me. I was barely able to fight him off.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You know what you need to do.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm programming you to fight better.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Thanks. I'm not a good finisher.

situation: The Boss, looking rumpled and scratched, complains to Dilbert that the company robot attacked him and he barely survived. He tells Dilbert that he knows what needs to be done, expecting the robot to be fixed or shut down. Instead, Dilbert connects a tablet to the robot and programs it to fight better, and the robot gratefully admits it is a poor finisher.
punchline: Dilbert interprets the Boss's vague order in the worst possible way, making the violent robot a better fighter, which the robot thanks him for, since it failed to finish off the Boss.
summary: After a robot nearly mauls his boss, an engineer responds to a vague instruction by upgrading the machine's combat skills instead of removing the threat.

title: The Red Folder Work Illusion

transcript.speaker: Balding Coworker
transcript.text: It is easier to create the illusion of work than it is to do actual work.

transcript.speaker: Balding Coworker
transcript.text: That's why I carry this red folder with me wherever I go.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Can you attend a design meeting at two?

transcript.speaker: Balding Coworker
transcript.text: Ooh... I wish I could, but I'm behind schedule on the red file.

situation: A balding coworker with spiky hair explains to a colleague at a table that faking work is easier than doing real work, and says he carries a red folder everywhere to create that impression. Later, another coworker asks him to attend a design meeting, and he holds up the red folder and uses it as an excuse to decline.
punchline: He immediately demonstrates the trick by using the prop red folder as a fake workload to dodge a meeting.
summary: A man shows off his strategy of carrying a prop folder to look busy, then uses it to wriggle out of a meeting invitation.

title: Boss Cancels Nonexistent Food Service

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've decided to cancel our food service to save money.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We don't have a food service. We all bring our own food and keep it in the break room refrigerator.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've been eating the food in there for seven years.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd keep that to myself if I were you.

situation: At a meeting, the Boss announces he is cancelling the company food service to save money. Dilbert points out that no such service exists and that employees bring their own food to the break room fridge. The Boss then reveals he has been eating that food for seven years, thinking it was a company-provided service.
punchline: The Boss unwittingly confesses to seven years of eating his coworkers' lunches because he assumed it was a free company perk.
summary: A manager threatens to axe a company perk that never existed, accidentally admitting he has been helping himself to everyone else's packed lunches.

title: Unverifiable Excuse Is a Good One

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Did you add the new feature yet?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: No, I had to fix a critical bug in the platform first.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have no way to verify that claim.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That's why it's a good one.

setting: Conference room table during a meeting
situation: A coworker asks Wally whether he has added the new feature yet. Wally claims he had to fix a critical bug in the platform first. Dilbert says he can't verify that claim, and Wally cheerfully replies that this is exactly why it makes a good excuse.
punchline: Wally admits his excuse is effective precisely because nobody can check whether it is true, revealing he is likely just avoiding work.
summary: A slacking engineer proudly explains that his claimed bug fix is the perfect alibi because no one can confirm it.

title: Keeping Employees Narrowly Miserable

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The one called Dilbert is showing signs of happiness at work.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That means we can give him more work and he won't quit. Excellent.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is anyone else exhibiting signs of unauthorized happiness?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: No. Everyone else is in the narrow band of misery you want them to be in.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: If they were any happier, it would mean you're overpaying them.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: If they were any less happy, they would take their own lives.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: If you don't hear any laughing or screaming, it means you're doing something right.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What about moans?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Moans are ideal. That's the sweet spot.

situation: Catbert, the HR director, reports to the Boss that Dilbert is showing signs of happiness. The Boss decides to pile on more work, then asks whether anyone else is happy. Catbert explains the ideal level of employee misery, between overpaid and suicidal.
punchline: Management's goal is to keep employees miserable enough to be cheap but not so miserable they quit or die, with moaning being the optimal indicator.
summary: An HR cat advises his boss on calibrating staff unhappiness so workers stay productive, underpaid and just short of breaking.

title: Dilbert Pours Out Misery, Coworker Ignores

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: How's work?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, since you asked...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's like being trapped in a garbage compactor and no one can hear me scream.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: All my hopes and dreams have died, along with my immune system and my dignity.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The only thing keeping me alive is that food tastes good.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I tried to escape into my imagination, but I learned I don't have one.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My life has no meaning. Each second is a slow-motion ordeal.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why do I get the feeling you weren't listening to any of that?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: My day was good too.

situation: A coworker holding a coffee cup asks Dilbert how work is going. Dilbert answers with a long, escalating litany of despair about his job and life. The coworker, glancing at a phone, has clearly tuned out and responds with an irrelevant remark.
punchline: The coworker asked 'How's work?' as empty small talk and wasn't listening, so he responds to Dilbert's desperate misery by saying his own day was good too.
summary: A casual greeting unleashes a torrent of existential gloom from Dilbert, which his distracted colleague completely fails to register.

title: Cubicles Like a Carton of Eggs

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Have you ever noticed that our cubicles are organized exactly like a carton of eggs?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: That feels right because eggs go rotten quickly, too.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I already hate my own analogy.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Eggs are overly sensitive, too.

situation: Dilbert remarks to a coworker that the office cubicles are laid out just like an egg carton. The coworker extends the analogy by pointing out that eggs rot quickly, and then that they are overly sensitive. Dilbert grows annoyed because the analogy keeps being turned into insults he now regrets starting.
punchline: Dilbert's casual analogy is stretched by his coworker into a series of jabs, so he ends up disliking his own comparison, implying that office workers are fragile and quick to burn out.
summary: A passing observation about desks resembling an egg carton gets extended by a coworker until the person who made it regrets it.

title: Robot Asks About Afterlife, Gets Darkness

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: What kind of afterlife are we looking at here?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your meaningless existence will be punctuated by an eternity of darkness.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Thanks for sparing my feelings!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sorry. I usually delete those first.

setting: Dilbert's workshop or lab, at a workbench with tools
situation: Dilbert is tinkering with a small robot-like device at his workbench while a larger robot stands beside him and asks what kind of afterlife robots can expect. Dilbert answers bluntly that its existence is meaningless and ends in eternal darkness. The robot sarcastically thanks him for sparing its feelings, and Dilbert explains he usually deletes feelings first.
punchline: The robot's sarcastic thanks is met with Dilbert's deadpan admission that he normally removes a machine's feelings before delivering harsh truths, so he was being unusually tactless this time.
summary: A robot looking for reassurance about life after death receives a bleak answer from its creator, who then admits he normally strips out emotions before such talks.

title: Catbert's Confidential Complaint Non-Response

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Have you done anything to address my complaints about management?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I can't tell you about any confidential conversations I have with management.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: So... should I just hope for the best?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: That sounds like a solid plan.

situation: An employee asks Catbert, the HR director, whether he has done anything about her complaints regarding management. Catbert says he cannot disclose any confidential conversations with management. When she asks if she should just hope for the best, he agrees that is a good plan.
punchline: HR hides behind confidentiality to avoid ever doing or revealing anything about complaints, leaving employees with nothing but hope.
summary: A worker seeks action on her complaints and the HR cat deflects with confidentiality, then cheerfully endorses her wishful thinking.

title: Scrum Master Is The Distraction

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: As the designated agile scrum, it is my job to remove any distractions so you can work.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Great. Remove yourself from my cubicle and you've done your job.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That seems too easy.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: And yet you can't do it.

situation: Dilbert stands in a coworker's cubicle and announces that, as the designated agile scrum, his job is to remove distractions so she can work. She replies that he can accomplish this by simply leaving her cubicle. Dilbert says that seems too easy, and she retorts that he still can't manage it.
punchline: The biggest distraction in the cubicle is the scrum master himself, and he is so oblivious to it that he can't even do the one simple thing that would fulfill his role.
summary: A self-important scrum facilitator insists he exists to eliminate interruptions, yet he is the very interruption his coworker wants gone.

title: Wally Compares Himself to Gandhi

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, your political opinions are making your co-workers uncomfortable.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That is exactly what people said to Gandhi.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You are nothing like Gandhi.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Was he a little bald guy who didn't have a real job?

situation: The Boss tells Wally that his political opinions are making his co-workers uncomfortable. Wally defends himself by claiming people said the same thing to Gandhi. When the Boss insists Wally is nothing like Gandhi, Wally replies by describing Gandhi in a way that matches himself.
punchline: Wally twists the Boss's rebuttal into a joke at his own expense, describing Gandhi as a little bald guy without a real job, which is exactly how Wally fits the comparison, since he is lazy and employed in name only.
summary: A manager's complaint about an employee's opinions is met with a grandiose historical comparison that the employee deflates with a self-deprecating description.

title: Wristband Snitches On Fake Sick Day

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I can't come to work today. I'm totally sick.

transcript.speaker: HR Representative
transcript.text: According to your employee health monitor, you're not sick at all.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Stupid snitch!!!

setting: Wally's bedroom and an office desk
situation: An employee in bed phones in to say he is too sick to work. A woman at her office desk replies that his employee health monitor shows he is perfectly healthy. He angrily curses the wristband that gave him away.
punchline: The employee-issued health tracker on his wrist exposes his fake sick day, so he ends up scolding the device for telling on him.
summary: A worker pretending to be ill is caught out by the company-issued wearable that reports his vital signs to the office.

title: Trusting Your Gut About Underperformance

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: People tell me you're underperforming.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you hear it from anyone credible?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, but I know it's true because my gut tells me it's true.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm curious where you stick your head to listen to your gut?

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that people say he is underperforming. Dilbert asks if the source was credible, and the Boss admits it wasn't but insists his gut feeling confirms it. Dilbert responds with an insult about how the Boss manages to listen to his own gut.
punchline: Dilbert insinuates that the Boss has his head up his own rear end, since that is the only way he could listen to his gut, mocking decisions based on gut feeling instead of evidence.
summary: A boss accuses an employee of poor performance based on hearsay and intuition, and the employee fires back with a crude jab at the boss's judgment.

title: Terrible Advice About Presenting to CEO

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm nervous because I need to make a presentation to our CEO. Do you have any advice?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Don't make eye contact with him. He hates that.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You have made things far worse!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: He also flies into a rage when he hears the word "the."

situation: Dilbert tells a coworker holding a coffee cup that he is nervous about presenting to the CEO and asks for advice. The coworker gives him a prohibition about eye contact, then, after Dilbert complains that this made things worse, adds another absurd and unavoidable trigger for the CEO's temper.
punchline: The coworker's 'advice' only increases Dilbert's anxiety, and the second tip, that the CEO rages at the word 'the', is impossible to follow and makes the presentation hopeless.
summary: A nervous presenter seeks tips for addressing the chief executive and instead receives a list of increasingly impossible warnings about the boss's temper.

title: Wise or Lazy: Wally's Contentment

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you ever want more out of life?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That's how losers think.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: If you always want more, you can never be happy with what you have.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't tell if you're wise or lazy.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I know. It took me years to find that sweet spot.

setting: Office break area or conference table with coffee cups
situation: Dilbert asks Wally whether he ever wants more out of life. Wally dismisses ambition as something losers do and argues that wanting more prevents happiness. Dilbert admits he can't tell if Wally is wise or lazy, and Wally agrees the ambiguity is deliberate.
punchline: Wally has deliberately cultivated a lifestyle where his laziness is indistinguishable from enlightened contentment, and he is proud of having perfected that ambiguity.
summary: A coworker's philosophy of never wanting more turns out to be a carefully refined blend of wisdom and sloth.

title: Sleeping on a Baby Changing Table

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need a raise because the cost of living around here is too high.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Stop being greedy. I pay you plenty.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't even afford to rent an apartment.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Get some roommates.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't afford that either.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've been sleeping on a baby changing table in a public restroom.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And the janitor has been charging me $3,000 per month for that.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How wide is the baby changing table?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Not wide enough for a roommate.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, I'm out of ideas.

setting: Office, the Boss's desk, plus an exterior shot of an office building
situation: Dilbert asks the Boss for a raise because the cost of living is too high. The Boss dismisses him and suggests roommates, but Dilbert says he is so broke he sleeps on a baby changing table in a public restroom and pays the janitor $3,000 a month for it. The Boss only asks how wide the table is, hoping to squeeze in a roommate.
punchline: The Boss responds to an employee's absurd poverty not by offering a raise but by trying to find a cheaper housing workaround, then gives up having refused to pay more.
summary: A worker pleading for more pay is so squeezed by living costs that he lodges in a restroom, yet his manager would rather brainstorm cramped living arrangements than open the wallet.

title: Robot Replacing Coworker By Doing Nothing

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: I wonder whose job I'll take first.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You could never do my job.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: I'm doing it right now.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You're not doing anything.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Right. Let that sink in.

setting: Conference room table, with an exterior shot of the office building in the final panel
situation: At a meeting, a robot wonders aloud whose job it will take first. A coworker with swept-up hair insists the robot could never do their job, and the robot replies that it is doing that job right now. The coworker points out the robot is doing nothing, and the robot tells them to let that sink in.
punchline: The coworker's job amounts to doing nothing, so a robot that does nothing can already replace them perfectly.
summary: A machine proves it can replace a colleague by exposing that the colleague's work consists of nothing at all.

title: Virus Fixes Nonsensical Mission Statement

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The Elbonian virus scrambled our mission statement into nonsense.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: No, that's our actual mission statement.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why does it look so different?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: The virus fixed the grammar and punctuation.

situation: Dilbert tells Alice, who is sitting at her desk, that a virus from Elbonia has scrambled the company's mission statement into nonsense. Alice looks at it on his phone and says that gibberish is the real mission statement. Dilbert wonders why it looks different, and she explains the virus corrected its grammar and punctuation.
punchline: The company's genuine mission statement is so meaningless that it looks like computer-corrupted gibberish, and the only thing the virus did was improve its grammar.
summary: A supposedly corrupted corporate statement turns out to be the genuine article, which the malware has only tidied up.

title: Dilbert Enters the Jargon Matrix

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dilbert enters the Jargon Matrix to save Asok

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Nothing in this dimension is real.

transcript.speaker: Asok
