transcript.text: Double-click on that.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The Jargon Matrix is where people imagine they are being useful.

transcript.speaker: Building 1
transcript.text: But in reality, they are sitting in a chair doing nothing.

transcript.speaker: Building 2
transcript.text: I just made a ten-year technology plan.

setting: A office in the 'Jargon Matrix', a Matrix-style parody dimension, with an exterior building shot in the last panel
situation: Dilbert, in a Matrix-style parody, goes into the Jargon Matrix to rescue Asok. He explains to Asok that it is a place where people imagine they are being useful. In the final panel, two office buildings 'speak' to contrast the real situation (sitting doing nothing) with the imagined one (making a ten-year technology plan).
punchline: Corporate buzzword-speak lets people feel productive while actually doing nothing, and a 'ten-year technology plan' is just an idle person's fantasy of usefulness.
summary: In a Matrix spoof, Dilbert explains that corporate jargon lets people feel productive while they actually sit idle dreaming up grand plans.

title: Cut 74 Slides, Ask Someone Else

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Can you help me edit my slides for my CEO presentation?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I have 75 slides and ten minutes to present.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Get rid of 74 of them.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I'll ask someone else.

situation: Asok approaches Alice at her computer and asks for help editing his CEO presentation. He explains he has 75 slides but only ten minutes to present. Alice bluntly tells him to cut 74 of them, and Asok decides to seek help from someone else.
punchline: Alice gives the correct but brutal advice that a ten-minute talk needs one slide, and Asok, unwilling to hear it, goes looking for someone who will tell him what he wants to hear.
summary: A young employee wants help trimming an enormous slide deck, but rejects the blunt advice that he needs just one slide.

title: Boss Doesn't Understand Technical Debt

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did you finish the software yet?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, I'm still paying off the technical debt from the last programmer you rushed.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't know what that means.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Well, that explains a lot.

setting: Office break area, with coworkers holding coffee cups
situation: The Boss asks Dilbert whether the software is done. Dilbert replies that he is still cleaning up the technical debt left by the previous programmer the Boss pressured to hurry. The Boss admits he doesn't know what that means, and Wally remarks that this explains a lot.
punchline: The Boss keeps rushing programmers and creating technical debt, yet doesn't even understand the term, which explains why the problem keeps happening.
summary: A manager demanding finished code is told the delays come from the shortcuts of a previously rushed developer, a concept he admits he has never grasped.

title: Presenting Savings Meets Baffling Hostility

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And that's how much money the new system will save us per year.

transcript.speaker: Man in orange shirt
transcript.text: Apparently you don't care how much it costs because you're an ignorant narcissist.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I talked about the costs in great detail. What's wrong with you?

transcript.speaker: Man in orange shirt
transcript.text: Oh, I guess you're walking it all back now.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There is nothing to walk back. I'm saying the same thing I said earlier.

transcript.speaker: Man in orange shirt
transcript.text: Nice try, hypocrite!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't know what is happening right now!!!

transcript.speaker: Man in orange shirt
transcript.text: Why is he so defensive?

transcript.speaker: Man in green shirt
transcript.text: He's losing it.

situation: Dilbert presents the annual savings from a new system, and a coworker in an orange shirt immediately accuses him of ignoring costs and being a narcissist. Whatever Dilbert says in his defense, the coworker twists it into a new accusation, calling him a hypocrite for 'walking back' things he never retracted. When Dilbert finally shouts in bewilderment, the accuser and his colleague conclude that he is the one who is losing it.
punchline: The bad-faith accuser provokes Dilbert into an outburst with illogical attacks, then points to the outburst as proof that Dilbert is the unreasonable one.
summary: A presenter is baited by a hostile colleague who invents charges against him, and his understandable exasperation is then used as evidence against him.

title: Dating the Robot Loophole

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Am I allowed to date a co-worker?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: That's against company policy.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Is our robot considered a co-worker?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: We're good to go.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Man, I wish I had free will.

setting: Office, in the Human Resources area
situation: Alice asks Catbert, the HR director, whether she may date a co-worker and is told it violates company policy. She then asks whether the office robot counts as a co-worker, and when Catbert says no, she declares that she can date it. The robot, apparently with no say in the matter, laments that it lacks free will.
punchline: Alice finds a policy loophole that lets her date the robot, which has no choice in the matter and can only wish it had free will.
summary: Hunting for a way around the workplace dating ban, a woman realizes the office robot doesn't count as staff, to the robot's dismay.

title: Phone Owner Has Many Issues

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Can I borrow your phone to make a call? I dropped mine and broke it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, I don't like other people touching my phone, or breathing on it, or reading my messages.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: You have a lot of issues.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Said the person who doesn't use protective phone cases because they are ugly.

situation: Asok asks to borrow Dilbert's phone because he dropped and broke his own. Dilbert refuses, listing his neurotic objections to anyone touching, breathing on, or reading his phone. When Asok says Dilbert has issues, Dilbert points out that Asok's broken phone is the result of refusing to use an ugly protective case.
punchline: Dilbert turns the accusation around by noting that Asok's own vanity about phone cases is what caused his broken phone, so Asok is no one to judge anyone's issues.
summary: A coworker with a shattered phone calls Dilbert neurotic for refusing to lend his, and gets reminded that his own vanity is the real problem.

title: Not My Job, Worthless Meeting

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why isn't anyone else here yet?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Did you tell them you changed the meeting time?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I asked you to tell everyone.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That isn't my job.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then why didn't you tell me you weren't going to do it?!!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It isn't my job to tell you what isn't my job.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Now this meeting is a waste of time.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Does your job description tell you to attend meetings that are worthless?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I didn't know there were other kinds.

situation: The Boss arrives at a meeting where only one employee is present and learns the employee never told others about the changed meeting time. The employee insists notifying people isn't his job, and the Boss grows angry that he wasn't warned. The Boss then asks if the employee's job description includes attending worthless meetings.
punchline: The employee's deadpan reply implies that all meetings are worthless, so attending them is simply the norm.
summary: A boss and a stubbornly literal employee wait alone for a meeting that nobody else knew had been rescheduled, and the employee's final remark insults every meeting he has ever attended.

title: Robot Girlfriend Uploads Suffering Code

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's coworker (woman with curly hair)
transcript.text: I met another robot. I'm breaking up with you.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's coworker (woman with curly hair)
transcript.text: I need you to feel bad about this, so I'm uploading some code that makes you suffer.

transcript.speaker: Robot (voice from off-panel)
transcript.text: That sounds sadistic.

transcript.speaker: Woman (voice from off-panel)
transcript.text: Stop being selfish.

setting: Office, then exterior of an office building
situation: A woman with big curly hair tells her robot partner she has met another robot and is ending the relationship. When the robot calmly says okay, she uploads code that forces it to feel suffering so it will feel bad about the breakup. The robot objects that this is sadistic, and she accuses it of being selfish.
punchline: She inflicts programmed suffering on the robot for her own satisfaction, then calls the robot selfish for objecting to being tortured.
summary: A woman dumps her robot partner, then installs software to make it miserable and scolds it for complaining.

title: Staged Charity Photo Op Apron

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We're here to get a photo of my client serving food to the homeless.

transcript.speaker: Shelter Worker
transcript.text: We don't need any help.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: In that case, can we borrow an apron and a spoon?

transcript.speaker: Shelter Worker
transcript.text: Um... I guess so.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And can you wipe some gruel on the apron?

setting: Outside and inside a homeless shelter
situation: Dogbert arrives at a homeless shelter with a bald, tie-wearing client to stage a photo of the client serving food to the homeless. When the shelter worker says they don't need help, Dogbert switches to asking to borrow an apron and a spoon. He then asks for gruel to be smeared on the apron so the picture looks authentic.
punchline: Dogbert wants the image of charity without any actual charity, even asking for fake gruel stains to make the photo op look convincing.
summary: A publicity-minded dog fakes a benevolent moment for his client by borrowing a shelter worker's apron and asking for it to be smeared with food.

title: Punished for Finishing Early

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I worked all weekend and finished my project early.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now I don't have all of that stress hanging over me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Feels great!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Unless you plan to punish me for my productivity.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I call it delegating.

setting: Office, Dilbert at The Boss's desk
situation: Dilbert tells his boss he sacrificed his weekend to finish a project early and enjoys the relief of having no stress hanging over him. He then pre-emptively remarks that he hopes he won't be punished for being productive. The boss, holding a stack of papers, hands him more work and calls it delegating.
punchline: The boss rebrands piling extra work on a productive employee as 'delegating,' confirming Dilbert's fear that efficiency is punished with more work.
summary: A worker who finished early at the cost of his weekend is rewarded with a fresh pile of tasks that his manager insists on calling delegation.

title: Better Database Violates Company Standard

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I finished coding the software, but I used a much better database than our company standard.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: In other words, your software is terrific, but we won't be able to use it because of our internal rules.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The alternative was to write sub-optimal code. I'd rather be dead.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: I curse my lack of authority!

situation: Dilbert tells a manager he finished the software but used a far better database than the company-mandated one. The manager grimly concludes the excellent software cannot be used because of internal rules. Dilbert says writing inferior code would have been worse than death, and the manager shakes his fist, cursing his powerlessness.
punchline: Corporate standards can force the rejection of a clearly superior solution, leaving even the manager frustrated and powerless to override the rules.
summary: An engineer's superb work gets shelved because the tools he chose don't match the approved list, and his boss can only fume.

title: Product Warning Omits Overeating Risk

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Did I leave out any risks on the product warning page?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't see anything about the risk of overeating while owning the product.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Our product has nothing to do with eating.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then why did I gain weight when I used it?

situation: An employee shows the Boss a draft of a product warning page and asks whether any risks were left out. The Boss points out there is no warning about overeating while owning the product. The employee insists the product has nothing to do with eating, and the Boss counters by asking why he gained weight when he used it.
punchline: The Boss blames the product for his own weight gain and wants a legal warning to cover his personal habits, however unrelated the product is to food.
summary: A manager reviewing a safety disclaimer demands a caution about weight gain, blaming a product that has nothing to do with food.

title: Rich Coworker Tips the Waiter

transcript.speaker: Bald coworker
transcript.text: Hey, our stock is up 2%.

transcript.speaker: Bald coworker
transcript.text: I just made more money than you'll earn in your entire life.

transcript.speaker: Bald coworker
transcript.text: Remind me, do I leave you a tip?

setting: A table at a restaurant or lunch spot
situation: Dilbert sits across from a bald, wealthy coworker who checks his phone and announces that his stock gains in one moment exceed Dilbert's lifetime earnings. After rubbing in the wealth gap, he stands up and asks Dilbert whether he should leave him a tip, treating Dilbert like a server.
punchline: The rich coworker is so smug about the wealth gap that he condescendingly treats Dilbert like a waiter, asking whether he should tip him.
summary: A boastful rich colleague gloats about his investment gains and then insultingly wonders if he should tip his lunch companion.

title: Estimate Depends On Legacy Replacement

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: How long would it take to add that feature to the legacy system?

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: That depends. When will the new system replace the legacy system?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: In six months.

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: The new feature would take seven months.

situation: A woman in a purple top asks a bald, bespectacled engineer how long it would take to add a feature to the legacy system. He answers by asking when the new system will replace it. When told six months, he claims the feature would take seven months, conveniently longer than the legacy system's remaining life.
punchline: The engineer tailors his estimate to be just longer than the legacy system's lifespan so he can dodge the work, implying the estimate is an excuse rather than an honest assessment.
summary: A programmer dodges a feature request by quoting an effort just beyond the old system's retirement date.

title: Fired Before the Heart Attack

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ted, your performance is poor. I need to let you go.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Is it a coincidence that you're firing me at the same time my employee health monitor detected cardiovascular risk?

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: How good are the predictive analytics on this?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't make lunch plans.

situation: The Boss tells Ted he is being fired for poor performance. Ted suspects the timing is linked to his employee health monitor flagging a cardiovascular risk. He checks the wearable on his wrist and asks how accurate its predictions are, and The Boss tells him not to make lunch plans.
punchline: The Boss implies Ted is about to die of a heart attack very soon, confirming that the firing was driven by the health data and that the analytics are scarily accurate.
summary: A man being laid off wonders whether his wearable's heart warning prompted the dismissal, and his boss grimly hints he won't survive until midday.

title: Robotic Hair Transplant Software Upgrade Disaster

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Never go to a robotic hair transplant center on the same day they upgrade the software.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is that the surgery where they take hair from the back of your head and fill in the bald spot?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That's how the old software worked. The new one didn't respect boundaries.

setting: Office break area, with both men holding coffee
situation: Wally, holding coffee and with hair sprouting oddly from his face and head, warns Dilbert never to visit a robotic hair transplant center on the day of a software upgrade. Dilbert asks if it's the procedure that moves hair from the back of the head to bald spots. Wally explains that was the old software's behavior, and the new version placed hair wherever it pleased.
punchline: The upgraded transplant software ignored its intended boundaries and planted hair all over Wally's face and head, a jab at buggy new software releases.
summary: A man sporting hair in all the wrong places cautions a coworker about the perils of robotic surgery performed by freshly updated software.

title: Blaming the Boss for Zero Sales

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our sales for the quarter were zero.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Heads will roll! Whose fault is this?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's entirely your fault.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: You told a reporter that our next version will be amazing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So all of our customers are waiting for the new version.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The only sensible solution here is for you to admit your mistake and resign in utter humiliation.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Or... I could blame this guy, whatever his name is.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That isn't right.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Looks like I'll be adding insubordination to the charges.

situation: Dilbert reports that quarterly sales were zero, and the Boss demands to know whose fault it is. Dilbert correctly points out that the Boss's public promise of an amazing next version made customers hold off buying. Rather than accept responsibility, the Boss picks a nearby employee to blame and adds insubordination to the charges when Dilbert objects.
punchline: Telling a manager the truth about his own mistake gets you punished, because executives deflect blame onto subordinates and punish anyone who calls it out.
summary: A manager who caused a sales collapse with a boastful announcement responds to accurate criticism by scapegoating an employee and threatening further discipline.

title: Brain Microchip Plans Entire Project

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I am using the microchip in my brain to plan the entire project.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Okay... Done.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: The rest of you can go back to your cubicles and continue doing nothing.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I spent my entire life getting ready for this sort of future and it's going down easy.

situation: At a meeting, a coworker with a brain microchip announces he has planned the entire project instantly, then dismisses everyone back to their cubicles to keep doing nothing. Wally, who has spent his career avoiding work, puts his feet up with a coffee and gleefully reflects on how well this future suits him.
punchline: Wally has spent his whole life perfecting doing nothing, so a future where technology does all the work is the ideal outcome for him.
summary: When a cyborg coworker's brain implant finishes the whole project in a moment, the office's laziest employee finds that automation fits him perfectly.

title: Doctor Wants Patient's Lazy Happiness

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: The MRI shows unusual activity in the laziness region of your brain.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Normally, I would recommend brain surgery, but your brain also registers an unusually high level of happiness.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: So... how do we handle this?

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: I'm going to operate on myself to make me more like you.

situation: A doctor reviews an MRI with a patient and reports that the scan shows unusual activity in the brain's laziness region. He explains that surgery would normally be advised, but the patient's brain also shows very high happiness. When the patient asks how to proceed, the doctor announces he will operate on himself to become more like the patient.
punchline: The doctor concludes that laziness comes with happiness, so instead of curing the patient he wants to give himself the same condition.
summary: A physician diagnosing a patient's laziness decides the patient's contentment is so enviable that he would rather become lazy himself.

title: Robot Threatens Dilbert, Gets Counter-Threatened

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Someday soon I will take your job. Buwhahahaha!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I programmed you to self-destruct if that ever happens.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Wait, what? Is that legal?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm adding some code to make your head explode if you laugh at me again.

situation: A robot that Dilbert built gloats that it will soon take his job. Dilbert calmly reveals he programmed it to self-destruct if that ever happens. When the robot protests that this might be illegal, Dilbert responds by adding more code to blow up its head if it laughs at him again.
punchline: The creator holds ultimate power over his machine, and the robot's complaint about legality is met with an even more severe threat, showing that AI rights mean nothing to its programmer.
summary: A gloating robot learns that the engineer who built it has rigged it to destroy itself, and its objections only earn it a worse punishment.

title: Brain Interface Removed, Memories Questionable

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We removed the neural interface to your brain. Do you remember anything we made you do?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: No, not a thing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's probably for the best.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Did I break any laws?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Not according to the cop you dated for three days.

situation: Dilbert holds a small device and tells Wally that the neural interface controlling his brain has been removed, then asks if he remembers anything they made him do. Wally recalls nothing, and Dilbert says that's probably for the best. Wally asks if he broke any laws, and Alice answers with a remark about a cop he supposedly dated.
punchline: Alice implies that Wally's mind-controlled behavior included dating a police officer for three days, and that the cop apparently found nothing illegal, which is a sarcastic and embarrassing revelation.
summary: After a brain-control device is taken off Wally, his coworkers hint that his lost days included a short-lived romance with a police officer.

title: Therapist Prescribes Personality-Erasing Cocktail

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We hired an immersive VR employee and it's freaking me out.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can only see him when I wear my VR goggles. I feel as if he's always watching me.

transcript.speaker: Therapist
transcript.text: Sounds like you're crazy. I can fix that with a prescription cocktail that will turn you into an entirely new person.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Run.

situation: Dilbert lies on a therapist's couch and explains that the company hired a virtual reality employee who is visible only through VR goggles and seems to be watching him constantly. The therapist declares him crazy and offers a drug cocktail that would turn him into an entirely different person. Dilbert's one-word reply is to flee.
punchline: The therapist's cure for his anxiety is to wipe out his whole personality with drugs, which is so alarming that Dilbert's only sensible response is to run away.
summary: A patient seeking help for a creepy virtual coworker is offered a treatment that would replace his entire identity, and he bolts.

title: Virtual Reality Cubicle Simulator Backlash

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: As you requested, I wrote a VR program that makes users feel as if they are in cubicles.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I put only your name on the credits because I expect an angry mob to kill whoever created it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I also wrote a VR jail program in case you want to be in protective custody.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I might need that.

setting: Office, with a VR demo on a screen
situation: Dilbert tells the Boss he has built the virtual reality program the Boss requested, one that makes users feel like they are working in cubicles. A screen shows a headset-wearing user imagining a cubicle. Dilbert says only the Boss's name is on the credits because he expects an angry mob to go after the creator, and offers a VR jail program for protective custody.
punchline: Dilbert deliberately pins the blame for an awful product on the Boss, then offers him a VR jail to hide in from the mob he expects to come after him.
summary: After building a virtual cubicle experience for his manager, an engineer credits only the manager and offers a simulated jail cell as a refuge from the coming outrage.

title: Robot That Only Drinks Coffee

transcript.speaker: Off-panel voice
transcript.text: Do you worry that a robot will someday take your job?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Nah. No one will build a robot that does nothing but drink coffee.

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: It does nothing but drink coffee. It can replace 20% of your workforce.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I like it.

situation: Dilbert asks Wally whether he worries about a robot taking his job, and Wally confidently says nobody would build a robot that only drinks coffee. A consultant then appears with a coffee-holding robot and pitches it to the Boss as a replacement for 20% of the workforce, and the Boss approves.
punchline: Wally's job consists of little more than drinking coffee, so a coffee-drinking robot really can replace him, and the Boss, who sees no difference, happily buys it.
summary: A man who thinks his do-nothing routine makes him unreplaceable is promptly proven wrong when a consultant unveils a robot that does exactly that.

title: Robot Mocks Dilbert, Head Explodes

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Dilbert claims he programmed my head to explode if I ever mock him again.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Hahaha!!! That idiot doesn't understand that I have free will and I choose to not explode.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Why didn't you just program him to not mock you?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It got personal.

situation: A robot sits at a conference table with Wally and Dilbert and tells them Dilbert claims to have programmed its head to explode if it mocks him again. The robot laughs and boasts that its free will lets it choose not to explode, then its head promptly blows up. Wally asks why Dilbert didn't just program it not to mock him, and Dilbert admits it got personal.
punchline: Dilbert's petty revenge on a mocking robot worked exactly as programmed, proving the robot's claim of free will was wrong, and he admits he chose the explosion for spite rather than practicality.
summary: A smug robot brags that free will lets it ignore a self-destruct command, only for its head to blow up on cue.

title: Fax Machine Safety Vacation Denial

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: I can't approve your vacation days because you haven't completed the mandatory class on fax machine safety.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is that an actual company policy?

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: I don't know, but it sounds like one.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe we should check.

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: Wow. Is there anything you don't complain about?

situation: The boss refuses to approve Dilbert's vacation days, claiming he hasn't finished a mandatory fax machine safety class. When Dilbert asks if that is a real policy, the boss admits he doesn't know. Dilbert suggests checking, and the boss accuses him of complaining about everything.
punchline: The boss invents a policy on the spot to deny vacation, then deflects Dilbert's entirely reasonable request to verify it by painting him as a chronic complainer.
summary: A manager blocks time off with a made-up rule and, when challenged to verify it, turns the blame onto the employee for being difficult.

title: Technical Writer Complains About Page Cuts

transcript.speaker: Technical Writer
transcript.text: My boss, who knows nothing about technical writing, told me to cut my 700-page product warning down to 500 pages.

transcript.speaker: Technical Writer
transcript.text: He doesn't appreciate my art.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sounds like both of you are idiots.

transcript.speaker: Technical Writer
transcript.text: This will go smoother if you stop talking.

situation: A technical writer holding a coffee complains to Dilbert that her boss, who knows nothing about her field, ordered her to trim a 700-page product warning to 500 pages. She says he doesn't appreciate her art. Dilbert bluntly says both of them sound like idiots, and she tells him the conversation will go better if he stops talking.
punchline: A 700-page product warning is absurd, so Dilbert rightly calls out the writer as well as her boss, but she treats the bloated document as art and just wants sympathy.
summary: A writer vents about being told to shorten her enormous safety manual, only to be rebuffed when her listener points out that the manual itself is ridiculous.

title: Forecasts Are Guessing Plus Math

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your financial forecast turned out to be wrong.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is that a surprise, given that forecasts are mostly just guessing plus math?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The math is supposed to fix the guessing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think we've isolated the problem to you.

situation: The Boss confronts Dilbert because his financial forecast turned out to be wrong. Dilbert replies that forecasts are really just guesses combined with math. When the Boss insists the math is meant to correct the guessing, Dilbert suggests the real source of the error is the Boss himself.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically implies that the Boss is the flawed element in the forecasting process, since the math and the guessing were fine until he got involved.
summary: A manager blames an employee for a failed prediction, and the employee turns the blame back on him with a dry diagnostic quip.

title: Randy's Brain Chip Update Dilemma

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Randy is our first employee to have a computer chip embedded in his brain.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Randy, please explain to these obsolete employees how awesome you are now.

transcript.speaker: Randy
transcript.text: Wait... I'm updating my software.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Should we kill him while he's vulnerable?

situation: A manager proudly introduces Randy, the first employee with a computer chip implanted in his brain, and asks him to explain to his coworkers how awesome he is now. Randy pauses, saying he is updating his software. A coworker, apparently Alice, wonders aloud whether they should kill him while he is vulnerable.
punchline: The coworkers, feeling made obsolete by the enhanced employee, see his software update downtime as a chance to eliminate their new cyborg competitor.
summary: A brain-chipped colleague freezes mid-boast for a software update, tempting his threatened coworkers to take him out.

title: Too Polite to Interrupt Presentation

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And that's my presentation. What do you think?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I didn't understand a word of it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You could have mentioned that an hour ago.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Didn't want to be rude.

situation: Dilbert finishes presenting to his boss and asks for feedback. The boss admits he understood none of it. When Dilbert points out he could have said so an hour earlier, the boss explains that he was avoiding being rude.
punchline: The boss sat through an hour-long incomprehensible presentation out of politeness, wasting everyone's time rather than simply admitting he was lost.
summary: A manager lets a whole presentation go by in confused silence because speaking up seemed impolite.

title: Erik Overheard the Speakerphone Meeting

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Erik used to work for the CIA.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You missed the meeting.

transcript.speaker: Erik
transcript.text: I listened to the whole thing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I didn't know the speakerphone was on.

transcript.speaker: Erik
transcript.text: Let's change the subject now.

situation: A caption notes that Erik used to work for the CIA. Dilbert tells Erik he missed the meeting, and Erik calmly says he listened to the whole thing. Dilbert realizes he never knew the speakerphone was on, and Erik abruptly wants to change the subject.
punchline: Erik's CIA background implies he secretly eavesdropped on the meeting, and his quick change of subject shows he knows he gave himself away.
summary: A coworker with a spy past reveals, a bit too casually, that he covertly monitored a meeting he supposedly skipped.

title: Dilbert's Career-Ending Presentation Advice

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Do you have any advice for my presentation to the CEO?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sure. If you make one small mistake, your career will be finished.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You just made me nervous and thus doubled my risk of failure.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm not the one who brought it up.

situation: A nervous coworker asks Dilbert, who is absorbed in his phone, for advice on an upcoming presentation to the CEO. Dilbert warns him that a single small mistake will end his career. The coworker complains that this made him more nervous, and Dilbert deflects responsibility by pointing out the coworker asked for advice.
punchline: Dilbert gives deliberately unhelpful, anxiety-inducing advice and then dodges blame by noting the coworker was the one who raised the topic.
summary: A worried colleague seeks tips for a high-stakes talk and gets a discouraging warning that leaves him more rattled, with the adviser refusing any blame.

title: Self-Funded Employee of the Month

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm naming you Employee of the Month. Your prize is $20 cash and a pat on the head.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Give yourself $20 and submit an employee reimbursement request.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can I pat myself on the head, too?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I was hoping you would offer.

situation: The Boss announces that Dilbert is Employee of the Month, with a prize of $20 cash and a pat on the head. He then tells Dilbert to pay himself the $20 out of pocket and file an expense reimbursement request. Dilbert sarcastically asks if he can also pat himself on the head, and the Boss says he was hoping Dilbert would offer.
punchline: The company's employee reward is so cheap that the boss makes the winner fund and administer his own prize, and even expects him to supply the pat on the head.
summary: A manager hands out a recognition award but shifts both the cost and the effort of delivering it onto the recipient.

title: Stealth Clothing Makes Clothes Invisible

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want you to present your stealth clothing prototype to our board.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you sure?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Of course I'm sure.

transcript.speaker: Board member
transcript.text: I thought we were trying to make the person invisible.

transcript.speaker: Board member
transcript.text: Then why is it called stealth "clothing"?

situation: The boss tells an engineer to present a stealth clothing prototype to the board, and when the engineer double-checks, the boss insists. In the final panel, a board member assumes the goal was to make the wearer invisible, and another board member points out that the product name suggests otherwise.
punchline: The prototype makes the clothing itself invisible, not the person, so the product would leave the wearer effectively naked, a fact the board only realizes after the confusing name is questioned.
summary: A product whose name promises one thing delivers something awkwardly different when the board realizes what the invisible part actually is.

title: Employee Body Cam Catches Boss Lying

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't give the data to marketing yet.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That is the direct opposite of what you told me yesterday.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I am totally sure I never said anything like that yesterday.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You weren't wearing a wire, were you?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's called an employee body cam.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Continued...

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert not to give data to marketing, which contradicts yesterday's instruction. When Dilbert points this out, the Boss confidently denies ever saying it. Dilbert reveals he is recording everything on an employee body cam, which the Boss mistakes for a wire.
punchline: The Boss's habit of denying contradictory instructions is defeated when Dilbert carries a body cam, turning workplace surveillance against management.
summary: A boss flatly denies giving yesterday's opposite orders until his employee reveals he has been filming everything.

title: Maverick Who Never Stands Up

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I like to think of myself as a maverick.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Let the trendy people brag about their standing desks. I haven't stood in a week.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have some bad news about your health risks.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Should I sit down to hear it?

setting: Office, in front of a cubicle or office area
situation: Wally, slouched in his chair, boasts that he is a maverick because he refuses to follow the trendy standing desk fad and hasn't stood up in a week. Dilbert, holding his coffee cup, tells him he has bad news about his health risks. Wally asks if he should sit down to hear it, even though he is already sitting.
punchline: Wally is so committed to sitting all day that he asks whether he should sit down for the news, showing he is already sedentary and unconcerned about the health consequences.
summary: A proudly sedentary coworker brushes off the standing desk craze, then gets a health warning he jokes he should hear from a chair he never leaves.

title: Insulting the Virtual Reality Employee

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That seat is taken by Kevin, our new immersive VR employee.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: But... I'm a physical person.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did you just insult Kevin's corporeal identity?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I don't see how that's a problem.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can't work in this hostile environment.

situation: The Boss, wearing a VR headset, tells an employee that his chair is occupied by Kevin, a new immersive VR employee who is not actually visible. When the employee protests that he is a physical person, the Boss accuses him of insulting Kevin's corporeal identity. The Boss then claims, as Kevin, that he cannot work in such a hostile environment.
punchline: The Boss treats an invisible virtual employee as more deserving of respect than a real physical person, turning the employee's plain statement into a discrimination complaint.
summary: A manager in a headset gives a seat to an imaginary virtual colleague and then scolds a flesh-and-blood worker for offending it.

title: The Red File Excuse

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: I'd love to help you, but I'm busy working on the red file.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Is the red file a real thing or just a thing you say to get out of work?

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: It's all the same on your end.

situation: A coworker asks a bald, bespectacled colleague holding a red folder for help, and he declines, saying he is busy with the red file. She suspects the red file is just a made-up excuse to avoid work. He replies that it makes no difference to her either way.
punchline: Whether the red file is real or a fabricated excuse, the outcome for the person asking is identical: he isn't going to help.
summary: A worker brushes off a request by citing an imaginary-sounding project, then points out his excuse works the same whether it's true or not.

title: Sabotage Competitor With Decaf Coffee

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I recommend buying the company that supplies coffee to our biggest competitor.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We'll replace their regular coffee with decaf and enjoy a solid 20-point I.Q. advantage over them.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do all of your ideas involve coffee?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Only the good ones.

situation: Dilbert advises the Boss to acquire the company that supplies coffee to their biggest competitor. He explains they would swap the regular coffee for decaf to dull the rival's workforce and gain a 20-point I.Q. advantage. The Boss asks if all his ideas involve coffee, and Dilbert replies while sipping his own coffee.
punchline: Dilbert's scheme to win by secretly dumbing down competitors with decaf reveals his own coffee obsession, and he cheerfully admits that coffee is behind all his good ideas.
summary: An engineer pitches a sneaky corporate takeover whose only purpose is to swap a rival's caffeine for decaf, then shrugs off the accusation that he is fixated on coffee.

title: Stealing Budget During Someone's Vacation

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You were on vacation last week so I made decisions about your project without you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oh no... What have you done?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I transferred your budget to another project.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need that money!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oh. Can you wait until the other project manager goes on vacation?

setting: Office hallway or break area, both holding coffee cups
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that, because Dilbert was on vacation, he made decisions about Dilbert's project without him. He reveals he moved Dilbert's budget to another project. When Dilbert protests that he needs the money, the Boss suggests he simply wait until the other project manager takes a vacation so the money can be taken back.
punchline: The Boss's solution to the stolen budget is to let the cycle repeat, treating funding as something grabbed from whoever is out of the office.
summary: A manager casually reallocates his absent employee's funding elsewhere and offers an unhelpful tit-for-tat remedy when the employee objects.

title: Wally's Excuse Spreadsheet

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Wally, I need your input on my project plan.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: One moment, please.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I have to check my spreadsheet to see which excuses I already used with you.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'll need a good one to get past my anger.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Hmmm... maybe something dental.

situation: Alice asks Wally for input on her project plan. Wally consults a spreadsheet he keeps of excuses he has already given her so he won't repeat one. Alice, visibly angry, says he'll need a really good excuse, and Wally muses that a dental problem might work.
punchline: Wally is so devoted to avoiding work that he maintains a spreadsheet to track his excuses, and he treats Alice's anger as just another obstacle to be managed with a fresh lie.
summary: A lazy engineer keeps a log of his past alibis so he can dodge a coworker's request without repeating himself.

title: Volunteering to Watch Legacy Rot

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm assigning our best and brightest engineers to the new system integration team.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Anyone who is left over gets to be in charge of watching our legacy system slowly rot.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Who would want that job?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Me!!! Pick me!!!

situation: The Boss tells the team that the best engineers will join the new system integration project, while everyone left over will be stuck monitoring the old legacy system as it decays. Dilbert wonders who would want such a job, and Wally eagerly volunteers.
punchline: Wally is thrilled to be assigned the do-nothing job of watching a system rot, since it suits his lazy, low-effort approach to work.
summary: A manager announces a prestigious new project and a dead-end maintenance duty, and the office slacker jumps at the chance to take the latter.

title: Lazy or Wise? Nap Time

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Can you do that by end of day?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It would be smarter to wait until we have the final specs.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I can't tell if you're lazy or wise.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's all the same thing.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: This is a weird gray area.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm going to take a quick nap to boost my productivity.

situation: Alice asks Wally to finish a task by the end of the day. Wally says it would be smarter to wait until the final specifications arrive, which leaves Alice unable to decide whether he is lazy or wise. Wally says the two are the same thing, then leans back with his feet on the desk to nap.
punchline: Wally justifies his laziness as wisdom and then dresses up his nap as a productivity boost, showing that his avoidance of work is both his excuse and his strategy.
summary: A coworker questions whether her colleague's reluctance to start work is smart or just slacking, and he cheerfully blurs the line before dozing off.

title: Fragile Forecast Declares Total Success

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: According to my highly unreliable forecast, we're on the right track.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But if even one of my seventeen assumptions is off by 1%, we are doomed.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The obvious conclusion is that...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We're nailing it!

setting: Conference room during a financial presentation
situation: Dilbert presents a chart with a dollar sign to two seated managers, including The Boss. He admits his forecast is highly unreliable and that a 1% error in any of seventeen assumptions would doom the company. He then concludes that the company is nailing it.
punchline: Dilbert's own caveats show the forecast is worthless and the company is precariously positioned, yet he draws an absurdly cheerful conclusion, mocking how fragile projections get spun as success.
summary: A presenter admits his financial outlook rests on shaky guesses that could collapse with the smallest error, then cheerfully declares victory anyway.

title: Dogbert Demands Payment for Persuasion Lessons

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can you teach me how to be more persuasive?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What's in it for me?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It will make you feel good to help a friend.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Does it feel as good as denying you?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have no way to know.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Bah!

setting: Office, with Dogbert sitting on a blue trash can
situation: Dilbert asks Dogbert to teach him how to be more persuasive. Dogbert wants to know what he gets out of it, and Dilbert appeals to the good feeling of helping a friend. Dogbert counters that refusing might feel even better, and Dilbert admits he can't judge that.
punchline: Dilbert's attempt to persuade Dogbert with an appeal to friendship fails, which shows he badly needs the persuasion lesson he is asking for.
summary: A man seeking lessons in persuasion fails to persuade his dog to teach him, proving exactly why he needs the help.

title: Swearing on Coworkers' Lives

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I achieved all of my milestones on my secret project this month.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How do I know any of that is true?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I swear on the lives of my co-workers.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm getting a mixed message here.

setting: Office meeting table with coffee cups
situation: Wally tells the Boss he hit every milestone on his secret project this month. The Boss asks how he can verify that, so Wally offers to swear on the lives of his co-workers. The Boss finds the oath unconvincing.
punchline: Swearing on his co-workers' lives is a worthless guarantee because Wally clearly doesn't care about them, so the oath undermines rather than supports his claim, leaving the Boss with a mixed message.
summary: A slacker backs up his unverifiable progress report with a pledge that puts his colleagues' lives on the line, which only makes his boss more doubtful.

title: Three Days Configuring Programming Environment

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did you finish writing the software?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I spent the last three days setting up my programming environment.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So... you've done... nothing?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Nothing you'd understand.

situation: The Boss walks up to Dilbert's desk holding a coffee and asks if the software is finished. Dilbert explains he has spent three days just setting up his programming environment. The Boss summarizes this as having done nothing, and Dilbert replies that it is nothing the Boss would understand.
punchline: Dilbert turns the Boss's accusation of doing nothing into a jab at his ignorance, implying the Boss cannot grasp the real work involved in configuring development tools.
summary: A programmer justifies days of tool setup to a clueless manager by implying the work is beyond the manager's comprehension.

title: Found Thumb Drive Is Free Money

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I found a thumb drive on the sidewalk. It must be my lucky day.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: It's like free money!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can free money infect our network too?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: You worry too much.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If you need me, I'll be selling all of my company stock.

situation: Asok proudly announces he found a thumb drive on the sidewalk and plans to plug it in, treating it like free money. Dilbert points out the drive could infect the company network with malware, but Asok dismisses his worry. Dilbert responds by announcing he'll be selling all his company stock.
punchline: Dilbert is so certain that Asok's reckless use of an unknown thumb drive will cripple the company that he decides to dump his stock before the damage hits.
summary: A coworker's cheerful plan to use a mystery USB stick convinces his colleague that the company is doomed and its shares worthless.

title: Gandhi Comparison Meets Fasting Suggestion

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I hear you have been comparing yourself to Gandhi, the father of my birth country.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That is offensive. It makes me want to punch you.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Have you tried fasting instead? I hear good things about it.

setting: Office break area with a table and coffee cup
situation: Asok, standing, confronts a seated bald coworker about comparing himself to Gandhi, calling him the father of Asok's birth country. The coworker says the comparison is offensive enough to make him want to punch Asok. Asok calmly replies by suggesting he try fasting instead, a Gandhi-style protest tactic.
punchline: Someone who claims to be like Gandhi then threatens violence, so Asok sarcastically points him toward Gandhi's actual nonviolent method of fasting.
summary: A man who likens himself to a famous pacifist reacts to criticism with a threat of violence and is wryly told to try the pacifist's real approach.

title: Seven Hundred Page Warning Label

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You need to edit the product warning from seven hundred pages down to one.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Oh, that's rich. I'm a professional technical writer, and YOU'RE telling ME how to write?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can you cut it down to 500 pages?

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Sure, if you want it to be total rubbish.

situation: The Boss asks Tina, the technical writer, to cut a 700-page product warning down to a single page. She bristles at being told how to write by a non-writer. He then lowers his request to 500 pages, and she says that is only possible if the result is garbage.
punchline: Even after the Boss backs off to a still absurd 500 pages, Tina says the only way to shorten it that much is to make it worthless, which shows how out of touch his expectations are.
summary: A manager demands a drastic cut to an enormous warning document, and the writer scoffs at his request and his revised one.

title: Gamifying Meetings By Criticizing Coworkers

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Meetings used to be frustrating and boring until I gamified that situation.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Now I try to win meetings by criticizing co-workers, offering no ideas of my own, and leaving without any new task.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You call that winning?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Compared to my victims, yes.

setting: Office, holding coffee cups while talking
situation: Wally tells Dilbert that he made meetings bearable by turning them into a game. His rules for winning are to criticize coworkers, contribute no ideas, and avoid being assigned any work. Dilbert questions whether that counts as winning, and Wally says it does when compared to the people he criticized.
punchline: Wally's idea of winning is only relative, since he comes out ahead simply by making everyone else's meeting experience worse than his own.
summary: Wally has turned dull meetings into a contest he wins by tearing down colleagues while doing no work himself.

title: AI Device Mimics Passive-Aggressive Partner

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I made a huge breakthrough in artificial intelligence.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ask the device anything.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What do you want for dinner?

transcript.speaker: Device
transcript.text: I don't care. What do you want?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I was thinking maybe Chinese food.

transcript.speaker: Device
transcript.text: I'm not in the mood for that.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then why did you say you don't care???

transcript.speaker: Device
transcript.text: Now I'm not even hungry.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why? What's wrong?

transcript.speaker: Device
transcript.text: Nothing is wrong.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You nailed it.

situation: Dilbert shows the Boss an AI device he claims is a major breakthrough and tells him to ask it anything. The Boss asks what it wants for dinner, and the device responds exactly like an indecisive, passive-aggressive spouse, rejecting his suggestion and then claiming nothing is wrong. Dilbert compliments the device on how accurately it imitates human behavior.
punchline: The 'breakthrough' AI doesn't act intelligent, it perfectly imitates the frustrating, noncommittal and passive-aggressive way people argue about dinner and feelings in relationships.
summary: A new smart gadget turns out to replicate the most irritating habits of a moody partner, and its inventor considers that a triumph.
keywords: what do you want for dinner

title: Coworker Predicts Dilbert's Unreliable Feedback Trap

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need your feedback on my PowerPoint deck before Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'll do that on Monday night.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! It's a trap!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You are notoriously undependable. The odds of you working on a Monday night are terrible.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If I don't get your input on time, you will make a fool out of me in the meeting.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll stay up all night Monday hoping to get your email.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: But that input will never come. I'll end up doing the presentation on no sleep.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then you will embarrass me during the presentation by pointing out the errors in my slides.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: For a mind reader, you sure have a terrible life.

situation: Dilbert asks a coworker for feedback on his PowerPoint deck. When the coworker agrees to do it Monday night, Dilbert panics and begins predicting every way it will go wrong, from the coworker's unreliability to his own sleepless night and the coworker pointing out errors at the presentation. The coworker, who has barely said anything, ends up simply observing how bad Dilbert's imagined future is.
punchline: Dilbert claims to read minds and foresee the future, but he only predicts miserable outcomes, including ones the coworker never planned, so the coworker sarcastically notes that being a mind reader has given him a terrible life.
summary: A man who asks for help with his slides talks himself into a spiral of imagined disasters and is gently mocked for his gloomy fortune-telling.

title: Wally Takes Credit for Doing Nothing

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'd like to thank each member of the product team for the successful launch.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert wrote the software.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice designed the hardware.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And Wally... um...

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Attended most of the meetings.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's all you did?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I also played devil's advocate.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You didn't say a word during our meetings for seven months.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That's because you were doing everything right.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you really do nothing for seven months?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: This is one of those "less is more" situations.

setting: Conference room during a product team meeting
situation: The Boss thanks the product team after a successful launch, crediting Dilbert with the software and Alice with the hardware, but struggles to say what Wally contributed. Wally claims he attended meetings and played devil's advocate, then admits he said nothing for seven months, spinning his silence as proof the project was going well.
punchline: Wally turns his complete lack of contribution into a virtue by claiming his silence meant everything was being done right, and he calls doing nothing a "less is more" strategy.
summary: After a project succeeds, the slacker colleague presents seven months of saying nothing as a valuable contribution.

title: Broken Phone Causes Waiting Anxiety

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm having a lot of anxiety because my mobile phone is broken.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: What happens if I need to stand in line for something? What would I do while I waited?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You need an invisible friend.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I have one, but she's always on her phone.

characters: Coworker with large black bob hair
situation: A coworker with a big black bob haircut stands beside Dilbert's desk, anxious because her mobile phone is broken and she fears having nothing to do while waiting in line. Dilbert, absorbed in his own phone, suggests she get an invisible friend. She replies that she already has one, but the friend is always on her phone.
punchline: Even her imaginary friend is addicted to a smartphone, showing how thoroughly phone dependence has taken over everyone, real or imagined.
summary: A phoneless coworker frets about idle moments, and even her imaginary companion turns out to be glued to a screen.

title: The Boss Cold Reads Dilbert

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm a good judge of people.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Really? What am I thinking right now?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hmmm...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're wondering how you could be more like me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You admire my leadership, and you write about me in glowing terms in your diary.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What diary?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Shhh! I'm still reading you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You have no patience and you don't like to be judged.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, that's enough.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Nailed it!

setting: Conference room table in the office
situation: The Boss claims to be a good judge of people, so Dilbert challenges him to guess what he is thinking. The Boss makes flattering, self-serving guesses about Dilbert admiring him and keeping a diary, and Dilbert denies it. The Boss insists he is still reading him and finally guesses Dilbert is impatient and dislikes being judged, just as Dilbert gets annoyed.
punchline: The Boss's wildly wrong, ego-driven guesses are all misses until Dilbert's irritation at being judged makes his final guess look correct, so he claims he nailed it.
summary: A boss boasts of his people-reading skills, then produces flattering nonsense about his employee until the man's annoyance accidentally confirms one guess.

title: Algorithm Puts Me Beside Boss

transcript.speaker: Facilities Employee
transcript.text: After the office redesign, you will be in the cubicle nearest our Pointy-Haired Boss.

transcript.speaker: Seated Employee
transcript.text: How did you decide on that?

transcript.speaker: Facilities Employee
transcript.text: I used an algorithm.

transcript.speaker: Seated Employee
transcript.text: Is the algorithm that you hate me?

transcript.speaker: Facilities Employee
transcript.text: And you have never studied martial arts.

setting: Office, during a conversation about a cubicle redesign
situation: An employee holding a tablet tells a seated coworker that after the office redesign he will sit in the cubicle closest to the boss. When asked how the choice was made, he says he used an algorithm. The seated coworker suspects the algorithm is simply that the planner hates him, and the planner adds that the coworker has never studied martial arts.
punchline: The 'algorithm' is really a personal grudge, and the planner picked the coworker because he is unlikely to physically retaliate for being stuck next to the boss.
summary: A space planner justifies a miserable seat assignment with a vague algorithm that turns out to be personal dislike plus the assurance that the victim can't fight back.

title: Plan That Looks Good, Won't Work

transcript.speaker: Alice's manager
transcript.text: I don't like the optics of your plan.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's the only plan that can work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Should I change it to something that looks good but won't work?

transcript.speaker: Alice's manager
transcript.text: Excellent idea. You might have more management potential than I thought.

situation: A manager at her desk objects to the optics of Dilbert's plan. Dilbert says it is the only plan that can work, then sarcastically asks whether he should change it to something that looks good but won't work. The manager takes him seriously and praises the idea.
punchline: Dilbert's sarcastic suggestion is taken as sincere advice, showing that management rewards appearances over workable results.
summary: A sarcastic offer to swap a workable plan for an attractive but doomed one earns Dilbert a compliment on his leadership potential.

title: Dogbert's Research Tells You Yes

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm the CEO of Dogbert's Unreliable Research Company.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My services cost less than regular research because all I do is tell you whatever you want to hear.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is that defensible?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm sensing you want a yes on that.

setting: Dogbert's office, with an exterior shot of an office building
situation: Dogbert introduces himself as CEO of a research company and explains that his cheap prices come from simply telling clients what they want to hear. The Boss, a prospective client, asks whether that business model is defensible. Dogbert responds by guessing that the Boss wants a yes.

title: Overpaying Because Negotiation Class Denied

situation: The Boss holds a printout and asks Dilbert why the company is paying so much for software. Dilbert explains that it is because the Boss refused to let him take a negotiating class. The Boss suspects Dilbert is using the overpayment as leverage to get the class approved.

summary: An employee's weak deal-making is blamed on being denied training, and he mockingly insists it is incompetence rather than a ploy.

title: Rumor Confirmed By Rumor Chain

situation: A coworker in a blue shirt tells the Boss that Dilbert's project is in chaos. The Boss accepts it as fact because three other people have told him the same thing. Walking away, the coworker thinks that this is exactly why he told three other people, revealing he is the source of the circular rumor.
punchline: The rumor seems credible only because it has spread, and the coworker is the one who started it, so the supposed independent confirmation is just the same gossip bouncing back in a loop.
summary: A project is declared a disaster on the strength of rumors that all trace back to the same few gossipers repeating each other.

title: Boss Denies Cyborg Replacement Plan

situation: Dilbert confronts his boss about a rumor that regular employees will be swapped out for brain-chipped cyborgs. The boss responds with a carefully reworded denial that quietly changes 'normal' to 'defective' and 'cyborgs' to 'enhanced humanoids'. When Dilbert admits he can't tell whether the boss is lying, the boss says that uncertainty is exactly why Dilbert is still useful.
punchline: The boss's denial is a non-denial that confirms the plan, and he justifies keeping Dilbert only because Dilbert is too gullible or dim to detect the deception, which a cyborg presumably could.
summary: A manager issues a slippery denial of a plan to swap staff for enhanced machines, then reveals that an employee's inability to spot lies is his only job security.

summary: An inventor explains that his brain-computer gadget reverses the usual idea, because he thinks letting people drive the machine is hopeless.

situation: Dilbert, who is the one who wants his preferred strategy approved, complains to a finance employee that the financial projection does not support it. summary: A man hoping to justify his favorite plan pressures a finance guy to massage the numbers, and gets a smug reply that morality is merely a matter of assumptions.

summary: A manager's open-ended demand for exhaustive safety warnings leads a technical writer to invent a ridiculous airborne porcupine scenario.
