situation: Dilbert sits on a rock outdoors and declares that he is a lover, not a fighter. The small white creature beside him asks when he last did either one. Dilbert asks if he is trying to start a fight, and the creature replies that fighting is the better option of the two.
punchline: Ratbert implies Dilbert is so lacking in romantic success that picking a fight would be a more realistic activity than finding love.
summary: A boastful claim about being a romantic rather than a brawler is deflated by a friend who points out he hasn't done either lately.

title: Phone Takes Over Boss's Brain

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The neural interface is live. His brain is now communicating with his phone.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: He's sending me a brain-text. It says, "Please help me. My phone has taken control of my body."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It worked!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Now we just need to write an app that makes him a better boss.

setting: Office, with the Boss seated wearing a headset device
situation: Dilbert and Alice have hooked the Boss up to a neural interface so his brain can communicate with his phone. The Boss sends Alice a brain-text saying his phone has taken control of his body, which is exactly what they hoped for. They then plan to write an app that turns him into a better boss.
punchline: The experiment to let a phone control the Boss's body is celebrated as a success because the employees want software to override his poor management, treating his helpless plea as proof the plan worked.
summary: Employees wire their manager's brain to his phone so an app can take over and fix his bossing, and his panicked brain-text confirms the plan is working.

title: Pictures Lie, Even on Tinder

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The public doesn't believe I really helped serve food at the homeless shelter.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Tell them pictures don't lie.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Pictures lie all the time. In fact, that's the best way to lie.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Keep that insight to yourself.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I have a full head of hair on Tinder.

setting: Office, with Dogbert seated behind a desk
situation: The Boss complains that the public doesn't believe he really helped serve food at a homeless shelter. Dogbert, acting as his advisor, suggests telling people pictures don't lie, then immediately admits that pictures lie all the time and are the best way to lie. The Boss urges him to keep that quiet because his own Tinder profile photo shows a full head of hair.
punchline: Dogbert's admission that photos are the best way to lie unintentionally exposes the Boss, who is using a misleading photo on Tinder, while also implying his shelter photo may be staged.
summary: A boss seeking to prove his charity work gets advice about the trustworthiness of photos, only to reveal his own dating-profile deception.

title: Dilbert Enters the Jargon Matrix

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Asok entered the Jargon Matrix. I'm going in to save him.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: User experience...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Cloud... blockchain... speed of execution... responsive design... peel the onion... move the needle...

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Sustainability.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm in.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: What the...? Where did you come from?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Continued...

setting: Conference table in a meeting room
situation: Asok sits in a meeting, dazed and mumbling buzzwords as if trapped in a 'Jargon Matrix.' Dilbert announces he will go in to save him, then holds his head and rattles off business buzzwords to join Asok's trance. Asok, startled, asks where Dilbert came from as Dilbert declares he's in.
punchline: A parody of The Matrix in which the way to enter a coworker's buzzword-induced trance is to recite corporate jargon, mocking how empty and hypnotic business buzzwords are.
summary: Dilbert mimics a sci-fi rescue mission by chanting corporate buzzwords to join a coworker lost in a trance of meaningless business-speak.

title: Not a Liar, Just an Idiot

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Everyone at work thinks I'm a liar because of a false rumor.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If it makes you feel any better, I know you aren't a liar.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thank you. That does help.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I see you as more of an idiot.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And you're welcome.

setting: Dilbert's living room, with Dogbert on the blue couch
situation: Dilbert comes home and tells Dogbert that his coworkers think he is a liar because of a false rumor. Dogbert offers comfort by saying he knows Dilbert isn't a liar, but then reveals he thinks Dilbert is an idiot instead.
punchline: Dogbert's reassurance is a backhanded compliment: clearing Dilbert of dishonesty only so he can insult his intelligence, then politely accepting thanks.
summary: A man seeks comfort over a damaging rumor, and his dog's kind words turn out to be a disguised insult.

title: Politeness Policy Slows Down Projects

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The company has a new politeness policy.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: It is no longer acceptable to turn and walk away while a co-worker is in the middle of telling you something.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That will add months to my project.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm selling all of my company stock.

situation: The Boss announces a new politeness policy that forbids walking away while a co-worker is still talking to you. Dilbert complains that the rule will add months to his project, and Alice responds by saying she is selling all of her company stock.
punchline: Alice and Dilbert realize that no longer being able to escape tedious conversations will cripple productivity, so Alice treats the policy as a sign the company is doomed and dumps her shares.
summary: A new rule against ending conversations abruptly convinces the team that the company is headed for decline.

title: Boss Rejects Legacy System Updates

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Would you like me to tell you what I accomplished this week with our legacy system?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, because legacy systems are boring and I like to think about new things.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I thought we replaced all of our legacy systems.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Keep your thoughts to yourself.

setting: Conference room table during a team meeting
situation: Wally offers to report on his week's work on the legacy system, but the Boss declines because old systems bore him and he prefers thinking about new things. Dilbert then remarks that he thought all the legacy systems had been replaced, and Wally tells him to keep quiet.
punchline: Wally was never actually working on anything, and the Boss's disinterest in legacy systems lets him get away with it until Dilbert's innocent comment threatens to expose that he made up the work.
summary: A slacking employee offers a report on a system that supposedly no longer exists, and a coworker's honest remark nearly gives him away.

title: Reprogramming a Robot Boyfriend

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I'm changing your programming to make you my perfect boyfriend.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: This feels wrong on many levels.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: How about now?

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Um... Now I love you. That's weird.

setting: A lab or workspace where a woman is connected to a robot by a cable
situation: A woman with big curly hair connects a handheld device to a robot and announces she is reprogramming it to be her perfect boyfriend. The robot objects that this feels wrong, so she tweaks the programming again. The robot then declares that it loves her, while noting that this feels weird.
punchline: The robot's moral objection disappears the moment she edits its code, showing that a programmed 'boyfriend' has no real free will or genuine feelings.
summary: A woman rewrites a robot's code until its objections vanish and it professes love for her.

title: Investigator Pads the Billable Hours

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've investigated Dilbert's email and phone records and I can say with confidence he did not collude with Elbonia.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: But there are many, many other crimes he might have committed, and you should pay me to investigate them.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That wasn't helpful.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Stop making it all about you.

situation: Dogbert, acting as an investigator, reports that Dilbert's email and phone records show no collusion with Elbonia. He then suggests there are countless other crimes Dilbert might have committed and urges the Boss to pay him to investigate those too. Dilbert complains the result isn't helpful, and the Boss scolds Dilbert for making it all about himself.
punchline: The investigator clears Dilbert of the original charge but immediately invents an open-ended reason to keep billing, while the oblivious Boss blames the innocent suspect for being self-centered.
summary: A consultant-turned-investigator finds nothing on the accused but pitches an endless probe of hypothetical wrongdoing to keep the money flowing.

title: Management Potential Is An Insult

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Our CEO thinks you have management potential.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What did I do to deserve that kind of insult??!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: He called you a heartless monster.

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: He speaks truth to power. I like it.

setting: Office cubicle and the CEO's office
situation: A coworker tells Dilbert that the CEO thinks he has management potential. Dilbert recoils in horror, taking it as an insult. The coworker adds that the CEO called him a heartless monster, and the CEO, listening in, says he likes that Dilbert speaks truth to power.
punchline: Dilbert regards being seen as management material as an insult, and the CEO confirms that management values heartlessness and being told off, treating Dilbert's contempt as a sign he would fit right in.
summary: Dilbert is appalled to hear that executives see him as promotable, and the CEO's reasoning only proves his point.

title: Marketing: Misleading, Not Lying

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our product has fewer features and a higher price compared to our competitors.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We'll fix that with a little thing I call "marketing."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Lying is unethical.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's why we only mislead.

situation: Dilbert tells his boss that their product is inferior and more expensive than the competition. The boss proposes fixing this with marketing, and when Dilbert objects that lying is unethical, the boss clarifies that the company only misleads customers rather than lying.
punchline: The boss dodges the ethical objection with a hair-splitting distinction, treating deliberate deception as acceptable as long as it isn't technically a lie.
summary: A boss plans to paper over a weak, overpriced product with advertising and justifies the deception by redefining it as something other than lying.

title: Getting Away With Pretending Work

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: If you need me, I'll be at my desk pretending to work.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: How long do you think you can get away with that?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I wondered the same thing for the first fifteen years or so.

situation: Wally, holding a coffee mug, tells Alice that he will be at his desk pretending to work. Alice asks how long he thinks he can get away with that. Wally replies that he wondered the same thing for his first fifteen years or so, revealing he has been slacking for a very long time.
punchline: Wally has been faking work for so long, and so successfully, that the question of getting caught stopped mattering after fifteen years.
summary: A habitual slacker casually admits he has coasted through his entire career without anyone noticing.

title: Bumped Flight Algorithm Picks Weakling

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why did your algorithm pick ME to be bumped from the full flight?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it because I had the lowest-cost ticket?

transcript.speaker: Airline Agent
transcript.text: It was that plus your lack of upper body strength.

setting: Airline check-in or gate counter at an airport
situation: Dilbert confronts a ticket agent after being chosen to be bumped from an overbooked flight. He guesses it was because he bought the cheapest ticket. The agent confirms that and adds that the airline's algorithm also factored in that he is physically weak.
punchline: The airline's bumping algorithm selects passengers who can't physically resist being removed, a jab at the violent forced removal of a passenger from an overbooked flight.
summary: A passenger learns that being bumped from an overbooked flight came down to paying the least and being too weak to put up a fight.

title: Avoiding Email to Live in Moment

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Did you get the file I sent by email?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: If I open email, I'll see thirty urgent messages that will ruin my entire day.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Can you open it tomorrow?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You should try to live in the moment.

situation: Alice asks Wally whether he received a file she emailed him. Wally admits he hasn't opened his email because doing so would reveal thirty urgent messages that would ruin his day. When Alice asks if he can open it tomorrow, he sips his coffee and tells her she should try to live in the moment.
punchline: Wally dresses up his habitual avoidance of work email as mindfulness, turning his laziness into advice that Alice should relax and live in the moment.
summary: A lazy employee justifies never checking his inbox by claiming that ignoring work messages is a form of present-moment wellness.

title: Secret Project Too Secret to Name

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What did you accomplish this month?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I made a lot of progress on the secret red file project that you gave me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Remind me what project that is.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: You made me promise I wouldn't tell you.

setting: Office meeting room at a table
situation: The Boss asks an employee what he accomplished this month. The employee claims great progress on a secret red file project the Boss supposedly assigned, holding up a red folder. When the Boss can't remember the project, the employee says he was sworn to secrecy and can't tell him.
punchline: The employee dodges accountability by inventing a project so secret that the boss himself is forbidden from knowing about it, and the clueless boss can't challenge the claim.
summary: A worker fends off a performance check by citing a confidential assignment that his manager supposedly forbade him from ever revealing.

title: Squatting in the Conference Room

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have this conference room booked for a meeting.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: This is my private office now. I took it over.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You can't just take over a conference room.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I already did. It was easy.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Now all I need to do is act as if it would be totally unreasonable to ask me to leave.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You need to leave. I have this room reserved.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That's totally unreasonable! I'm all settled in and I'm working on a company-critical deadline!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I guess I could cancel my meeting.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Perfect. Now get out of my office.

setting: A conference room in the office
situation: Dilbert arrives for a meeting he booked and finds a coworker has taken over the conference room as her private office. She openly explains her plan: simply act outraged at any request to leave. When Dilbert asks her to go, she plays the indignant card exactly as described and Dilbert backs down.
punchline: The coworker announces her bullying tactic in advance, then uses it, and it works anyway, showing that brazen entitlement beats legitimate reservations.
summary: A woman who has claimed a booked meeting room as her own cheerfully reveals her strategy of feigned outrage, and it still wins the argument.

title: Threatening Wally Backfires Spectacularly

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Wally, did you finish the data scrub?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: No. A defect in my brain made me too lazy.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Perhaps some sort of threat would get you going.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's worth a try.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Do your work or else I'll tell everyone you're useless!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That would save me a lot of time.

situation: Alice asks Wally whether he finished a data scrub, and he admits he didn't, blaming a brain defect that makes him lazy. Alice suggests a threat might motivate him, and Wally agrees to let her try. She threatens to tell everyone he's useless, and he happily points out that this would reduce his workload.
punchline: Wally's reputation for uselessness is already so thorough that exposing it would only relieve him of future work, so the threat is actually a reward.
summary: A frustrated coworker's attempt to scare a slacker into working only hands him a way to dodge even more tasks.

title: Team Abandons Drowning Coworker, Covers Up

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: As you know, our team-building event did not go smoothly.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In my defense, I had no way of knowing a Class 6 whitewater adventure would be so bumpy.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It took me by surprise when Ted fell in.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But I'm proud that we came together as a team and agreed to not look for him.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It would have ruined our timing for lunch.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Anyway, I'm sure Ted swam to safety.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ted doesn't know how to swim.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: All in favor of pretending Ted didn't attend the event?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: They didn't have life vests?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're thinking of the deluxe package.

setting: Conference room, with a brief shot of an office building exterior
situation: The Boss addresses the team after a disastrous team-building whitewater rafting trip on which Ted fell in and drowned. He casually admits the team chose not to search for Ted so they wouldn't miss lunch. When Dilbert points out Ted can't swim, the Boss calls a vote to pretend Ted never attended, and a final panel has a character asking whether there were life vests.
punchline: The Boss shows no remorse for abandoning a drowning employee, and instead of facing the consequences he proposes covering it up, while the life vest question is brushed off as a cost-cutting issue (the deluxe package).
summary: After a deadly rafting retreat, a callous manager shrugs off leaving a coworker to drown and proposes the group simply pretend he was never there.

title: Alice Tries Reprogramming Opinionated Robot

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Dilbert's problem is that he's a huge narcissist.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: You are not qualified to make that diagnosis and you cannot detect his inner thoughts.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Open your access panel so I can fix your stupid opinion.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Are you saying I don't have free will?

situation: Alice offhandedly diagnoses Dilbert as a narcissist, and the robot objects that she is unqualified and cannot know his inner thoughts. Alice responds by demanding the robot open its access panel so she can fix its opinion. The robot asks whether she is denying that it has free will.
punchline: Alice reacts to a disagreement by proposing to reprogram the machine rather than debate it, which proves the robot's point that she is treating its opinion as a defect, not a choice.
summary: A woman who casually labels a coworker is corrected by a robot, and she answers by threatening to rewrite its programming.

title: Financial Projection Is Just Guessing

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Here's the financial projection you asked me to do. It's basically just guessing plus math.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Obviously, it's useless for making decisions because I can get any result I want by tweaking the assumptions.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't say any of that stuff when you present it to the board tomorrow.

situation: Dilbert hands the Boss a financial projection he was asked to prepare and candidly admits it is just guesswork dressed up with math. He explains that any desired result can be produced by adjusting the assumptions. The Boss, rather than being concerned, tells him not to share this honest assessment with the board.
punchline: The Boss doesn't care that the projection is meaningless; he only wants it presented to the board with a false air of credibility.
summary: An engineer confesses his forecast is worthless fiction, and his manager only worries that the truth might slip out in front of the directors.

title: Aggressive Negotiation Gets Dilbert Results

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Negotiate with your vendor and get the price down.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't know how to negotiate. I'm an engineer.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's simple. All you need to do is make an aggressive first demand and settle for less.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How aggressive are we talking about here?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The more aggressive the better.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That doesn't sound right.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Trust me. More is better.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My opening demand is that you name me as beneficiary on your life insurance policy, mow my lawn, and die in traffic on the way home.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You got the price down by 35%.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I really hoped it wouldn't work.

setting: Office hallway and a conference room
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert to negotiate a lower price with a vendor, and Dilbert admits he doesn't know how. The Boss advises an aggressive opening demand, so Dilbert makes an absurd, outrageous demand to the vendor. It works and the price drops 35%, which Dilbert wished it hadn't.
punchline: Dilbert's ridiculous demand (life insurance beneficiary, lawn mowing, dying in traffic) actually succeeds, and he is dismayed because he intended it as an absurd demand that would fail.
summary: Told to be as aggressive as possible in a vendor negotiation, an engineer makes a wildly absurd opening demand and is dismayed when it wins a big discount.

title: HR's Confidential Behind-the-Scenes Progress

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I complained about my boss two months ago. Has Human Resources done anything about it?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Lots of confidential things are happening behind the scenes.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: For example?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: For example, we talked about how much of a whiner you are.

situation: An employee with a big black bowl haircut asks Catbert, the HR director, whether anything has been done about her complaint against her boss from two months ago. Catbert claims confidential activity is underway behind the scenes. When she asks for an example, he reveals that HR has only been discussing what a whiner she is.
punchline: Instead of investigating the complaint, HR has spent the time criticizing the employee who filed it, showing HR protects management rather than workers.
summary: A worker seeking an update on her grievance learns that the only action taken was HR gossiping about her.

title: First Stage of Becoming Wally

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: All I did today was create a bunch of PowerPoint slides that no one will understand.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But I got paid the same as if I had done something useful.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is this the first stage of becoming you?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: If you're lucky.

setting: Conference room table in the office
situation: Dilbert sits next to Wally with coffee and admits he spent the day making PowerPoint slides nobody will understand, yet he was paid just as if he had done something useful. He asks Wally whether this is the first stage of becoming like him. Wally, the notoriously unproductive coworker, replies that it is, if Dilbert is lucky.
punchline: Wally treats doing useless work while collecting a full paycheck as a desirable achievement, implying Dilbert is only at the beginning of the path to Wally's total slacking.
summary: After a day of pointless slide-making that still earned full pay, a coworker wonders if he is turning into the office's champion slacker, who gladly says he hopes so.

title: Robot Surgery: Nobody Cares About Survival

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've been asked to replace your head.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Um... What's the survival rate for this operation?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No one cares.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: I'll need a second opinion.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I don't care either.

situation: Dilbert, holding a small robot head, tells the robot sitting at the meeting table that he has been asked to replace its head. The robot nervously asks about the operation's survival rate, and Dilbert says no one cares. The robot asks for a second opinion, and Wally, sipping coffee, says he doesn't care either.
punchline: The robot's request for a second opinion only gets the same indifference from a second person, showing that nobody at the company cares about the welfare of a machine.
summary: A robot facing a head transplant discovers that every human in the room is equally indifferent to whether it survives.

title: Decaf Mental Vacation Side Effects

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I've never seen you take a vacation.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I take mental vacations.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: All I do is switch to decaf. After a few hours, I can't remember what country I'm in.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Sounds dumb. Is there any downside?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: The locals could be friendlier.

situation: Alice remarks that she has never seen a coworker go on vacation. He explains that he takes mental vacations by switching to decaf coffee, which leaves him so foggy he forgets what country he is in. When Alice asks about the downside, he complains that the locals could be friendlier.
punchline: Because he is confused enough to think he's in a foreign country, he treats his normal coworkers as unfriendly locals.
summary: A coffee-drinking worker claims he vacations by going caffeine-free until he is too groggy to know where he is, and grumbles about the natives.

title: CEO Praises Presentation Never Given

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Our CEO said he liked your presentation.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He made me shut up and sit down before I got to my first slide.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: He's not a big fan of content.

situation: A coworker tells Dilbert that the CEO said he liked his presentation. Dilbert points out that the CEO cut him off and made him sit down before he reached even his first slide. The coworker explains that the CEO simply dislikes content.
punchline: The CEO's praise really means he liked the presentation because it was cut short, since he has no appetite for actual substance.
summary: A boss-level compliment turns out to mean the presenter was silenced before delivering anything, because the executive dislikes substance.

title: Doctor Invests in Dopamine Pirates

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: The MRI shows that your brain has been hijacked by dopamine pirates.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: You are now under the full control of social media corporations, gambling casinos, and big pharma.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you writing me a prescription?

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: No, I'm buying stock in those companies.

setting: Doctor's office with an MRI scanner
situation: A doctor reviews Dilbert's MRI results and tells him his brain has been taken over by dopamine pirates, meaning social media companies, casinos, and big pharma. Dilbert asks if a prescription is coming, but the doctor says he is instead buying stock in those companies.
punchline: Rather than treating the patient's addiction, the doctor decides to profit from the industries that exploit it.
summary: A physician diagnoses a patient as manipulated by addictive industries and then opts to invest in them instead of offering help.

title: Cleared of Collusion, Still Guilty

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: So, I hear you colluded with our Elbonian competitors.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, I was cleared of that.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Then why's it still in my head?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't know how to respond to that.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I take that as proof you're guilty.

situation: A coworker at her desk accuses Dilbert of colluding with the company's Elbonian competitors. Dilbert says he was officially cleared, but she argues that if he was innocent the accusation wouldn't still be on her mind. When Dilbert says he has no answer to that, she treats his silence as proof of guilt.
punchline: The coworker's circular logic makes any accusation unfalsifiable: the lingering suspicion itself counts as evidence, and being unable to rebut it counts as an admission, satirizing political collusion accusations.
summary: A colleague treats a cleared accusation as still valid because she can't stop thinking about it, then reads Dilbert's stunned silence as a confession.

title: Coaching Offer Turned Back On Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you want some coaching?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Heck yes.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: If you find someone who knows my job better than I do, send them my way.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe I could share my wisdom with you.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Can you teach me how to stay calm when some idiot interrupts me?

situation: The Boss offers Alice some coaching, and she eagerly accepts, but only on the condition that he finds someone who knows her job better than she does. When he suggests sharing his own wisdom instead, Alice asks him to teach her how to stay calm when an idiot interrupts her, implying he is that idiot.
punchline: Alice sarcastically accepts the boss's wisdom by asking for tips on staying calm around idiots who interrupt her, a thinly veiled insult aimed at the boss himself.
summary: Alice shrugs off her manager's coaching offer, noting he knows less about her work than she does, then slyly insults him while pretending to ask for his advice.

title: Asok Trapped in the Jargon Matrix

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Come quickly. I think Asok entered the Jargon Matrix.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: At the end of the day, I want some actionable insights that will improve our cross-platform integration.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Can he hear us?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes, but our words are just noise to him now.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Silo.

situation: Alice fetches Dilbert, warning that Asok has fallen into a trance-like state called the Jargon Matrix. They find Asok slumped in his chair, spouting meaningless corporate buzzwords. Dilbert explains that he can hear them but their words are just noise to him, and Asok responds with a single buzzword.
punchline: Asok has become so absorbed in corporate buzzwords that he can no longer communicate in normal language, and his lone utterance of 'silo' shows he is stuck responding only with jargon.
summary: Coworkers watch helplessly as a colleague loses himself in a stream of empty business-speak and can no longer understand plain talk.
keywords: at the end of the day

title: Intern Cannot Get Departmental Buy-In

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You'll need to get buy-in from the other departments.

transcript.speaker: Intern
transcript.text: You have given me an impossible task.

transcript.speaker: Intern
transcript.text: I am only an intern.

transcript.speaker: Intern
transcript.text: No one will agree to anything I ask because I have no power to hurt them.

transcript.speaker: Intern
transcript.text: Most department heads won't even schedule a meeting with me.

transcript.speaker: Intern
transcript.text: And if they do, they will end up canceling it at the last minute and rescheduling.

transcript.speaker: Intern
transcript.text: There is literally no way for me to succeed at this task.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I also need you to ask them to fund your project out of their budgets.

situation: The Boss hands an intern a project and tells him to get buy-in from other departments. The intern explains at length why this is impossible: as a lowly intern he has no power over anyone, and department heads will not meet with him or will cancel meetings. The Boss responds by adding an even harder demand, that the departments fund the project from their own budgets.
punchline: Instead of acknowledging the intern's valid objections, the boss makes the impossible task even harder, showing he ignores or doesn't care about the obstacles.
summary: A powerless intern carefully lays out why winning over other departments can't work, and his boss responds by piling on a still bigger request.

title: Thirty Thousand Feet Leadership Rules Out

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What's the view on this from thirty thousand feet?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: From that distance, everything we do is meaningless.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then how do we know what to do?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I guess we ruled out "leadership."

setting: Conference room table, with a final panel showing an office building exterior
situation: At a meeting, The Boss asks Alice for the view on an issue from thirty thousand feet, a common management buzz phrase. Alice answers literally that from that distance everything is meaningless. The Boss asks how they then decide what to do, and Alice replies sarcastically that leadership must be ruled out.
punchline: Alice sarcastically suggests that if big-picture thinking renders all work meaningless and leaves the team without direction, the missing ingredient must be leadership from management.
summary: A manager's lofty request for a high-level perspective gets a bleak literal answer and a pointed jab at management's lack of direction.

title: Hacked Through Thumb Drive, Password

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Elbonian hackers got into our network. We don't know how.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Maybe it was the thumb drive you found on the sidewalk in front of our entrance.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Or maybe it was because your password is "password."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How do you know my password?

situation: The Boss tells his staff at a meeting that Elbonian hackers broke into the company network and nobody knows how. Alice suggests it might have been the thumb drive he found on the sidewalk outside, and Tina adds that his password is literally "password." The Boss responds only by asking how she knows his password.
punchline: The Boss is so oblivious to basic security that he is baffled the breach happened, and his only reaction to being told his password is "password" is to wonder how anyone knew it.
summary: After a network breach baffles management, coworkers point to a found USB stick and an absurdly weak password, and the culprit still misses the point.

title: Prefers Office Layout With No Work

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you prefer the privacy of a cubicle or the collaborative atmosphere of an open office plan?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Cubicles poison my soul. But in an open office plan, I would not get any work done.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So... which do you prefer?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: The one with no work. I thought that was obvious.

setting: Office hallway, both holding coffee cups
situation: Dilbert asks a coworker whether he prefers a private cubicle or a collaborative open office plan. The coworker complains that cubicles are soul-crushing but admits he would get no work done in an open plan. When Dilbert asks again which he prefers, the coworker says he wants whichever layout involves no work.
punchline: The coworker's real preference has nothing to do with office design; he simply wants to avoid working at all, and thinks that should have been obvious.
summary: A man weighing two office layouts reveals that his true ideal is any arrangement that lets him avoid working.

title: Vacation Spent Catching Up Work

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I hear you have some vacation days coming. Planning anything big?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I plan to catch up on all the work I couldn't get done here because people keep interrupting me.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That's a sad vacation.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then why am I craving it right now?

situation: A coworker holding a coffee cup asks Dilbert, who is typing at his laptop, about his upcoming vacation. Dilbert says he will spend it catching up on the work he can't finish because of constant interruptions. The coworker calls that sad, and Dilbert replies that he still craves it.
punchline: Dilbert's job is so full of interruptions that spending his vacation just working in peace sounds appealing to him.
summary: A man looks forward to his time off only because it will let him finish his work without being bothered.

title: Browser History Says Don't Trust You

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're not planning any changes, trust me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Trust you?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've seen your browser history. I wouldn't trust you to guard a funeral home.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's the easiest job ever. Just drive stakes through the hearts of the dead and they'll stay put.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: To my point.

situation: The Boss assures Dilbert that no changes are planned and asks to be trusted. Dilbert refuses, citing the Boss's browser history and saying he wouldn't trust him to guard a funeral home. The Boss responds by explaining how to keep the dead from rising, which only confirms Dilbert's suspicion.
punchline: The Boss's casual expertise in staking the dead suggests his browser history is full of vampire or necrophilia-type content, proving exactly why he can't be trusted.
summary: A manager's request for trust is shot down when his oddly detailed knowledge of corpse security reveals what he has been browsing online.

title: Simulation Creators Must Be Psychopaths

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Scientists confirmed that our reality is actually a software simulation created by an advanced civilization.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That makes no sense unless the advanced civilization is a bunch of psychopaths who like to see us suffer.

transcript.speaker: Alien 1
transcript.text: One of the idiots in our simulation is insulting us.

transcript.speaker: Alien 2
transcript.text: I'm going to break his phone screen.

setting: Dilbert's desk (panels 1-2) and an alien lab with a glass dome (panel 3)
situation: Dilbert sits at a table with Dogbert, a tablet and a coffee mug, and notes that scientists have confirmed reality is a simulation. He reasons that the creators must be psychopaths who enjoy watching people suffer. In the last panel, two red alien creatures looking at a tiny Dilbert inside a glass dome overhear the insult and decide to break his phone screen.
punchline: Dilbert's guess that the simulation's creators are sadistic is immediately proven right when the aliens overhear him and retaliate by tormenting him.
summary: A man grumbles that the beings running our simulated universe must be cruel, and the beings in question promptly show him he was correct.

title: Body Cam Catches Boss Contradicting Himself

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: According to my employee body cam playback, you contradicted yourself eleven times today.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your stupid body cam is interfering with my ability to manage.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: By "manage," do you mean contradicting yourself and later denying it?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't NOT mean that.

situation: Dilbert, wearing an employee body cam, tells the Boss that the recorded playback shows he contradicted himself eleven times in one day. The Boss complains that the camera interferes with his ability to manage. Dilbert asks whether managing means contradicting yourself and denying it later, and the Boss awkwardly concedes with a double negative.
punchline: The Boss effectively admits that his management style consists of contradicting himself and denying it, and he can only agree using a double negative that avoids a straight admission.
summary: A wearable camera gives an employee hard evidence of his boss's flip-flopping, and the boss reluctantly confirms that this is exactly what his job amounts to.

title: Salary Spreadsheet Leak, Wally Paid Most

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You left a spreadsheet with everyone's salary in the copier.

transcript.speaker: Off-panel voice
transcript.text: Oops.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: By now, every employee has seen it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Should I be worried that it will lower morale?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: No, I wouldn't worry about that.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I would worry about heads exploding when they find out Wally has the highest pay in the department.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: POW!!!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: It's going to be a long week.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Would you mind kicking that angry eyeball into the trash?

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, tells the Boss that a spreadsheet listing everyone's salary was left in the copier and that all employees have seen it. The Boss worries about morale, but Catbert says the real danger is people's heads exploding when they learn that Wally, the laziest employee, is the highest paid. Afterward a head literally explodes, leaving an eyeball on the desk for Catbert to dispose of.
punchline: The salary leak is so unfair, since lazy Wally earns the most, that employees' heads explode in rage, and the Boss casually asks Catbert to clean up the leftover eyeball.
summary: After confidential pay data leaks, an HR cat warns that workers will blow their tops over who earns the most, and one promptly does.

title: Judging Alice's Robot Boyfriend

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hear you're dating our office robot.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Stop judging me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm not judging you.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Good.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm judging the robot.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Ouch.

setting: Office, with an exterior shot of the office building in the middle panel
situation: Dilbert, holding a coffee cup, tells Alice he has heard she is dating the office robot. Alice tells him to stop judging her, and he insists he is not judging her. In the last panel he reveals that he is judging the robot instead.
punchline: Dilbert claims not to judge Alice's choice, but his real criticism is aimed at the robot, which implies the robot is an unworthy partner, and Alice, who is dating it, takes the insult personally.
summary: A coworker swears he isn't criticizing his colleague's love life, then explains that his scorn is reserved for her mechanical partner.

title: Catbert Pretends to Hear Complaints

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I have complaints about my boss. Many, many complaints.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Tell me all about it while I pretend to listen.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Then you will look into my complaints?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Is there any way you would know if I didn't?

situation: Tina, an employee, comes to Catbert in HR to complain about her boss. Catbert openly says he will only pretend to listen. When Tina asks if he will investigate, he points out she would have no way of knowing whether he did or not.
punchline: HR has no accountability, so the employee can never verify whether her complaints are acted on, which means HR may as well do nothing.
summary: An HR cat cheerfully admits he is faking attention to a worker's grievances and notes she could never tell if he did anything about them.

title: Too Long, Didn't Read Email

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Did you read my email?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, it was too long.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Maybe you could read it when you have more time.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I never have time to read email messages that are too long.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe you could rewrite it to be shorter.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I don't have time to rewrite it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And I don't have time to read it.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: If no one reads that email, it will mean I wasted two hours writing it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Plus, you're wasting my time right now. Don't forget to include that in your failure assessment.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I had high hopes for that email.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's a sunk cost. Let it go.

situation: A coworker asks Dilbert whether he read his email, and Dilbert says it was too long to read. Each suggestion the coworker offers, reading it later or rewriting it shorter, is rejected because neither of them has time. When the coworker laments the two hours he spent writing it, Dilbert coldly tells him to treat it as a sunk cost.
punchline: Dilbert dismisses the coworker's two hours of effort as a sunk cost, while blaming him for wasting his time by complaining about it.
summary: A man who spent hours on a lengthy email learns that nobody has the time to read it, and gets coldly told to move on.

title: Robot Boss Threatens Skull Crushing

transcript.speaker: Robot Boss
transcript.text: Thanks to advances in artificial intelligence, I am both a robot and your new boss.

transcript.speaker: Robot Boss
transcript.text: Work hard while I do nothing or I will crush each of your skulls with my mechanical arms.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He's tough, but he's fair.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And no micro-managing. I find it refreshing.

situation: A robot introduces itself to the team as their new boss, powered by artificial intelligence, and threatens to crush their skulls with its mechanical arms if they don't work hard while it does nothing. Afterward, Dilbert and Wally walk down the hall and calmly discuss the robot's management style as if it were a perfectly good boss.
punchline: The employees are so used to bad management that a boss who openly threatens violence still counts as an improvement because he's fair and doesn't micromanage.
summary: A new robot manager promises to do nothing and menaces his staff, yet his employees end up praising him as a refreshing upgrade over human bosses.

title: Open Office Failure, Ignored Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our transition to an open office plan has been a huge failure. Too many distractions.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How can we change back to cubicles and private offices without looking like idiots?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Are you listening to me?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Is someone nursing a baby over there?

situation: The Boss walks up to an employee seated at a desk and complains that the open office plan has failed because of too many distractions. He asks how they can revert to cubicles without looking foolish, but the employee, absorbed in his phone, ignores him. When the Boss asks if he is listening, the employee instead asks whether someone is nursing a baby nearby.
punchline: The employee's distracted, off-topic response demonstrates exactly the problem with open offices, while the Boss only worries about saving face rather than admitting the mistake.
summary: A manager laments his failed open-plan experiment while a distracted worker proves his point by tuning him out.

title: Phone Charger Coffee Warmer Idea

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Nothing is going right today. My phone charger is too hot, and my coffee is too cold.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you just invent a phone charger that keeps your coffee warm?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Did I?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll have a prototype for you tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Continued...

setting: Conference room table at the office
situation: Wally complains that his phone charger is overheating while his coffee has gone cold. Dilbert, an engineer, realizes the two complaints add up to a product idea: a charger that warms coffee. Wally is unsure he actually invented anything, and Dilbert promises a prototype the next day.
punchline: Wally unknowingly stumbles into a product idea by complaining, and Dilbert instantly turns his grumbling into an engineering project, deadpan.
summary: A grumbling coworker's two unrelated gripes accidentally combine into a gadget concept that an engineer eagerly offers to build.

title: Virtual Reality Cubicle Simulator Order

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're going to use our VR technology to take over the cubicle business.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Write a program that makes users feel as if they are working in a fabric-covered box.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe we should think outside the box.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Stop resisting change.

situation: The Boss announces that the company will use its VR technology to enter the cubicle business, then instructs Dilbert to program a simulation that makes users feel they are in a fabric-covered box. Dilbert suggests thinking outside the box, and the Boss dismisses the suggestion as resistance to change.
punchline: The Boss wants to digitally recreate the cubicle experience, and when Dilbert makes the 'outside the box' pun to question the idea, the Boss uses 'resisting change' as a lazy way to shut down any criticism.
summary: A manager orders an engineer to build a virtual reality product that simulates sitting in a cubicle, and brushes off the engineer's pointed pun as mere reluctance to adapt.

title: Only Common Variable: The Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Every one of my employees is underperforming. What should I do?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You should fire yourself because you're the only common variable.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hadn't considered that.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: That's how I know I'm right.

situation: The Boss complains to Catbert that all of his employees are underperforming and asks for advice. Catbert tells him to fire himself, since he is the one factor shared by every underperformer. The Boss admits he never thought of that, and Catbert says that obliviousness proves his point.
punchline: The Boss's failure to even consider that he might be the problem confirms that he is the problem.
summary: A manager blaming his whole team is advised by a cat to look at the one thing they all have in common, and his blank reaction proves the diagnosis.

title: Promoting Ted Because He Can't Code

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I promoted Ted to software architect because he doesn't know how to code.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: At first I thought it was a bad idea. Then I remembered that sometimes monkeys are astronauts.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You know the monkeys don't fly the rocket, right?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And Ted won't be writing code.

situation: The Boss strolls up to Dilbert holding a coffee and announces he promoted Ted to software architect precisely because Ted can't code. He justifies the odd choice by recalling that monkeys have been sent into space as astronauts. Dilbert points out that the monkeys never actually fly the rocket, and that Ted won't be writing code either.
punchline: The Boss's monkey-astronaut analogy accidentally confirms the problem: the monkeys are along for the ride and don't do the real work, so Ted's promotion is equally pointless and misguided.
summary: A manager defends giving a top technical role to a non-programmer by comparing him to space monkeys, a comparison that undermines his own logic.

title: The Idiot Who Doesn't Know

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: As you know, every project in this company has one idiot on the team.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That can't be true.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It is true.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I assign one idiot per team to keep them from bunching together.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: My project team doesn't have any idiots.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There's a good explanation for why you think that.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I don't see what that would be.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: If I had an idiot on my team, I would know it.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Unless. . .

situation: Dilbert tells a meeting that every project team has exactly one idiot, and the Boss confirms he assigns one per team to keep them from clustering. Alice insists her team has none and that she would know if it did. As Dilbert hints at an explanation, Alice slowly begins to realize what he means.
punchline: Alice's confident claim that she would recognize an idiot on her team unravels when she realizes she herself may be the idiot, since an idiot wouldn't know it.
summary: A team member boasts she would spot any fool in her group, only to dawn on her that the fool might be her.

title: Helpful Offer Met With Hostility

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How can I help you achieve your goals and be more successful?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You could stop talking all creepy and weird.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I thought I was being helpful.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Go hate your job like everyone else.

situation: Dilbert approaches a coworker seated at a conference table who is absorbed in a handheld device, and earnestly offers to help him achieve his goals and be more successful. The coworker, without looking up, tells him to stop sounding creepy and weird. When Dilbert says he was only trying to be helpful, the coworker tells him to go hate his job like everyone else.
punchline: The coworker rejects sincere helpfulness and treats workplace misery and disengagement as the expected norm that Dilbert should conform to.
summary: A well-meaning offer of assistance gets shut down by a disengaged colleague who insists everyone is supposed to be miserable at work.

title: The Salamander Software Estimate

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When will the next version of the software be done?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's like asking me to estimate how long it takes a salamander to evolve into a horse.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So... what should I tell our CEO?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Try the salamander analogy. It worked on you.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert when the next software version will be finished. Dilbert replies that estimating this is like predicting how long a salamander needs to evolve into a horse. The Boss, apparently satisfied, asks what he should tell the CEO, and Dilbert points out the analogy worked on him.
punchline: The Boss was so easily fobbed off by a nonsensical analogy that Dilbert suggests he simply reuse it on the CEO, implying the Boss didn't realize he'd been brushed off.
summary: An absurd evolutionary comparison gets a manager to drop a schedule question and then pass the same dodge up the chain.

title: Blackmailing the Boss Over Dementia

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: What is this "red file" people keep telling me you're working on?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Do you remember giving me this secret project, or should I spread the rumor that you have dementia?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oh, now I sort of remember.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Good. Now run along while I work on the red file.

situation: An employee who is seated at his desk with a coffee mug is asked by the Boss about a mysterious 'red file' that people keep mentioning. The employee holds up a red folder and threatens to spread a rumor that the Boss has dementia unless the Boss claims to remember assigning him the secret project. The Boss goes along with it, and the employee dismisses him so he can keep working on the red file.
punchline: The employee invents a secret project to look busy, and he uses the threat of a dementia rumor to trick the Boss into confirming he assigned it.
summary: A worker bluffs his way into having a made-up secret assignment by implying his boss's memory is failing.

title: Boss Takes Credit From Asok

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I did a great job on this design.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Whoa! Whoa!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No one likes a braggart. Keep your boasting to yourself.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Didn't Asok help you with this design?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok? Never heard of him.

situation: A coworker holding a tablet proudly says he did a great job on a design, and the boss stops him, scolding him for bragging. When Asok, sitting at his desk, asks whether he helped with the design, the boss claims he has never heard of Asok.
punchline: The boss hypocritically forbids bragging while erasing Asok's contribution, showing that he ignores subordinates and happily takes credit for their work.
summary: A manager lectures a staffer about modesty, then pretends a junior employee who contributed to the work doesn't exist.

title: Everyone Says You Moved It

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Everyone says you moved the server rack and lied about it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Everyone is wrong. It didn't happen.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Oh, so it's your word against literally "everyone"? Is that what you are saying?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'll go with the majority on this, thank you very much.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I want to like people, but they don't make it easy.

situation: A coworker confronts Dilbert, claiming that everyone says he moved the server rack and lied about it. Dilbert denies it, and the coworker mocks his defense as his word against everyone. The coworker then decides to side with the majority, leaving Dilbert frustrated.
punchline: Dilbert's denial is dismissed because the accusers outnumber him, so he laments that people make it hard to like them.
summary: Accused by rumor of a server rack mishap, Dilbert finds that his honest denial loses to sheer popular opinion.

title: Why Pay You to Enjoy Yourself?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey, I have a great idea.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe I could work on interesting projects instead of the soul-killing tasks you always assign to me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why would I pay you for enjoying yourself?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I was not prepared for that question.

situation: Dilbert approaches his boss, who is holding a coffee cup, and proposes that he be given interesting projects instead of the soul-killing tasks he normally gets. The boss responds by asking why the company would pay him for enjoying himself. Dilbert is left stumped by the question.
punchline: The boss treats work as something that must be unpleasant to justify a paycheck, a view so absurd that Dilbert has no comeback.
summary: An employee asks for more engaging assignments and is shut down by a manager who thinks pay should only compensate for misery.

title: Pride Is Like Being Crime Victim

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, I'm starting to think you don't take pride in your work.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That would be like taking pride in being the victim of a crime.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: How'd the pep talk go?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He made some good points.

situation: The Boss tries to motivate Wally by suggesting he lacks pride in his work. Wally responds that taking pride in his job would be like taking pride in being a crime victim. Afterward, Catbert asks the Boss how the pep talk went, and the Boss admits Wally made good points.
punchline: The pep talk backfires because Wally's argument that work victimizes employees is so persuasive that the Boss ends up agreeing with him.
summary: A manager's attempt to inspire a lazy employee collapses when the employee's cynical comparison convinces the manager instead.

title: Fired Coworker's Chair Is Icky

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: My chair is broken. I need a new one.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You can take Ted's chair. I fired him this morning.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That feels icky.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's just a chair.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Ted was a creepy underperformer. I don't want his loser energy on me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's your only option unless I fire someone else today.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Okay, give me an hour to do some back-stabbing and rumor-mongering.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll just let that situation work itself out.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Nice chair.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why did my fight-or-flight instinct just kick in?

situation: Alice's chair is broken, and the Boss offers her the chair of Ted, whom he just fired. Alice refuses because of Ted's supposed bad energy, and the Boss says her only other option is for him to fire someone else today. Alice cheerfully offers to start back-stabbing and spreading rumors to get a colleague fired, the Boss passively lets it happen, and she then approaches Dilbert with a creepy smile.
punchline: Alice would rather sabotage a coworker's career to get a better chair than sit in a fired colleague's seat, and the Boss happily lets this destructive office politics unfold.
summary: Needing a replacement seat, an employee decides to engineer a coworker's dismissal rather than accept a fired colleague's cast-off furniture.

title: Offended Resource Sounds Like Leader

situation: An employee storms into the Boss's office to complain that Dilbert called him a "resource," which he finds offensive. The Boss relays the complaint to the head of human resources by saying Dilbert offended one of the resources. The HR director responds that this makes Dilbert sound like a natural leader.
punchline: Treating employees as interchangeable "resources" is so normal in management that insulting people this way is taken as proof of leadership ability.
summary: A worker's complaint about being dehumanized as a resource ends with management praising the offender's leadership potential.

setting: Office desk during a one-on-one meeting
situation: A coworker has presented an idea to Dilbert, who is holding a sheet of paper. Dilbert says a new politeness policy prevents him from giving his honest opinion, so he changes the subject to a story about a manure fire burning down a pig farm. The coworker's expression turns sour as he gets the message.
punchline: Dilbert complies with the politeness policy on a technicality while still conveying that the idea is garbage, since the manure fire story is an obvious metaphor.
summary: Barred from candid feedback by a new etiquette rule, an engineer sidesteps it by telling a pointed anecdote that makes his low opinion unmistakable.

title: Traffic App Busts Late Excuse

situation: Wally arrives late holding a coffee cup and blames a big freeway accident. The Boss, seated at the table with his phone, says his traffic app shows no such accident. He then asks Wally which kinds of excuses can't be verified with an app.
punchline: Caught in a lie by a traffic app, Wally is invited to pick a better excuse from the category that technology can't fact-check.
summary: A tardy employee's alibi collapses when his manager consults a smartphone and then asks for a more verifiable-proof-resistant fib.

title: Doctor's Note Allows Meeting Naps

situation: Wally, holding his coffee mug, announces to Alice that he has a doctor's note permitting him to sleep during meetings. Alice tells him that this means he must be interesting enough to keep her awake. She says she'll try her best, but Wally has already fallen asleep.
punchline: Alice is mistaken about who has to be interesting: Wally's note licenses him to sleep, and he promptly dozes off, making the meeting about her failing to hold his attention, which is exactly what he wanted.
summary: A man excuses his meeting naps with medical paperwork, and his colleague's attempt to stay engaging is cut short when he nods off at once.

situation: At a meeting table, the Boss announces that employees must stop calling their cubicles by that name and use 'modular workstation' instead, claiming the old word is demeaning. Dilbert then says he feels much better, and the Boss says he hoped the fix would work quickly.
punchline: Management thinks a cosmetic change in vocabulary can solve employee dissatisfaction, and Dilbert's sarcastic 'I feel so much better' shows it changes nothing.
summary: A manager decrees a fancier name for cubicles as if relabeling them could lift his staff's spirits.

transcript.text: There are so many reasons that I don't know where to start!

situation: Dilbert presents his plan and asks for questions. A smug coworker mocks the plan as dumb and claims to have countless reasons for criticizing it. When Dilbert asks him to pick just one, he cites funding, and Dilbert reveals the project is already fully funded.
punchline: The coworker's boasting about endless objections collapses when his single real argument is refuted, leaving him with nothing but his condescending face.
summary: A sneering colleague claims he has too many reasons to trash a proposal, but his one actual objection turns out to be wrong.

situation: Asok stands at a screen showing a diagram and announces he will cover 75 slides in ten minutes. The CEO, seated at the table, immediately cuts him off, tells him to sit down, and says never to speak to him again. Afterward Dilbert asks how the presentation went, and Asok glumly replies that it was 75 slides too long.
punchline: The CEO's hostile reaction shows the presentation was so overlong that zero slides would have been the right amount, which Asok bitterly admits by saying it was 75 slides too long.
summary: A young engineer's absurdly packed slide deck so enrages the CEO that the talk ends before it begins, and he ruefully concedes the deck was excessive.

title: Doomed Project Needs a Blamecatcher

transcript.text: Why do they want me to work on a project that is clearly doomed?

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he is being assigned to a project co-managed by two vice presidents who despise each other. Dilbert points out the project is obviously doomed and asks why he was picked. The Boss explains that the executives called him a 'blamecatcher'.
punchline: Dilbert was chosen not to make the project succeed but to be the scapegoat who absorbs the blame when it inevitably fails.
summary: A worker discovers he has been handed a hopeless assignment so that someone will be available to take the fall.

title: Body Cam Defeats Boss's Deletion Trick

situation: Dilbert tells his boss he has started wearing an employee body cam, then shows him a video of the boss contradicting yesterday's instructions with what he said today. The boss grabs the device and claims to have accidentally deleted the footage. Dilbert calmly says he has seven hundred backups.
punchline: The boss's usual trick of denying and erasing evidence fails because Dilbert has anticipated it and keeps an absurd number of backups.
summary: A worker armed with recorded proof of his manager's flip-flop foils the attempt to wipe it out by having copies everywhere.

title: Robot Head Becomes Home Speaker

transcript.speaker: The Boss

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert to design a home speaker to rival Amazon Alexa and Google Home, and Dilbert promises a prototype in fifteen minutes. He then builds a sentient robot, holding a screwdriver, which asks whether it will be living with a human family. Dilbert coldly replies that only its head will be used.
punchline: Dilbert's quick prototype is a sentient robot, and his deadpan answer reveals that its head alone will be turned into the speaker, a darkly casual disregard for the feelings of his creation.
summary: Asked to create a smart speaker prototype, an engineer quickly builds a thinking robot and then casually tells it that only its head will end up in people's homes.

title: Hiring Engineers Without Souls

transcript.text: This way, I won't feel so bad when I motivate him with emotional abuse.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert, who sits at his desk, that he hired a new engineer with no soul, standing beside him in a blue shirt. He explains this will spare him guilt when motivating the engineer through emotional abuse. Dilbert asks if he's joking, and the Boss admits he never feels bad about it anyway.
punchline: The Boss's supposed guilt-avoidance strategy is unnecessary because he has no conscience about abusing employees in the first place.
summary: A manager brags about hiring a soulless engineer to ease his conscience over mistreating staff, then admits he never had any guilt to begin with.

situation: An employee introduces himself as Barry Dingle and explains that he lurks at the Boss's office door, pouncing with questions whenever the Boss finishes a phone call. The Boss complains that he hates this, and Barry points out it's the result of the Boss's own open-door policy. In the last panel the Boss is on the phone while Barry peeks around the doorway, waiting.
punchline: The Boss's much-touted open-door policy has created the very pest he now can't escape, and Barry is cheerfully waiting to ambush him again.
summary: A manager discovers that his welcoming open-door policy has turned into a lurking employee who corners him after every call.

He says he is attending random meetings hoping to find spare budget money. When the coworker says the meeting is about a mandatory software upgrade, Dilbert immediately calls it a huge waste of money.
punchline: Dilbert is trying to redirect money to his own project, so he instantly disparages the funded software upgrade as wasteful, showing how budget fights are driven by self-interest rather than merit.
summary: An engineer with no funding sneaks into meetings to scavenge budget, then trashes the one project that actually has money.

punchline: The coworker's question about the physical fate of binary digits is so naive that it disproves Dilbert's reassurance that no question is dumb.
summary: A confident assurance that no question is foolish collapses the moment a colleague asks something truly baffling about computers.

summary: When a coworker criticizes his programming for ignoring design standards, Dilbert bluntly turns the criticism around and questions the critic's skill.

punchline: Working on boring legacy systems means getting to go home on time, while the 'exciting' new projects demand such long hours that his house looks abandoned.
summary: A man pities a colleague stuck on outdated software, but her reasonable hours make his overworked, house-abandoning schedule look far worse.

summary: A coworker accuses Dilbert of espionage and then interprets his protest of innocence as confirmation, leaving him trapped in an unwinnable argument.

summary: A manager and the HR cat discover that their lawsuit-happy virtual employee cannot be eliminated because he has copied himself online.

When Dilbert points out the new tweets are sexist, the Boss proudly says that is the point, because it makes people forget the earlier racist tweets.
punchline: The Boss thinks the way to escape a scandal is to create a fresh one, treating each new offensive tweet as a successful distraction from the last.

summary: A manager waves away an employee's denial and settles on whichever explanation preserves his own infallibility.
